•	The employer can save on the costs of supervising the employees against shirking.
(Any ONE of the above with brief explanation, 2 marks)
Disadvantage for the employees:
•	As their incomes fluctuate with the company's revenue, they have to bear risk.		(2 marks)

questions.topic: B2 · Ch210 · Factors of production
questions.text:
Mr Wong runs a trading company. The salaries of the salespersons are a certain percentage of the company's profits. 
(a)	Explain the advantage of this payment method to Mr Wong.	(2 marks)
(b)	What is the disadvantage of paying profits as salaries to the salespersons? Suggest ONE way to solve this problem.	(4 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	•	It can increase the salespersons' incentive to work and their productivity.
	•	It can shift some risks to employees.
	(Any ONE of the above with brief explanation, 2 marks)

(b)	•	The salespersons have to bear a higher risk (unstable income). They receive no salaries if the company makes no profit.	(2 marks)

	•	Another type of wage payment, such as time rate, can be used along with this wage payment method. This can make salespersons' salaries more stable.		(2 marks)

questions.topic: B2 · Ch210 · Factors of production
questions.text:
Dr Chan has employed two nurses to help him at the clinic. They are paid on a time rate.
(a)	Explain why the nurses are paid on a time rate.	(4 marks)
(b)	Is the occupational mobility of nurses higher than that of doctors? Explain.		(3 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	•	The work of nurses is not standardised.
	•	The contribution of nurses is difficult to measure.
	•	The nurses can pay more attention to service quality as they do not have to hurry.
	(Any TWO of the above with explanation, 2 marks × 2 = 4 marks)

(b)	•	Yes, the occupational mobility of nurses is higher.	(1 mark)
	•	Their training is more general / less specialised than that of doctors. 
	•	Their income is lower and hence their cost of changing occupation is lower.
	(Any ONE of the above with explanation, 2 marks × 1 = 2 marks)

questions.topic: B2 · Ch210 · Factors of production
questions.text:
Mr Cheung is a university professor. The university hires two assistants to assist in his research work.
(a)	Explain which method the university should adopt to pay the assistants.	(5 marks)
(b)	Compare the occupational mobility of Mr Cheung and his assistants.	(3 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	•	Time rate	(1 marks)
	•	It is difficult to measure the output of the assistants. Time rate is simple and easy to administer.	(2 marks)
	•	The assistants can pay more attention to product quality as they do not have to hurry. 	(2 marks)

(b)	•	Mr Cheung's occupational mobility is lower.	(1 mark)
	•	Since Mr Cheung's monetary reward is higher, his cost of changing job is higher.	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B2 · Ch210 · Factors of production
questions.text:
Mr Lee runs a store in North Point by himself and sells egg puffs. He bears unlimited liability.
(a)	To what type of ownership does the store belong?	(1 mark)
(b)	To what factor of production does Mr Lee belong? Explain your answer.	(4 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Sole proprietorship	(1 mark)

(b)	He is an entrepreneur as he bears a business risk and makes business
	decisions.	(2 marks)
	He belongs to labour as he provides physical and mental effort when he cooks egg puffs.	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B2 · Ch210 · Factors of production
questions.text:
Mr Chan opened a shark fin retail shop in Tsueng Kwan O last year. He employed only two salespeople who are paid on a time rate. The table below shows the income of both Mr Chan and his employees last year. 

	Period 1 Income ($)	Period 2 Income ($)	Period 3 Income ($)	Period 4 Income ($)	
Mr Chan	30,000	24,000	-3,000	-5,000	
Employee	20,000	20,000	20,000	20,000	

(a)	List TWO factor(s) of production employed by Mr Chan.	(2 marks)
(b)	Refer to the table above. Can you explain why Mr Chan's return fluctuated last year while his employees' return remained constant?	(4 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	•	Labour: the effort provided by the two employees
	•	Capital: the shop in Tseung Kwan O
	•	Capital: products to be sold, e.g. shark fin
	•	Entrepreneurship: the effort provided by the owner, Mr Chan
(Any TWO of the above, 1 mark × 2 = 2 marks) 

(b)	•	The return for labour is usually stipulated in contracts.	(1 mark)
	•	Their factor services have to be paid whether the firm earns a profit or not.		(1 mark)
	•	The return for entrepreneurship is uncertain as the sales of a product are not guaranteed.	(1 mark)
	•	Entrepreneurs have to bear the risk of fluctuating profits and may even suffer losses.	(1 mark)

questions.topic: B2 · Ch210 · Factors of production
questions.text: Miss Fong is a bank manager, who is responsible for decision-making and management. Explain if she is an entrepreneur.	(3 marks)
questions.answerText:
•	No, she is labour.	(1 mark)
•	The main role of an entrepreneur is risk bearing, but she need not bear risk.		(2 marks)

questions.topic: B2 · Ch210 · Factors of production
questions.text: Explain whether an air conditioner in a restaurant is capital.	(4 marks)
questions.answerText:
Capital is a man-made resource used by producers to help production.	(2 marks)
An air conditioner in a restaurant is a man-made resource which helps provide better catering services. Hence, it is capital.	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B2 · Ch210 · Factors of production
questions.text:
Suppose the government agrees to the construction of a new highway connecting Tuen Mun to Kowloon in the near future.
(a)	To what type of factors of production does this new highway belong to? Explain.		(2 marks)
(b)	Explain if there is any change in the 
	(i)	occupational mobility; and 
	(ii)	geographical mobility 
	of workers living in Tuen Mun.	(4 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Capital. It is a man-made resource to help production, e.g., transportation.		(2 marks)

(b)	(i)	No change as the construction of the highway does not affect the willingness and ease of a worker to change from one occupation to another.	(2 marks)
	(ii)	Increases as workers in Tuen Mun can now move from one place to another more easily than before.	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B2 · Ch210 · Factors of production
questions.text:
Kay Tse is a popular singer in Hong Kong.
(a)	To which kind of factors of production does she belong?	(2 marks)
(b)	An economics teacher said, 'When Kay buys more clothes for her shows, her capital increases.' Explain why the teacher is correct.	(4 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Labour	as she provides human effort, both mental and physical, that can be used in production.	(2 marks)

(b)	•	Capital refers to man-made resources used by producers to help production.		(2 marks)
	•	Her clothes are capital for her as they are man-made resources used by Kay in the provision of entertainment services.	(1 mark)
	•	People find her performance more enjoyable if she wears more beautiful clothes at her shows, i.e. her productivity increases.	(1 mark)

questions.topic: B2 · Ch210 · Factors of production
questions.text:
The Shatin to Central link is a railway that will connect Tai Wai to Admiralty. Estimates are that it will be completed by 2020.
(a)	To which type of factor of production does this new railway belong? Explain.		(2 marks)
(b)	Explain if there is any change in the  
	(i)	occupational mobility; and 
	(ii)	geographical mobility 
	of workers living in Shatin.	(4 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Capital. This is a man-made resource to help production, e.g., transportation.		(2 marks)

(b)	(i)	No change as the railway does not affect the willingness and ease of a worker to change from one occupation to another.	(2 marks)
	(ii)	Increases as workers in Shatin can now move from one place to another more easily than before.	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B2 · Ch210 · Factors of production
questions.text:
It has been said that when Leonardo Da Vinci first came to del Verrocchio's studio, he was told to draw eggs all the time.
(a)	To which type of factor of production does the studio belong? Explain.	
		(2 marks)
(b)	If Da Vinci broke two eggs when he was practising and del Verrocchio bought two new eggs later, was there any capital accumulation?	(2 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Capital. This is a man-made resource to help production, e.g., teaching.	(2 marks)

(b)	Since capital formation equals capital depreciation, there was no capital accumulation.	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B2 · Ch210 · Factors of production
questions.text:
(a)	List TWO features of capital.	(2 marks)
(b)	Explain why an increase in investment will raise future consumption at the cost of present consumption.	(4 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	•	Capital is man-made resources, i.e. it has been processed. 
	•	Capital can be used to increase the productivity of other factors or replace other factors.
	•	An increase in capital means present consumption is forgone for more future consumption.
	(Any TWO of the above, 1 mark × 2 = 2 marks)
	
(b)	•	Investment is the production or purchase of capital.	(1 mark)
	•	When scarce resources are allocated to produce capital, fewer resources will be used to produce consumer goods for present consumption.	(2 marks)
	•	An increase in capital can raise productivity and more consumer goods can be produced for consumption in future. Future consumption hence increases.		(1 mark)

questions.topic: B2 · Ch210 · Factors of production
questions.text:
The table below shows the amount of capital formation and capital depreciation of Office A last year.

Item	Capital formation ($)	Capital depreciation ($)	
Printers	6,000	2,700	
Scanners	34,000	30,000	
Projectors	10,000	12,000	

(a) What is capital accumulation?	(2 marks)
(b) Compute the amount of capital accumulation in the period.	(2 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	The difference between capital formation and capital depreciation is the change in capital stock. The net increase in capital stock is called capital accumulation.		(2 marks)

(b) Capital accumulation
	= Capital formation - capital depreciation
	= $(6,000 + 34,000 + 10,000 - 2,700 - 30,000 - 12,000)
	= $5,300 		(2 marks)

questions.topic: B2 · Ch210 · Factors of production
questions.text:
Identify the situations in which 
(a)	gold is land;	(3 marks)
(b)	gold is capital.	(3 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	•	Land refers to natural resources that can be used in production.	(1 mark)
	•	Gold ores in the gold mines are classified as land as they are gifts from nature, not involving human effort.	(2 marks)

(b)	•	Capital includes all man-made resources used by producers to help production.	(1 mark)
	•	Gold which has been extracted from gold mines and then purified for further production (e.g., for ornament and industrial purposes) is classified as capital as it has become a man-made resource used by producers to help production.		(2 marks)

questions.topic: B2 · Ch210 · Factors of production
questions.text:
Louis said, 'Lake water is land.'
Eddie said, 'No, lake water is capital.'
Explain separately in what situation each of the above is correct.	(4 marks)
questions.answerText:
•	Land includes all the natural resources that can be used in production.	(1 mark)
•	When the lake water is not processed, it is land. In this situation, Louis is correct.	(1 mark)
•	Capital refers to all man-made resources used by producers to help production.		(1 mark)
•	When the lake water is processed (e.g., lake water in a man-made lake) and used to help production (e.g., fish breeding or water activities). In this situation, Eddie is correct.	(1 mark)

questions.topic: B2 · Ch210 · Factors of production
questions.text:
Suppose Medic Ltd has discovered a plant which can cure most cancers. According to Medic Ltd, this plant can only be grown in the Amazon Basin and cannot be artificially propagated (人工培植).
(a)	To which factor of production does the plant belong? Explain.	(2 marks)
(b)	Medic Ltd later makes the plant into a pill for sale in the market. Do you think the price elasticity of supply for the pill is high or low? Explain.	(3 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	•	Land	(1 mark)
	•	Because it is a natural resource that can be used in production (for medical use). 	(1 mark)

(b)	•	Price elasticity of supply is low.	(1 mark)
	•	Because the production of the pill requires the use of a plant which can only be naturally grown in the Amazon Basin, independent of the price. Production of the pill is therefore inflexible.	(2 marks)

Structured Questions

questions.topic: B2 · Ch210 · Factors of production
questions.text:
A logistics company has drivers, warehouse workers, engineers and managers.
(a)	What economic principle is illustrated by the above phenomenon? List THREE reasons why the principle can increase labour productivity?	(4 marks)
(b)	The drivers receive a monthly salary of $9,000 and take part in a profit-sharing scheme.	
	(i)	From the viewpoint of the company, explain ONE disadvantage of a monthly salary.	(2 marks)
	(ii)	From the viewpoint of the drivers, explain ONE advantage of the above payment method.	(2 marks)
(c)	Give ONE example of how engineers can increase the labour productivity of 	drivers.		(2 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Division of labour	(1 mark)
	•	Practice makes perfect
	•	Choosing the most suitable person for the job
	•	Stimulus to mechanisation
	•	Saves time in training
	(Any THREE of the above or other reasonable answers. 1 mark × 3 = 3 marks)

(b)	(i)	•	Drivers may shirk as their income does not directly depend on their contribution. Productivity therefore may decline.
		•	More supervision is needed as the company has to assign and monitor the work of its drivers. Therefore, this entails a higher administrative cost.
		(Any ONE of the above. 2 marks)
	(ii)	Drivers can earn more if the firm earns a larger profit.	(2 marks)

(c)	The engineers can keep the trucks in good condition so that the trucks can run better. Drivers can transport their cargoes more quickly.	(2 marks)
	(Accept other reasonable examples)

questions.topic: B2 · Ch210 · Factors of production
questions.text:
Advances in technology are reducing the demand for labour. Companies today are using robots to replace labour on production lines. Robots never get injured or fatigued, which means they are more 'hard-working' than human workers.
(a)	According to the above information, how will wages change if the cost of producing robots decreases?	(7 marks)
(b)	What are the factor incomes of capital and labour respectively?	(4 marks)
(c)	How will the increase in robots affects affect the productivity of labour?	(2 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Indicate on the diagram:
	•	The supply curve of robots shifts rightwards.	(1 mark)
	•	The price of robots decreases.	(1 mark)
	•	The demand curve of labour shifts leftwards.	(1 mark)
	•	Wage decreases.	(1 mark)
	     
	Verbal elaboration:
	•	If the cost of producing robots decreases, the supply of robots increases. Therefore, the price of robots decreases.	(1 mark)
	•	The information in the question indicates that robots and labour are substitutes. Therefore, when the price of robots decreases, the demand for labour will decrease.	(2 marks)

(b)	Capital: interest	(2 marks)
	Labour: wage	(2 marks)

(c)	It will increase the productivity of labour.	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B2 · Ch210 · Factors of production
questions.text:
The following table shows information about two car factories.
	Factory A	Factory B	
No. of workers employed
Output (units)
No. of working hours per worker	20
1,000
10	30
900
5	

(a)	In which types of production are the workers in the car factories engaged? Which type of factor of production do the workers provide?	(2 marks)
(b)	Which factory has a higher labour productivity? Explain your answer.	(5 marks)
(c)	Suggest TWO possible reasons why a factory may have higher productivity than another.		(4 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Secondary production	(1 mark)
	Labour	(1 mark)
(b)	Labour productivity of Factory A 
	= [1,000 ÷ (20 × 10)] units/working hour	(1 mark)
	= 5 units/working hour	(1 mark)
	Labour productivity of Factory B
	= [900 ÷ (30 × 5)] units/working hour	(1 mark)
	= 6 units/working hour	(1 mark)
	Therefore, factory B has a higher labour productivity.	(1 mark)

(c)	•	The health condition of workers is better.
	•	The average educational level of workers is higher and workers receive more training.
	•	The quantity and quality of other factors of production are higher.
	•	The working conditions are better.
	•	The method of organising workers is more efficient.
	•	Workers are rewarded with higher wage rates or better job prospects.
(Any TWO of the above, 2 marks × 2 = 4 marks)

questions.topic: B2 · Ch210 · Factors of production
questions.text:
May owns a restaurant. The waiters at her restaurant are paid with tips, plus their basic salary. Customer orders are processed with a computer. 
(a)	Explain ONE advantage and ONE disadvantage to the waiters of being paid with tips.		(4 marks)
(b)	Which factor of production do May and the waiters provide?	(2 marks)
(c)	The computer used in the restaurant becomes outdated. How does this affect the change in capital stock? Show the formula to support your answer.	(3 marks)
(d)	The interest rate has decreased. Explain how this affects the capital stock at May's restaurant.	(2 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Advantage to the waiters:
	•	Workers can earn more by providing a high standard of services.	(2 marks)
	Disadvantage to the waiters:
	•	Workers bear risk as their incomes fluctuate with tips.	(2 marks)

(b)	May: Entrepreneurship.	(1 mark)
	Waiters: Labour.	(1 mark)

(c)	Change in capital stock = Capital formulation - Capital depreciation	(2 marks)
	The increase in capital depreciation due to capital obsolescence will lead to the decrease in capital stock.	(1 mark)

(d)	When the interest rate decreases, the cost of buying the capital decreases. Thus, May will buy more capital and the capital stock at her restaurant will increase.
			(2 marks)

questions.topic: B2 · Ch210 · Factors of production
questions.text:
The following table shows information about a factory in 2014 and 2015.

Year	2014	2015	
 No. of workers employed 
 Output (units)
 No. of working hours per worker	60
160,000
44	66
150,000
40	

(a)	How can labour productivity be measured?	(2 marks)
(b)	Find the change in 
	(i)	labour supply and 
	(ii)	labour productivity 
	of the factory from 2014 to 2015 based on the above information.	(8 marks)
(c)	Suggest TWO reasons to account for the above change in labour productivity.	
					(4 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Labour productivity is measured by output produced per working hour of labour.	(2 marks)

(b)	(i)	Labour supply in 2014 = (60 × 44) = 2,640 working hours	(1 mark)
		Labour supply in 2015 = (66 × 40) = 2,640 working hours	(1 mark)
		Therefore, labour supply in 2015 has been unchanged.	(1 mark)
	(ii)	Labour productivity in 2014
		= [160,000 ÷ (60 × 44) ] units/working hour	(1 mark)
		= 60.61 units/working hour	(1 mark)
		Labour productivity in 2015
		= [150,000 ÷ (66 × 40)] units/working hour	(1 mark)
		= 56.82 units/working hour	(1 mark)
		Therefore, the labour productivity in 2015 has decreased.	(1 mark)

(c)	•	The health condition of workers has worsened.
	•	The average level of educational attainment and training received by workers has dropped.
	•	The quantity and quality of other factors of production have decreased.
	•	The working conditions have become poorer.
	•	The method of organising workers has become less efficient.
	•	The incentive to work has worsened.
	(Any TWO of the above, 2 marks × 2 = 4 marks)

questions.topic: B2 · Ch210 · Factors of production
questions.text:
Study the following production information about Country A.

Year	2011	2015	
Number of workers	100		120		
Average working hours of workers	2,340		1,820		
Total output (units)	100,000		120,000		

(a)	Calculate the average labour productivity of Country A in 2011 and 2015.		(4 marks)
(b)	Suggest THREE reasons to account for the change in labour productivity of 
Country A.	 (7 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	•	Average labour productivity in 2011
		=  unit/working hour	(1 mark)
		= 0.43 unit/working hour	(1 mark)
	•	Average labour productivity in 2015
		=  unit/working hour	(1 mark)
		= 0.55 unit/working hour	(1 mark)

(b)	The average labour productivity has increased because:	(1 mark)
	•	the health condition of workers has improved.
	•	the average level of educational attainment and training received by workers has raised.
	•	the amount of capital has increased and/or the quality of capital has improved and/or the technological level has advanced.
	•	the working conditions have improved.
	•	the method of organising workers has become more efficient.
	• 	incentive to work has improved.
	(Briefly explain any THREE of the above, 2 marks × 3 = 6 marks)

questions.topic: B2 · Ch210 · Factors of production
questions.text:
Karen runs a boutique. The salesgirls at her shop are paid by a commission which is a certain percentage of the total revenue, in addition to their basic salary.
(a)	Explain ONE advantage to Karen and one disadvantage to the salesgirls of adopting this payment system.	(4 marks)
(b)	Suppose the demand for products from Karen's boutique decreases. Explain the effect on the income of the salesgirls with the aid of a demand-supply diagram.		(7 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Advantages to Karen:
	•	Workers have a higher incentive to provide a high standard of services.
	•	She can save on the costs of supervising the standard of services.
	•	Part of the business risk can be shifted to the workers.
	(Any ONE of the above, 2 marks)
	Disadvantage to the salesgirls:
	•	Compared with a time rate, their income will be more unstable since part of their income depends on sales revenues.	(2 marks)

(b)
	(2 marks)	
	•	If demand for the products falls, the equilibrium price and the quantity transacted will fall.	(2 marks)
	•	Therefore, the total revenue will fall (P0 × Q0 ( P1 × Q1).	(1 mark)
	•	The commission given to the salesgirls will decrease.	(1 mark)
	•	The total income of the salesgirls for them will fall.	(1 mark)

questions.topic: B2 · Ch210 · Factors of production
questions.text:
There are different positions at a school, such as teachers, computer officers, clerks and laboratory technicians.
(a)	To which type of production does teaching belong? Explain.	(3 marks)
(b)	To which factor of production does a teacher belong? Explain.	(3 marks)
(c)	State TWO advantages to a school of practising division of labour.	(4 marks)
(d)	Arrange, from the highest to the lowest, the occupational mobility of the following posts: teachers, principal, clerks.	(3 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	•	Tertiary production	(1 mark)
	•	Teaching is the provision of educational services.	(2 marks)

(b)	•	Labour	(1 mark)
	•	Teachers provide the human effort, both mental and physical, in the provision of educational services. 	(2 marks)

(c)	•	Assigning the right person to do the right job
	•	Practice makes perfect
	•	Saving time in training
	•	Saving time in moving around jobs
	•	Fewer capital goods are needed in production and hence the school can afford to provide sufficient tools for teachers to improve productivity
	(Any TWO of the above, 2 marks × 2 = 4 marks)

(d)	Clerks ( teachers ( principal	(3 marks)

questions.topic: B2 · Ch210 · Factors of production
questions.text:
In Hong Kong, the police force is divided into different departments, such as operations, crime, security, etc.
(a)	Identify the type of division of labour in this case. Give TWO disadvantages of division of labour in the police force.	(3 marks)
(b)	To which factor of production does a police officer belong? Explain.	(3 marks)
(c)	What is the wage payment method for police officers in Hong Kong? Explain ONE advantage of this method to the employer (Hong Kong government) and police officers, respectively.	(5 marks)
*(d)	To reduce the turnover of police officers, an academic suggests increasing the wage level of police officers. Explain whether an increase in the wage level will reduce the occupational mobility of police officers.	(3 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Complex division of labour	(1 mark)
	Disadvantages:
	•	Work becomes dull and monotonous
	•	Loss of job satisfaction
	•	Over-interdependence
	•	Limited skills of police officers
	•	Greater risk of unemployment
	(Briefly explain any TWO of the above, 1 mark × 2 = 2 marks)

(b)	•	Labour	(1 mark)
	•	In maintaining law and order, a police officer provides human effort, both mental and physical.	(2 marks)

(c)	•	Time rate	(1 mark)
	•	Advantage to the employer: 
		-	no need to measure the exact contribution of police officers
		-	police officers can pay more attention to services quality
		(Briefly explain any ONE of the above, 2 marks × 1 = 2 marks)
	•	Advantage to police officers: more stable income/ do not need to face the risk of income fluctuation	(2 marks)

(d)	•	Yes.	(1 mark)
	•	If wages are increased, the opportunity costs for police officers of changing jobs, which are their wages as police officers, are higher. Therefore, their occupational mobility will decrease.	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B2 · Ch210 · Factors of production
questions.text:
Eddie runs a computer store. He hires some salespeople and a clerk.
(a)	Suggest the methods of wage payments for the salespeople and the clerk to Eddie and list TWO reasons for each suggestion.	(6 marks)
(b)	What are the roles of Eddie in running the computer store? List THREE of them.		(3 marks)
(c)	Both Eddie and the clerk get returns from the computer store. Name their returns respectively and list TWO differences between them.	(4 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	•	Salespeople: a 'basic salary plus commission' scheme	(1 mark)
		Reasons:
		This can increase their incentives to work and they will provide a high standard of services. Besides, Eddie can save on the cost of supervising the salespeople.	(2 marks)
	•	The clerk: a time rate	(1 mark)
		Reasons:
		It is simple and easy to administer. Eddie can save much of the cost of measuring the clerk's contribution. Moreover, the clerk may pay more attention to the quality of work.	(2 marks)

(b)	•	Bearing business risk	(1 mark)
	•	Making major business decisions	(1 mark)
	•	Managing other factors of production	(1 mark)

(c)	•	Eddie's return: profits	(1 mark)
	•	The clerk's return: wages	(1 mark)
	Differences:
	•	Wages are usually stipulated in contracts while profit is uncertain because the sales of a product are not guaranteed. 	(1 mark)
	•	The return for labour must be positive while the return for an entrepreneur may be negative if the firm experiences a loss.	(1 mark)

questions.topic: B2 · Ch210 · Factors of production
questions.text:
Mr Lee runs a fashion shop. He hires an executive to run the daily operation.
(a)	To which kind of factors of production do Mr Lee and the executive belong respectively? Are their returns the same? Explain.	(8 marks)
(b)	The shop hires many staff, such as designers, salespersons and cleaning workers, etc. 
	(i)	Identify the type of division of labour practised in the shop.	(1 mark)
	(ii)	Compare the occupational mobility of a designer and a salesperson.	(3 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	•	Mr Lee is an entrepreneur. He makes major decisions and bears risks.		(2 marks)
	•	The executive is labour; he / she provides human effort in production.		(2 marks)
	•	Their returns are different: Mr Lee's returns are profits; the executive's returns are wages.	 (2 marks)
	•	Profits are uncertain and realised only after production and sales, while wages are known before production.	(1 mark)
	•	Wages are relatively steady while profits are unstable and can even be negative.	(1 mark)

(b)	(i)	Complex division of labour	(1 mark)
	(ii)	•	The occupational mobility of a designer is lower than that of a salesperson.	(1 mark)
		•	A designer receives more training and his/her income is higher. Therefore, his/her opportunity cost of changing jobs is higher.	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B2 · Ch210 · Factors of production
questions.text:
Explain if the following sentences are correct:
(a)	In economics, reclaimed land is land.	(3 marks)
(b)	In economics, the supply of land will not increase.	(3 marks)
(c)	In economics, the supply of land does not involve opportunity cost.	(3 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	•	Incorrect.	(1 mark)

questions.text:
* Which of the following statements about the relationship between marginal product, average product and total product is correct? 
A.	When marginal product increases, total product increases. 
B.	When marginal product decreases, total product decreases. 
C.	Average product is total product divided by the quantity of fixed factors. 
D.	None of the above
questions.answerText:
For Option A, suppose the marginal product of the nth unit of a variable factor (e.g., labour) is -5 units of output, while the total product using n units of labour is 100 units of output. If the marginal product of the (n＋1) th unit of labour is -3, the marginal product increases (from -5 to -3), while the total product using (n＋1) units of labour decreases to 97 (100 - 3) units of output. Therefore, Option A is incorrect. 
For Option B, suppose the marginal product of the nth unit of labour is 10 units of output, while the total product using n units of labour is 100 units of output. If the marginal product of the (n＋1) th unit of labour is 5 units of output, the marginal product decreases (from 10 to 5) and the total product using (n＋1) units of labour increases from 100 units of output to 105 units of output. Therefore, Option B is incorrect.

questions.answerText:
Recall that the factory employs five workers. 
When there is one absentee, the drop in total product is 400 units. Hence, the marginal product of the first absentee is 400 units, which is the MP of the 5th worker.
When there are two absentees, the drop in total product is 775 units. Hence, the marginal product of the second absentee is 375 units (775 units - 400 units), which is the MP of the 4th worker. You can find the marginal product of the rest of the workers using the same method.

(c)	What is the effect of this measure on average cost and marginal cost of production?	(4 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Yes, because it does not vary with the level of output.	(2 marks)
(b)	Any two reasonable examples	(2 marks)
	Examples: electricity fee, costs of raw materials
(c)	•	Average cost = Total cost ÷ Units of output	(1 mark)
	•	Since total cost of production decreases and the level of output remains unchanged, average cost must decrease.	(1 mark)
	•	Marginal cost of the nth unit = TC of n units - TC of (n - 1) units	(1 mark)
	•	Since the total cost of n units and that of (n - 1) units decrease by the same amount, marginal cost of production remains unchanged.	(1 mark)
	OR
	•	The change in the fixed cost will not affect the marginal cost.	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B2 · Ch211 · Production in the short run and long run
questions.text:
Ms Chan runs a cake shop in Causeway Bay. Suppose the power company raises the electricity charge by 5%.
(a)	Do electricity charges belong to fixed cost or variable cost? Explain.	(2 marks)
(b)	Give ONE example of the shop's fixed cost and variable cost, respectively.		(2 marks)
(c)	What is the effect of an increase in electricity charges on total cost and marginal cost?	(5 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Electricity charges belong to variable cost because it varies with the level of output.	(2 marks)
(b)	Any one reasonable example for each type of cost
	Example of fixed cost: rent	(1 mark)
	Example of variable cost: costs of raw materials	(1 mark)
(c)	•	Total cost = Total fixed cost + Total variable cost	(1 mark)
	•	Since total variable cost increases and total fixed cost remains unchanged, total cost must increase.	(1 mark)
	•	MC of the nth unit of output = TC of n units - TC of (n-1) units	(1 mark)
	•	In raising electricity charges by 5%, the higher the consumption of electricity, the greater the increase in electricity charges.	(1 mark)
	•	Therefore, the increase in TVC of n units will be greater than that of (n-1) units, marginal cost will increase.	(1 mark)

questions.topic: B2 · Ch211 · Production in the short run and long run
questions.text:
Tom opens supermarkets. He finds that if he increases all the inputs to increase outputs, the average cost will increase. Give THREE possible reasons for this.	
				(6 marks)
questions.answerText:
This is because the scale of the supermarket is too large and it suffers from diseconomies of scale. 
•	It needs to pay a higher marketing cost to maintain its market share as the markets approach saturation.
•	The complex organisational structure of a large supermarket may delay decisions, block communication and weaken coordination. This increases its average cost of production.
•	A bank may charge a higher interest rate to compensate for the higher risk of lending too much money to a large supermarket.
•	As a large supermarket increases its employment of resources, the firm may have to buy them from more expensive sources or use more expensive substitutes.
(Any THREE of the above or other reasonable answers. 2 marks × 3 = 6 marks)

questions.topic: B2 · Ch211 · Production in the short run and long run
questions.text:
Suggest TWO reasons why a large logistics company usually has a cost advantage.	
				(4 marks)
questions.answerText:
The possible reasons are as follows:
•	A large logistics company can afford to have better machines (e.g., trucks) since the cost can be spread over a larger output.
•	A large logistics company can have specialisation among managers and attract more productive professionals to work for it. Thus, productivity can be increased and the average cost of production can be reduced.
•	A large logistics company can raise funds at a lower average cost.	
•	A large logistics company can enjoy a larger discount when buying inputs in bulk, and this can lower its average purchasing cost.
•	A large logistics company can spread its advertising costs over a larger output. Hence, it can cut its average cost of marketing.
•	A large logistics company can diversify its input sources, products and markets to reduce the risks of a rise in costs or a fall in sales.
(Any TWO of the above or other reasonable answers. 2 marks × 2 = 4 marks)

questions.topic: B2 · Ch211 · Production in the short run and long run
questions.text: Suggest TWO possible reasons why a large supermarket chain usually has a cost advantage over a small store.	(4 marks)
questions.answerText:
The possible reasons are as follows:
•	A large supermarket chain can afford to have better machines (e.g., cash registers) since the cost can be spread over a larger output.
•	A large supermarket chain can have specialisation among managers and attract more productive professionals to work for it. Thus, productivity can be increased and the average cost of production can be lowered.
•	A large supermarket chain can raise funds at a lower average cost.	
•	A large supermarket chain can enjoy a larger discount when buying inputs in bulk, and this can lower its average purchasing cost.
•	A large supermarket chain can spread its advertising costs over a larger output. Hence, it can cut its average cost of marketing.
•	A large supermarket chain can diversify its input sources, products and markets to reduce the risks of a rise in cost, production disruption and a fall in sales.
	(Any TWO of the above or other reasonable answers. 2 marks × 2 = 4 marks)

questions.topic: B2 · Ch211 · Production in the short run and long run
questions.text: State the differences between diminishing marginal returns and diseconomies of scale.	(6 marks)
questions.answerText:
Diminishing marginal returns: 
•	Relate to the input-output relationship in the short run.	(1 mark)
•	As more variable factors are added to a given quantity of fixed factors, the marginal product eventually drops, ceteris paribus.	(2 marks)
Diseconomies of scale:
•	Relate to the cost-output relationship in the long run. 	(1 mark)
•	Disadvantages associated with too large a scale of production which results in higher average costs.	(2 marks)

questions.text:
* A teacher says, 'In the short run, it is impossible for the total product of a firm to keep increasing. However, it is possible in the long run.'
Is the teacher correct? Explain.	(5 marks)
questions.answerText:
•	For the first half, it depends.	(1 mark)
•	According to the law of diminishing marginal returns, marginal product decreases eventually. However, whether the total product can keep increasing depends on whether the marginal product decreases to a negative figure; if it decreases to a negative figure, the total product cannot keep increasing. •	On the other hand, a firm eventually suffers diseconomies of scale in the long run. Although average cost increases with output, total product can still increase continuously. 	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B2 · Ch211 · Production in the short run and long run
questions.text: List THREE reasons that explain why the average costs of big supermarkets are lower than those of small supermarkets.	(6 marks)
questions.answerText:
This is because big supermarkets can benefit from economies of scale:
•	A big supermarket can afford to buy better equipment to raise productivity and can fully utilise it. Hence, the average cost of production drops.
•	A big supermarket can have specialisation among managers and attract more productive professionals to increase productivity. Thus its average cost of production drops.
•	A big supermarket can bargain for a lower borrowing rate and can issue shares to avoid paying interest. Hence, its average cost of capital drops.
•	A big supermarket can enjoy a larger discount when buying its inputs in bulk, so that its average cost of purchases drops.
•	A big supermarket can spread its advertising costs over a larger output. Hence, its average cost of marketing drops.
•	A big supermarket can afford research and development to develop new technology to lower its average cost of production. 
(Any THREE of the above or other reasonable answers. 2 marks × 3 = 6 marks)

questions.topic: B2 · Ch211 · Production in the short run and long run
questions.text: List THREE reasons to explain why the average cost at a food factory increases when it expands its scale of production.	(6 marks)
questions.answerText:
This is because the scale of the factory is too large and it suffers from diseconomies of scale. Reasons for diseconomies of scale:
•	The complex organisational structure of a large factory may delay decisions, block communication and weaken coordination. This increases its average cost of production.
•	A bank may charge a higher interest rate to compensate for the higher risk of lending too much money to a large factory. This raises its average cost of production.
•	As a large factory increases its employment of resources, the firm may have to buy them from more expensive sources or use more expensive substitutes. This raises its average cost of purchasing resources.
•	A large factory may suffer from saturation of the local market. Exploring overseas markets increases its average cost of marketing.
(Any THREE of the above or other reasonable answers. 2 marks × 3 = 6 marks)

questions.topic: B2 · Ch211 · Production in the short run and long run
questions.text:
* Student X: When a firm expands its output level and enjoys economies of scale, the average cost of production and total cost of production will decrease.
Is he correct? Explain.	(4 marks)
questions.answerText:
•	Economies of scale: When a firm increases its output by expanding its scale of production (i.e. increasing the employment of all factors by the same proportion), the average cost of production will decrease.	(2 marks)
•	However, the total cost of production may increase or decrease, depending on whether the marginal cost is positive or not. Therefore, the statement is incorrect.	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B2 · Ch211 · Production in the short run and long run
questions.text:
'When a firm reduces its scale of production, the average cost increases. This means the firm suffers from diseconomies of scale.'
Is this statement correct? Explain.	(6 marks)
questions.answerText:
•	Economies of scale: When a firm increases its output by expanding its scale of production (i.e., increasing the employment of all factors by the same proportion), the average cost of production will decrease.	(2 marks)
•	Diseconomies of scale: When a firm increases its output by expanding its scale of production (i.e., increasing the employment of all factors by the same proportion), the average cost of production will increase.	(2 marks)
•	When the firm reduces its scale, the average cost increases. In other words, when the firm expands its scale, the average cost decreases. Hence, the firm enjoys economies of scale, instead of suffering from diseconomies of scale. Therefore, the statement is incorrect.	(2 marks)

(b)	Reasons:
	•	A larger firm can afford to buy better equipment to raise productivity and can fully utilise it. 
		Hence, the average cost of production drops.
	•	A larger firm can have specialisation among managers and attract more productive professionals to increase productivity. Thus, its average cost of production drops.
	•	A larger firm can bargain for a lower borrowing rate. Hence, its average cost of capital drops.
	•	A larger firm can enjoy a larger discount when buying its inputs in bulk, so that its average cost of purchases drops.
	•	A larger firm can afford research and development to develop new technology to lower its average cost of production. 
	(Any THREE of the above or other reasonable answers. 2 marks × 3 = 6 marks)


(c)	Advantage:
	•	Holders of debentures are creditors, not owners of the company. They therefore have no voting rights and the existing shareholders' power of controlling the company is not diluted.	(2 marks)
	Disadvantage:
	•	The company must pay interest to the bond holders regardless of its financial condition.	(2 marks)
	(Accept other reasonable answers)

questions.topic: B2 · Ch211 · Production in the short run and long run
questions.text:
Suppose the government imposes a per-unit sales tax on tissue manufacturers in order to reduce waste.
(a)	What are the effects of the tax on the average cost and the marginal cost of producing tissues? Explain.	(4 marks)
(b)	Facing enduring promotion from environmental groups, some people replace tissues by handkerchiefs. With the aid of a demand-supply diagram, explain under what situation the equilibrium price of tissues will increase when the imposition of a sales tax and the above event take place simultaneously.	(6 marks)
(c)	Mr Lee is a sole proprietor of a tissue manufacturing firm. To produce handkerchiefs, he needs to purchase new machines. Instead of borrowing from banks, he raises funds by forming a partnership with Miss Ma. Explain ONE advantage and ONE disadvantage of forming a partnership over borrowing from banks.	(4 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	•	Average cost = Total cost ÷ Total output. Total cost increases by per-unit tax times total output.	(1 mark)
	•	The tax will increase the average cost.	(1 mark)
	•	Every unit of output is taxable.	(1 mark)
	•	So the tax will increase marginal cost by the amount of the per-unit tax.		(1 mark)

(b)	Verbal elaboration:
	•	The sales tax will decrease the supply of tissues (S0 → S1).	(1 mark)
	•	The demand for tissues will decrease when people replace tissues by handkerchiefs (D0 → D1).	(1 mark)
	•	If the supply decreases more than the demand, the equilibrium price will increase (P0 → P1).	(2 marks)
	Indicate on the diagram:
	(2 marks)

(c)	Advantages:
	•	Mr Lee need not bear interest.
	•	There are more sources of capital.
	•	There is a wider scope of specialisation.
	•	Cost and risk sharing is possible.
	(Any ONE of the above with explanation or other reasonable answers, 2 marks) 
	Disadvantages:
	•	Mr Lee has to bear the consequences of mistakes committed by other partners.
	•	Longer decision-making time is required and decision making is less flexible.
	•	Transfer of ownership is more difficult.
	(Any ONE of the above with explanation or other reasonable answers, 2 marks)

questions.topic: B2 · Ch211 · Production in the short run and long run
questions.text:
Mr Yeung is a sole proprietor of a printing factory which prints textbooks for publishers in Hong Kong. The following information is extracted from a report on Mr Yeung's factory:

No. of workers absent from work	Reduction of books printed	
1	200	
2	500	
3	900	
4	1,400	
5	2,000	

(a)	State the law of diminishing marginal returns.	(3 marks)
*(b)	Are the data consistent with the law? Explain your answer.	(4 marks)

(c)	Suppose Mr Yeung wants to increase the productivity of workers by increasing the number of printing machines. He therefore asks his best friend, Mr Wong, to join him and together they form a private limited company.
	(i) What are the features of a private limited company in comparison with a sole proprietorship?	(2 marks)
	(ii)	With the capital from Mr Wong, Mr Yeung doubled the number of machines and the number of workers in their factory. However, the total output has less than doubled. Suggest TWO reasons to account for this.	(4 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	The law states that when a variable factor is added continuously to a given quantity of a fixed factor, the marginal return or marginal product (of the variable factor) will eventually decrease, ceteris paribus.	(3 marks)

(b)	Suppose there are N workers in total. When one worker is absent, the drop in total output is 200, which is the marginal product of the Nth worker. When two workers are absent, the additional drop in total output is 300 (= 500 － 200), which is the marginal product of the (N - 1)th worker. …

Number of workers	Marginal product	
N - 5	-	
N - 4	600	
N - 3	500	
N - 2	400	
N - 1	300	
N	200	
		(3 marks)
	Since the marginal product of workers decreases with the number of workers, the data are consistent with the law of diminishing returns.	(1 mark)

(c)	(i)	•	The firm is an independent legal entity.
		•	The firm has lasting continuity.
		•	Owners bear limited liability, instead of unlimited liability
		•	Separation of ownership and management
		•	Wider source of capital
		•	Larger extent of specialisation
		•	Distant relations with employees and customers
		•	Higher profits tax rate
	
		(Any TWO of the above or other reasonable answers. 1 mark × 2 = 2 marks)
	(ii)	The printing factory is suffering from diseconomies of scale:
		•	The complex organisational structure of a large factory may delay decisions, block communication and weaken coordination. This raises its average cost of production.
		•	A bank may charge a higher interest rate to compensate for the higher risk of lending too much money to a large factory. This raises its average cost of production.
		•	As a large factory increases its employment of resources, the firm may have to buy them from more expensive sources or use more expensive substitutes. This raises its average cost of purchasing resources.
		•	A large firm may suffer from saturation of the local market. Exploring overseas markets raises its average cost of marketing.
		(Any TWO of the above with a brief explanation or other reasonable answers. 2 marks × 2 = 4 marks)

questions.topic: B2 · Ch211 · Production in the short run and long run
questions.text:
Miss Chan is a sole proprietor of a farm. The following is from a report on her farm:

No. of workers absent	Total output (units)

(c)	Miss Chan wants to expand the scale of her farm. She invites Mr Lam to invest in the farm. Suppose Mr Lam wants to confine his maximum loss to his investment in the farm.

questions.answerText:
(a)	The law states that when a variable factor is added continuously to a given quantity of fixed factors, the marginal return or marginal product (of the variable factor) will eventually decrease, ceteris paribus.	(3 marks)

(b)	Suppose there are N workers. When one worker is absent, the drop in total output is uncertain, which is the marginal product of the Nth worker. When two workers are absent, the drop in total output is 200 (=1,890 - 1,690) units, which is the marginal product of the (N - 1) th worker. …

No. of workers	Marginal product (units)	
N - 5	-	
N - 4	150	
N - 3	160	
N - 2	180	
N - 1	200	
N	-	
		(3 marks)
Since the marginal product of workers increases with the number of workers, the data cannot illustrate the law.	(1 mark)

(c)	(i)	Private or public limited company / Limited company	(1 mark)
		•	The firm is an independent legal entity.
		•	The firm has lasting continuity.
		•	Owners bear limited liability, instead of unlimited liability
		•	Separation of ownership and management
		•	Wider source of capital
		•	Larger extent of specialisation
		•	Distant relations with employees and customers
		•	Higher profits tax rate
		(Any TWO of the above or other reasonable answers. 1 mark × 2 = 2 marks)

	(ii)	Capital		(1 mark)
		It is a man-made resource that can be used to help production. It has been processed by human effort.	(1 mark)

questions.topic: B2 · Ch212 · Expansion of firms
questions.text:
Study the following extract from the annual report of a company.

Last year, our company's business was poorer than expected: since we concentrate on clothing exported to the United States, the poor economic performance of the US economy last year was a disaster for us. Total profit has decreased by 56% compared with the year before. As a result, our company will start a series of business expansions to diversify our business.

(b)	Explain TWO advantages of the business expansion named in (a).	(4 marks)
questions.answerText:

Because these two types of expansion can help product diversification.	(1 mark)
(b)	•	It can enjoy economies of scale.
	•	It can extend its brand name to other products.
	•	It can reduce risk through product diversification.
	•	It can have more efficient use of resources held by another firm (for integration only).
	•	It can invest in other more profitable industries (for conglomerate expansion only).
	•	Any other relevant advantages
	(Any TWO of the above with explanation, 2 marks × 2 = 4 marks)

questions.topic: B2 · Ch212 · Expansion of firms
questions.text:
Study the following conversation between the managers of Twinkling Star Limited, a toy manufacturer.

Manager A: As demand for toys has been falling in recently years, we should combine with another toy manufacturer.
Manager B: I disagree. We should combine with a publisher instead.

			(1 mark)

	Because they supply unrelated products.	(1 mark)
(b)	Advantages of horizontal integration to Twinkling Star Limited:
	•	It can benefit from economies of scale.
	•	It can increase its market share.
	•	It can reduce competition.
	•	It can reduce duplication of facilities.
	•	Any other relevant advantages
	(Any of the above with explanation, 2 marks)
	Advantages of conglomerate integration to Twinkling Star Limited:
	•	It can enjoy economies of scale.
	•	It can extend its brand name to other products.
	•	It can reduce risk through product diversification.
	•	It can have more efficient use of resources held by another firm.
	•	It can invest in other more profitable industries.
	•	Any other relevant advantages
	(Any of the above with explanation, 2 marks)

questions.topic: B2 · Ch212 · Expansion of firms
questions.text:
(a)	Identify TWO similarities and TWO differences between the motives of lateral integration and conglomerate integration.	(4 marks)

questions.topic: B2 · Ch212 · Expansion of firms
questions.text:
Name and explain the type of integration a firm should engage in if:
(a)	it wants to lower its average costs.	(3 marks)
(b)	it wants to reduce the number of substitutes available in the market.	(3 marks)
(c)	it wants to reduce the time spent on finding and negotiating with suitable and reliable suppliers.	(3 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	All types of integration can achieve this.	(1 mark)
	As the scale of production increases, the firm can enjoy economies of scale, which lowers average costs.	(2 marks)
(b)	Horizontal integration	(1 mark)
This can reduce the number of competitors and thus reduce the number of substitutes available in the market.	(2 marks)
(c)	Vertical backward integration 	(1 mark)
With subsidiaries supplying inputs, the firm can reduce the time spent on finding and negotiating with suppliers. Moreover, the supply of inputs is secured through this type of integration.	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B2 · Ch212 · Expansion of firms
questions.text:
Innomax Interior Design Limited provides not only interior design services; it also undertakes decoration projects. The following table shows its rates of return:

Year	2000	2001	2002	2003	2004	2005	
 Rate of return	-20%	5%	-5%	-10%	6%	-1%	

(a)	Which type of production does the company participate in? Explain.	(3 marks)
(b)	To reduce fluctuation in the rate of return, Innomax Interior Design Limited plans to integrate with another firm. Which types of firms can it integrate with? Explain with an example.	(3 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Secondary production and tertiary production	(1 mark)
	Decoration works turn raw materials into finished goods.	(1 mark)
	Interior design is a service.	(1 mark)
(b)	It can integrate with firms which are in entirely different businesses.	(1 mark)
	Any industry which is unrelated to interior design or decoration, e.g., Chinese restaurants	(1 mark)
	This is because even when the interior design business fails, the loss may be compensated for by a gain in another business. As a result, the overall rate of return can be stabilised.	(1 mark)
	(Accept other reasonable example that involves lateral integration.)

Structured Questions

questions.topic: B2 · Ch212 · Expansion of firms
questions.text:
Beef and fish are substitutes. Ken is the owner of a company that sells beef. He is deciding whether to integrate with a cattle farm or a company that sells fish.
(a)	Explain what type of expansion is involved if his firm integrates with a cattle 
farm. List ONE possible motive.	(3 marks)
(b)	Explain what type of expansion is involved if his firm integrates with a company that sell fish. List ONE possible motive that is different from (a).	(3 marks)
(c)	Suppose the supply of beef decreases.
	(i)	What will be the change in the total revenue of the company that sells beef?
			(4 marks)
	(ii)	What will be the change in the total revenue of the company that sells fish?	
		(4 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	(Vertical) Backward expansion	(1 mark)
	Because the firm expands into a preceding stage of production.	(1 mark)
	Possible motives:
	•	Enjoy economies of scale
	•	Better use of resources that another firm has
	•	Extend its brand name to other products
	•	Secure the supply of inputs
	•	Reduce expenses for transactions of inputs
	•	Any other relevant motives
	(Any ONE of the above, 1 mark)

(b)	Conglomerate expansion	(1 mark)
	Because the firm expands into a business of unrelated products.	(1 mark)
	Possible motives:
	•	Enjoy economies of scale
	•	Better use of resources that another firm has
	•	Extend its brand name to other products
	•	Spread risk through product diversification
	•	Invest in other more profitable industries
	•	Any other relevant motives
	(Any ONE of the above, 1 mark)


(c)	(i)	The price of beef will increase and the quantity transacted will decrease.	
				(2 marks)
			The change in the total revenue is uncertain, depending on the elasticity of 
demand.	(2 marks)
	(ii)	As the price of beef will increase, the demand for fish will increase.	(1 mark)
		The price and the quantity transacted of fish will increase.	(2 marks)
		Therefore, the total revenue will increase.	(1 mark)

questions.topic: B2 · Ch212 · Expansion of firms
questions.text:
In 2012, Eslite Bookstore opened a branch in Hong Kong, which is its first one outside Taiwan.
(a)	Explain what type of expansion is involved in the above expansion.	(2 marks)
(b)	Explain TWO advantages of the above expansion.	(4 marks)
(c)	In which type of production is the bookstore involved?	(1 mark)
(d)	In the production of books, authors create the content, publishers publish the book and bookstores sell them. What kind of economic principle is involved? Explain TWO advantages of this arrangement.	(5 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Lateral expansion	(1 mark)
	Because branches in Hong Kong and Taiwan are related but not competitive.
			(1 mark)
(b)	•	Enjoy economies of scale
	•	Extend its brand name to other markets
	•	Spread risk through market diversification
	•	Any other relevant advantages
	(Any TWO of the above with explanation, 2 marks × 2 = 4 marks)

(c)	Tertiary production	(1 mark)

(d)	Division of labour	(1 mark)
	Advantages:
	•	The right person can be assigned to do the right job. For example, authors may be good at creating the content but bad at marketing the books.
	•	This saves workers' time in shifting between different tasks. For example, authors can just stay at home to write the books.
	(Accept any other reasonable answers, 2 marks × 2 = 4 marks)

questions.topic: B2 · Ch212 · Expansion of firms
questions.text:
There was a greater demand for smartphones, but the factory could not buy the machines within a month. Therefore, it employed more part-time workers and continued to produce on Sundays. After a month, the factory successfully took over another phone manufacturer and so had more machines to produce the phones than it had before.
(a)	Identify the kind of business expansion involved.	(2 marks)
(b)	Explain TWO possible motives of the above expansion.	(4 marks)
(c)	Did the factory operate in the short run or long run one month earlier? Explain your answer.	(2 marks)
(d)	The factory cannot increase its output by just adding part-time workers. State the economic principle illustrated in this situation.	(3 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Horizontal expansion	(2 marks)

(b)	•	Enjoy economies of scale
	•	Increase market share
	•	Reduce competition
	•	Reduce duplication of facilities
	•	More efficient use of resources held by another firm
	(Any TWO of the above with explanation, 2 marks × 2 = 4 marks)

(c)	As the number of machines cannot be increased, machines are a fixed factor in this case. Because there is a fixed factor, the factory operates in the short run.	
			(2 marks)

(d)	The law of diminishing marginal returns, which states that when a variable factor is added continuously to a given quantity of fixed factors, the marginal product of the variable factor will eventually decrease, ceteris paribus.	(3 marks)

questions.topic: B2 · Ch212 · Expansion of firms
questions.text:
A Korean television broadcaster opens a shop in Hong Kong to sell their drama products.
(a)	Which type of expansion is involved in the above expansion?	(2 marks)
(b)	Explain TWO advantages of the above expansion.	(4 marks)
(c)	In which types of production is the shop involved?	(1 mark)
(d)	Explain why the staff at the shop are paid according to their working hours.	
			(2 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	(Vertical) Forward expansion	(2 marks)

(b)	•	Enjoy economies of scale
	•	Extend its brand name to other products
	•	Secure market outlets for outputs
	•	Reduce transaction expenses
	(Any TWO of the above with explanation, 2 marks × 2 = 4 marks)

(c)	Tertiary production	(1 mark)

(d)	The work of the staff is non-standardised and it is too costly to measure their contribution.
	(Accept any other reasonable answer, 2 marks)

questions.topic: B2 · Ch212 · Expansion of firms
questions.text:
Study the following newspaper extract.

After Peach Fashion took over Cool Shirts, some Cool Shirts shops were closed. All Cool Shirts shops which were retained after the takeover were renamed Peach Fashion. Peach Fashion is also expanding outside Hong Kong. It has obtained approval to open stores in Heilongjiang (黑龍江).	

(a)	Identify and name the TWO kinds of business expansion involved.	(2 marks)
(b)	After integrating with Cool Shirts, Peach Fashion closed some shops. It found that the average cost of the company decreased.
	(i)	Give THREE reasons to explain why the average cost of the company decreased.	(6 marks)
	(ii)	Some customers have said the quality of products is now better. Explain why this has happened.	(2 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Takeover of Cool Shirts: horizontal expansion or integration	(1 mark)
	Expanding in Heilongjiang: lateral expansion	(1 mark)

(b)	(i)	(	Since the scale of production is larger after the integration, Peach Fashion can enjoy economies of scale. 	(2 marks)
		(	Peach Fashion closed down some stores to avoid duplication of facilities. This saves on rental and equipment costs. 	(2 marks)
		(	The integration reduces competition. Hence, Peach Fashion can cut its expenditure on advertising and offer fewer special benefits to customers. 
				(2 marks)
	(ii)	Because of the larger scale, the combined company may be able to afford better machines and equipment and may spend more on research and development to improve the quality of products.	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B2 · Ch212 · Expansion of firms
questions.text:
Suppose a bus company plans to acquire a football team and raises $800 million by issuing new shares to the public.
(a)	Which type of expansion is involved in the above acquisition? Explain.	(2 marks)
(b)	Explain TWO advantages of the above acquisition to the bus company.	(4 marks)
(c)	The bus company chooses to raise capital by issuing shares instead of bonds.
	(i)	To which type of business ownership does the bus company belong?	(1 mark)
	(ii)	Describe THREE features of this type of business ownership.	(6 marks)
	(iii)	Explain ONE advantage and ONE disadvantage to the bus company of issuing shares over issuing bonds.	(4 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Conglomerate expansion	(1 mark)
	Because the bus company expands into a business of unrelated products.	(1 mark)

(b)	•	It can enjoy economies of scale.
	•	It can extend its brand name to other products.
	•	It can reduce risk through product diversification.
	•	It can have more efficient use of resources held by another firm.
	•	It can invest in other more profitable industries.
	•	Any other relevant advantages
	(Any TWO of the above with explanation, 2 marks × 2 = 4 marks)

(c)	(i)	Public limited company	(1 mark)
	(ii)	• 	An independent legal entity
		• 	Limited liability
		• 	Separation of ownership and management
		•	More sources of capital
		• 	Lasting continuity
		•	Weaker incentive to improve efficiency
		•	More distant relationship with employees
		•	More distant relationship with customers
		•	Can invite public subscription for its shares
		•	Needs to disclose its financial accounts to the public
		•	One to an unlimited number of shareholders
		•	Complicated and expensive set-up procedure
		•	Higher profits tax rate than sole proprietorships and partnerships
		•	Any other relevant features
		(Any THREE of the above with explanation, 2 marks × 3 = 6 marks)
	(iii)	The advantage of issuing shares:
		•	No interest burden
		•  	No redemption obligation
		•	Issuing more shares reduces the debt-to-equity ratio, making it easier to have more bank loans.
	(Any ONE of the above with explanation, 2 marks)
		The disadvantage of issuing shares:
		•	New shareholders may influence company decisions.
		•	Higher risk of being taken over is incurred.
		(Any ONE of the above with explanation, 2 marks)

questions.topic: B2 · Ch212 · Expansion of firms
questions.text:
PARKnSHOP is one of the largest supermarket chains in Hong Kong. In recent years, it has opened many superstores in different areas of Hong Kong.
(a)	Name the type of production PARKnSHOP is involved in.	(1 mark)
(b)	Is the expansion internal or external? Explain.	(2 marks)
(c)	Suggest TWO reasons for the expansion mentioned above. 	(4 marks)
(d)	At a superstore, a variety of goods, including fresh vegetables, fresh poultry and cooked food, are sold. The environment at the superstore is also cleaner and tidier than a traditional market.
	With the aid of a diagram, explain the effect of superstore openings on the equilibrium price, the quantity transacted and the total revenue of the same goods sold in traditional markets.	(6 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Tertiary production	(1 mark)

(b)	Internal expansion	(1 mark)
	Because PARKnSHOP expands on its own without combining with other firms.	
				(1 mark)

(c)	It can benefit from economies of scale.	(2 marks)
	It can increase its market share.	(2 marks)

(d)	(	Since the goods sold in superstores and those sold in traditional markets are substitutes for each other, the demand for the goods sold in traditional markets will fall (D0 ( D1).	(1 mark)
		(2 marks)
	•	The equilibrium price decreases (P0 ( P1).	(1 mark)
	•	The quantity transacted decreases (Q0 ( Q1).	(1 mark)
	•	Total revenue (= equilibrium price × quantity transacted) falls.	(1 mark)

questions.topic: B2 · Ch212 · Expansion of firms
questions.text:
From 2010 to 2014, Sun Hung Kai Properties (SHK) has opened YATA (一田百貨) branches in different locations in Hong Kong. SHK also opened YATA branches in some of its shopping arcades.
(a)	Is internal or external expansion involved when SHK opens YATA branches in its shopping arcades? Explain.	(2 marks)
(b)	SHK's core business is the development of property for sale and investment. Explain TWO reasons why SHK opened YATA branches.	(4 marks)
(c)	Suppose an AEON department store has already been established in one of SHK's shopping arcades. How will AEON's sales revenue be affected if SHK opens a YATA branch in the same shopping arcade? Explain with the aid of a supply-demand diagram.	(6 marks)
(d)	Suppose YATA found that its average cost fell after three more branches had been opened. Explain the fall in average cost.	(5 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Internal expansion	(1 mark)
	Because SHK expands on its own without combining with other firms.	(1 mark)

(b)	•	It can enjoy economies of scale.
	•	It can spread risk through product diversification.
	•	It can invest in other more profitable industries.
	•	Any other relevant reasons
	(Any TWO of the above with explanation, 2 marks × 2 = 4 marks)

(c)	•	Since goods sold in YATA and AEON are in substitute demand, the demand for goods sold in AEON will fall (D0 ( D1). 	(1 mark)
		(2 marks)
	•	The equilibrium price decreases (P0 ( P1).	(1 mark)
	•	The equilibrium quantity decreases (Q0 ( Q1).	(1 mark)
	•	Hence, total sales revenue (= equilibrium price × equilibrium quantity) will decrease.	(1 mark)

(d)	This is because YATA benefits from economies of scale.	(1 mark)
	Sources of economies of scale:
	•	A larger firm can afford to buy better equipment to raise productivity and can fully utilise its equipment.
	•	A larger firm can have specialisation among managers and attract more productive professionals to increase productivity.
	•	A larger firm can bargain for a lower borrowing rate and can issue shares to avoid paying interest.
	•	A larger firm can enjoy a larger discount when buying its inputs in bulk.
	•	A larger firm can spread its advertising costs over a larger output.
	•	A larger firm can diversify its input sources, products and markets.
	(Any TWO of the above with brief explanation, 2 marks × 2 = 4 marks)

questions.topic: B2 · Ch212 · Expansion of firms
questions.text:
In Country X, Firm A specialises in innovating and designing cars while Firm B specialises in manufacturing cars. Suppose Firm A acquires Firm B.
(a)	From the perspective of Firm A, to which type of expansion does this belong? Explain.	(2 marks)
(b)	Explain TWO advantages of this type of expansion.	(4 marks)
(c)	Productivity increases after the acquisition. Explain, with the aid of a supply-demand diagram, the effects on the equilibrium price and quantity of cars.		(5 marks)
(d)	Suppose instead of acquiring Firm B, Firm A acquires a film production company. What would motivate Firm A to take such an action? Explain TWO possible reasons.	(4 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Vertical forward expansion by expanding into a later stage of production of the same product, i.e., from innovating and designing to producing.	(2 marks)

(b)	•	It can enjoy economies of scale.
	•	It can extend its brand name to other products.
	•	It can secure market outlets for outputs.
	•	It can reduce expenses in transactions.
	•	Any other relevant advantages
	(Any TWO of the above with brief explanation, 2 marks × 2 = 4 marks)

(c)	•	The increase in productivity lowers the production cost and raises the supply  (S0 ( S1).	(1 mark)
		(2 marks)

	•	The equilibrium price decreases (P0 ( P1).	(1 mark)
	•	The equilibrium quantity increases (Q0 ( Q1).	(1 mark)

(d)	•	It can reduce risk through product diversification.
	•	It can utilise resources held by the film production company more efficiently.
	•	It can invest in more profitable industries.
	•	It can extend its brand name to other products.
	•	Any other relevant reasons
	(Any TWO of the above with brief explanation, 2 marks × 2 = 4 marks)
