questions.topic: B4 · Ch419 · Monopoly pricing
questions.text: A monopoly under simple monopoly pricing must be inefficient. Do you agree? Explain.	(5 marks)
questions.answerText:
Agree.
A monopolist will maximise profit by producing at the output level where MR = MC.	(1 mark)
Under simple monopoly pricing, the MR curve lies below the demand curve. As a result, at the profit-maximising output level, the price is greater than MR and, hence, the price is greater than MC.	(2 marks)
This means that the MB of the good to consumers exceeds the MC of producing the last unit (MB > MC). There is underproduction of output. Deadweight loss exists at this output level.	(2 marks)
(Graphical illustration is also accepted.)

questions.topic: B4 · Ch419 · Monopoly pricing
questions.text: * 'If firms operating in a perfectly competitive market combine and monopolise the market, both consumers and the combined firm must suffer under simple monopoly pricing.' Suppose the demand and cost curves remain unchanged before and after the integration. Comment on this statement using separate diagrams.	(8 marks)
questions.answerText:
The statement is wrong.
After the perfectly competitive market is monopolised, output decreases (Qc ( Qm) and the market price increases (Pc ( Pm).	(1 mark)
It is true that consumers must suffer as they enjoy less output at a higher price. The consumer surplus decreases after the market is monopolised.	(2 marks)
However, the combined firm can sell its output at a higher price, though less output is sold, to maximise its profit. The producer surplus increases after the market is monopolised. Thus, the combined firm will benefit.	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B4 · Ch419 · Monopoly pricing
questions.text: * Explain why output levels in a perfectly competitive market and a monopoly under simple monopoly pricing are different even though profit-maximising conditions in both markets are the same. Assume that the demand and cost curves are the same in both markets.	(6 marks)
questions.answerText:
Sellers in both markets will produce at the output level where MR = MC. 	(1 mark)
However, when a monopolist practises simple monopoly pricing, MR < P. As a result, at the profit maximising output level (where MR = MC), MC < P, and this means MC < MB (because consumers will buy the quantity where MB = P).	(2 marks)
By comparison, in a perfectly competitive market, sellers are price takers and the equilibrium output level is where MC = MB.	(2 marks)
Given that the demand and cost curves are the same in both markets, the output levels in the two markets are different.	(1 mark)
(Graphical illustration is also accepted.)

questions.topic: B4 · Ch419 · Monopoly pricing
questions.text:
Neway's market share in the Hong Kong karaoke market is nearly 90%. Explain whether the following practices by Neway constitute price discrimination.
(a)	It charges higher prices at Neway CEO branches, which are more luxurious than other branches.	(3 marks)
(b)	Customers who come at night are charged higher prices.	(3 marks)
(c)	Full-time students are charged lower prices.	(3 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	No.	(1 mark)
	The services provided at Neway CEO branches are superior to other branches.
	(2 marks)
(b)	No.	(1 mark)
	As more people go to Neway at night, the cost of serving a customer at night is higher. Also, all customers face the same 'higher prices' at night.	(2 marks)
(c)	Yes.	(1 mark)
	The cost of serving students and other customers is the same. Therefore, the price difference should be due to reasons other than cost differences.	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B4 · Ch419 · Monopoly pricing
questions.text:
(a)	Define price discrimination.	(2 marks)
(b)	Explain whether the following practices constitute price discrimination.
	(i)	Students are offered a $6 discount for a lunch set.	(3 marks)
	(ii)	For the same concert, the price of some balcony (樓座) seats is higher than rear stall (大堂後座) seats.	(3 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Price discrimination is the practice of charging different buyers different prices for the same good for reasons other than differences in costs.	(2 marks)
(b)	(i)	Yes.	(1 mark)
		Provided that the lunch set is the same for students and non-students, the price difference is for reasons other than differences in costs.	(2 marks)
	(ii)	No.	(1 mark)
		Balcony seats and rear stall seats offer different levels of enjoyment. They are not the same good.	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B4 · Ch419 · Monopoly pricing
questions.text:
Classify the following practices into different degrees of price discrimination. Explain your answer briefly.
(a)	A telecommunications company charges customers $300 each month for the first 2GB mobile data and $250 for the next 2GB of data.	(3 marks)
(b)	A Japanese mobile phone manufacturer retains more products for the domestic market and charges a lower price, and sells less in foreign markets at a higher price. (Suppose the production costs for domestic and foreign markets are the same.)	(3 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	This is second-degree price discrimination 	(1 mark)
	as the producer charges different prices for different blocks of mobile data usage.	(2 marks)
(b)	This is third-degree price discrimination	(1 mark)
	as the manufacturer charges different prices in two market segments.	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B4 · Ch419 · Monopoly pricing
questions.text:
MTR has introduced the MTR City Saver (港鐵都會票) that allows 40 single journeys covering designated urban stations for a fixed price.
(a)	Who are more likely to buy the MTR City Saver? People who often take high-fare rides or those who often take low-fare rides?	(1 mark)
(b)	Explain whether the MTR City Saver is a price discrimination arrangement. If it is, state the type of price discrimination to which it belongs.	(4 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	People who often take high-fare rides are more likely to buy the MTR City Saver.
	(1 mark)
(b)	Yes.	(1 mark)
The pricing arrangement separates frequent high-fare riders from other passengers. They are charged lower prices but not because the cost of serving them is different.	(2 marks)
This is third-degree price discrimination.	(1 mark)

questions.topic: B4 · Ch419 · Monopoly pricing
questions.text:
Hong Kong Disneyland has three types of one-day admission tickets, namely Adult, Child (aged 3-11) and Senior (aged 65 or above). The prices of Adult, Child and Senior tickets are $499, $355 and $100, respectively.
(a)	What is price discrimination?	(2 marks)
(b)	Is the above pricing arrangement an example of price discrimination? If yes, to which type of price discrimination does it belong?	(3 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Price discrimination is the practice of charging different buyers different prices for the same good for reasons other than differences in costs.	(2 marks)
(b)	Yes. This is because different prices are charged to adults, children and the elderly even though the costs of serving them are the same.	(2 marks)
	This belongs to third-degree price discrimination (market segmentation) because different prices are charged in three different market segments.	(1 mark)
	(Accept other reasonable answer.)

questions.topic: B4 · Ch419 · Monopoly pricing
questions.text:
John says, 'Having a dish of Yangzhou fried rice in a restaurant at lunchtime is more expensive than having one at teatime in the same restaurant. The restaurant is practising first-degree price discrimination.'
Mary says, 'I think the discount that the restaurant offers to students is an example of first-degree price discrimination.'
Comment on John and Mary's statements. 	(6 marks)
questions.answerText:
John's statement is wrong because the portion size of the Yangzhou fried rice served at lunchtime and teatime is usually different. The portion size of dishes at teatime is usually smaller. Even if the size is the same, the marginal cost of serving a customer a dish of Yangzhou fried rice at lunchtime (the peak hour of business for a restaurant) is much higher than at teatime. Therefore, the practice is not price discrimination.
	(4 marks)
Mary's statement is also wrong. A student discount is an example of third-degree discrimination instead of first-degree discrimination. The restaurant charges different prices in two market segments, students and non-students.	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B4 · Ch419 · Monopoly pricing
questions.text:
Give ONE reason to explain why the following producers may fail to practise price discrimination effectively.
(a)	A small meat stall in Hong Kong charges frequent customers a lower price but other customers pay a higher price.	(2 marks)
(b)	Hong Kong Disneyland charges local visitors a lower price but tourists pay a higher price.	(2 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	The meat stall does not have enough monopoly power to control output and prices. Consumers can easily switch to other sellers. (Accept other reasonable answers.)	(2 marks)
(b)	The market is not separable. If Hong Kong Disneyland does not check every visitor's identity document, local people buying tickets at a lower price may resell them to tourists who have to pay a higher price. (Accept other reasonable answers.)	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B4 · Ch419 · Monopoly pricing
questions.text:
Some large tutorial schools in Hong Kong offer scholarships and tuition fee refunds to students who obtain excellent results in public examinations.
(a)	Explain why this arrangement can be an example of price discrimination and state to which type of price discrimination it belongs.	(3 marks)
(b)	Suggest TWO conditions for successful implementation of this type of price discrimination.	(4 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	This can be an example of price discrimination because tuition fees for bright students are effectively lower than those for normal students even though they receive the same tuition services.	(2 marks)
It belongs to third-degree price discrimination.	(1 mark)
(b)	Conditions for successful implementation of third-degree price discrimination:
•	The tutorial schools must have some monopoly power to control prices. This means that if a tutorial school raises tuition fees for normal students (while lowering tuition fees for bright students), not all of them would be able to switch to other tutorial schools.
•	The tutorial schools are able to segment the market. In other words, it is difficult for bright students to resell their tutorial services to normal students.
•	Bright students and normal students must have different demand elasticities. Otherwise, tutorial schools cannot increase their profit by charging bright students lower tuition fees while charging normal students higher tuition fees.
•	The information cost for the tutorial schools is low, i.e., they can easily distinguish between bright students and normal students. (In fact, the information cost is low because students who want to get scholarships or tuition fee refunds will voluntarily provide their public exam results to the tutorial schools.)
(Any TWO of the above, 2 marks ( 2 = 4 marks)

questions.topic: B4 · Ch419 · Monopoly pricing
questions.text:
(a)	Define perfect price discrimination and market segmentation.	(4 marks)
(b)	Contrast these two pricing arrangements.	(4 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Perfect price discrimination is the practice of charging each buyer according to the buyer's maximum willingness to pay for each extra unit of the good.	(2 marks)
Market segmentation is a situation where the seller charges different prices in two or more market segments at the same time.	(2 marks)
(b)	Under perfect price discrimination, different consumers pay different prices for every unit consumed. Under market segmentation, consumers in different market segments pay different prices, while consumers in the same market segment face the same price.	(2 marks)
	Moreover, market segmentation requires different demand elasticities between buyers but perfect price discrimination does not.	(2 marks)
	(Accept other correct differences between the two pricing arrangements.)

questions.topic: B4 · Ch419 · Monopoly pricing
questions.text:
(a)	Are the following examples of price discrimination? Explain.	
(i)	A Taiwanese bubble tea chain charges consumers a higher price for bubble tea at its shop in Mongkok than in Yuen Long. 	(2 marks)
(ii)	Towngas offers a 50% discount to the elderly. 	(2 marks)
*(iii)	A bakery offers a 30% discount on its bread after 7 pm every day.	(2 marks)
(iv)	A butcher usually charges his frequent customers a lower price.	(2 marks)
(b)	Give TWO reasons to explain why it is possible to practise price discrimination in the above cases.	(4 marks)
(c)	Are the price discrimination arrangements in (a) necessarily profitable? Why?
	(2 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	(i)	No. The shops are located in different districts. The rental expense of a shop in Mongkok is likely higher than that in Yuen Long. Hence, the cost of serving bubble tea at the Mongkok shop is higher.	(2 marks)
(ii)	Yes. The cost of providing gas to the elderly and non-elderly is the same.		(2 marks)
(iii)	No. Bread freshness drops during the day. Fresh bread and stale (不新鮮) bread are not the same good to consumers. Moreover, all customers receive the 30% discount after 7 pm.	(2 marks)
(iv)	Yes. The cost of selling meat to a frequent customer is the same as that of selling to a non-frequent customer.	(2 marks)

(b)	In cases (ii) and (iv), the sellers can practise price discrimination because the following conditions are satisfied:
•	The sellers have monopoly power
•	The markets are separable
•	The sellers have low information costs
•	Buyers have different demand elasticities
(Any TWO of the above, 2 marks ( 2 = 4 marks)

(c)	No. Whether it is profitable to practise price discrimination depends on the benefits and costs of doing so. Even if the information cost and transaction cost are low in both cases, it is still not profitable to do so if the costs outweigh the benefits.	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B4 · Ch419 · Monopoly pricing
questions.text:
Every year, a Lunar New Year fair is held at Victoria Park. At the fair, a wide variety of merchandise like flowers, toys, Feng Shui products, etc., can be found. Suppose many small stalls sell a Feng Shui product called Pixius (貔貅). Pixius is a durable good.
(a)	Different stalls at the fair sell Pixius at different prices. Does this constitute price discrimination? Explain your answer.	(3 marks)
*(b)	A stall lowers the price of Pixius on the last day of the fair. Does this constitute price discrimination? Explain your answer.	(4 marks)
(c)	A stall sells Pixius to different customers at different prices at a particular time during the fair. Does this constitute price discrimination? Explain your answer.		(3 marks)
(d)	List THREE conditions for price discrimination.	(3 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	No. This is because different shops have different costs. They may source Pixius from different suppliers. Moreover, their rental and wage expenses are different.		(3 marks)

(b)	No. The Pixius products that have not yet been sold at the fair have to be transported to and stored in other places. Since additional costs and effort are being incurred to sell them later, the future return is lower. The opportunity cost of selling a Pixius at the fair is the return of selling the Pixius after the fair. As the end of the fair gets closer, the likelihood of selling the stock at the original price is lower and lower, and the cost of selling Pixius at the fair decreases. Moreover, all customers on the last day of the fair can buy Pixius at the lower price. They are not charged different prices.	(4 marks)

(c)	Yes. The cost at the same stall of selling Pixius to different customers should be the same at a particular time during the fair. Thus, the price difference is not due to the cost.	(3 marks)


(d)	Conditions for price discrimination:
•	Monopoly power
•	Separable market
•	Different demand elasticities
•	Low information costs for the seller
•	Buyers have different information costs
(Any THREE of the above, 1 mark ( 3 = 3 marks)

questions.topic: B4 · Ch419 · Monopoly pricing
questions.text:
Toda Island is a remote and isolated island. Mr Villa is able to get all of the fishermen on the island to work for him. His company is now the only supplier of fish on Toda Island.
(a)	The following diagram shows the demand and marginal cost (MC) curves that 
Mr Villa's company faces.
	
	Suppose the company adopts simple monopoly pricing.
	(i)	Show the profit-maximising output and monopoly price on the above figure. Explain your answer briefly.	(5 marks)
	(ii)	Indicate the efficient output and deadweight loss on the above figure. Explain the cause of the deadweight loss.	(3 marks)
(b)	Mr Villa has discovered the country of Redland, located on a continent, and set up branches there. Production costs in Redland and on Toda Island are the same. The company now charges the same prices in both places. 'To make more profit, I can charge every consumer the maximum amount that he is willing to pay for each extra unit of my product,' Mr Villa said.

	(i)	Which type of price discrimination is Mr Villa talking about? Explain why it is difficult to carry out this type of price discrimination.	(2 marks)
	(ii)	Suppose consumers on Toda Island are isolated from those in Redland and that the demand for fishery products in Redland is less elastic than it is on Toda Island. Suggest a type of price discrimination and briefly explain how it should be carried out.	(3 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	
	(i)	Indicate on the diagram:
		(	Correct marginal revenue curve	(1 mark)
		(	Profit-maximising output	(1 mark)
		(	Monopoly price	(1 mark)
		Verbal elaboration:
		The company will produce at the output level where MR is equal to MC.
			(1 mark)
		The company will use the demand curve to determine the monopoly price at the profit-maximising output level.	(1 mark)
	(ii)	Indicate on the diagram:
		(	Efficiency output	(1 mark)
		(	Deadweight loss	(1 mark)
		Verbal elaboration:
		The deadweight loss is caused by underproduction as output is lower than the efficient level.	(1 mark)


(b)	(i)	First-degree price discrimination.	(1 mark)
		It is very costly to find information about each buyer's demand curve.
	(1 mark)
	(ii)	Third-degree price discrimination.	(1 mark)
		Mr Villa should sell less and charge a higher price in Redland and sell more and charge a lower price on Toda Island.	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B4 · Ch419 · Monopoly pricing
questions.text:
Roberto has a monopoly on salt in a small coastal city in the country of Nephalem. He faces the following demand schedule. 

Price ($)	Output (units)	
48	1	
42	2	
36	3	
30	4	
24	5	
18	6	

The marginal cost is constant at $12 and the total fixed cost is $10.
(a)	Find the profit-maximising output and the corresponding price and profit.
	(6 marks)
(b)	Define price discrimination.	(2 marks)
(c)	List TWO conditions of price discrimination.	(2 marks)
(d)	Over time, Roberto has become the only salt seller in Nephalem. Roberto's production bases are in the eastern coastal region. Explain whether the following behaviours necessarily constitute price discrimination.
	(i)	Roberto sells salt in the western region of Nephalem at a higher price than in the eastern region.	(3 marks)
	(ii)	Roberto offers a discount to restaurants which buy in large quantities.
	(3 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	
Price ($)	Output (units)	MR ($)	MC ($)	
48	1	48	12	
42	2	36	12	
36	3	24	12	
30	4	12	12	
24	5	0	12	
18	6	-12	12	
		(2 marks for marginal revenue)
	The profit-maximising output is 4 units where MR = MC = $12.	(1 mark)
	The monopoly price = $30	(1 mark)
	The corresponding profit = TR - TC = $120 - ($48 + $10) = $62	(2 marks)

(b)	Price discrimination is the practice of charging different buyers different prices for the same good for reasons other than differences in costs.	(2 marks)

(c)	(	The seller has monopoly power
	(	Separable market
	(	Different demand elasticities
	(	Low information costs for the seller
	(	Buyers have different information costs
	(Any TWO of the above, 1 mark × 2 = 2 marks)

(d)	(i)	No.	(1 mark)
		The price difference may be due to the extra cost of transporting salt from production bases in the eastern region to the western region.	(2 marks)
	(ii)	No.	(1 mark)
		As the restaurants buy salt in large quantities, Roberto may enjoy economies of scale when supplying those restaurants. Therefore, the discount may be due to lower production costs.	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B4 · Ch420 · Anti-competitive behaviours
questions.text:
(a)	What are the possible motives of anti-competitive behaviours? Explain ONE of them.	(2 marks)
(b)	How do anti-competitive behaviours affect different parties in the market? Give TWO effects.	(2 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Firms may engage in anti-competitive behaviours to increase their market power and thus increase their profits. (Accept other reasonable answers.)	(2 marks)
(b)	Anti-competitive behaviours may restrict market competition, increase market prices, reduce output, reduce consumers' choices, and reduce consumer surpluses. (Any TWO of the above or other reasonable answers, 1 mark ( 2 = 2 marks)

questions.topic: B4 · Ch420 · Anti-competitive behaviours
questions.text:
(a)	What are horizontal agreements?	(1 mark)
(b)	Suppose Wellcome, China Resources Vanguard and ParkNShop, the three leading supermarket chains, colluded to set minimum prices for their products. Into which type of horizontal agreement did they enter? What would the effects of this type of horizontal agreement be?	(4 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Horizontal agreements are agreements among competitors in the same market to restrict competition.	(1 mark)
(b)	This is price-fixing or a price agreement.	(1 mark)
	The supermarket chains can avoid price competition among themselves.	(1 mark)
	Prices can be raised.	(1 mark)
	Therefore, the supermarket chains can earn higher profits.	(1 mark)

questions.topic: B4 · Ch420 · Anti-competitive behaviours
questions.text:
(a)	How can firms increase profits by entering into an output agreement?	(2 marks)
*(b)	What condition would make an output agreement effective?	(3 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Under an output agreement, firms can jointly restrict total output in order to raise the price of a good. As a result, they can earn more profit.	(2 marks)
(b)	As the price under an output agreement is higher, a firm is able to earn more profit by selling more output secretly at the agreed higher price. If any firm does so, the total output level will increase beyond the quota level. The price will then fall below the agreed price. Therefore, for an output agreement to be effective, members of the cartel should be able to prevent individual members from selling more than the quota.	(3 marks)

questions.topic: B4 · Ch420 · Anti-competitive behaviours
questions.text:
(a)	What will the effects be if competitors in a market enter into a market allocation agreement?	(2 marks)
(b)	Why didn't major electrical appliance retailers in Hong Kong form a cartel and divide the market? Give TWO reasons.	(4 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	If competitors in a market enter into a market allocation agreement, they divide the market and agree not to compete with each other. This allows them to raise prices and earn more profit in their own markets.	(2 marks)
(b)	•	There are many small electrical appliance retailers in the market and free entry into the market. Hence, even if large retailers form a cartel, they may not be able to become monopolists in their own territories and increase prices.
	(2 marks)
	•	As Hong Kong is small, consumers are able to shop in different districts. Therefore, it is difficult for retailers to divide the market.	(2 marks)
	(Accept other reasonable answers.)

questions.topic: B4 · Ch420 · Anti-competitive behaviours
questions.text: What is bid-rigging? Why is it difficult for bidders to engage in bid-rigging in auctions for stalls at the Lunar New Year fair? Explain.	(4 marks)
questions.answerText:
Bid-rigging is an agreement among competitors to conspire in contract bidding, public tenders or auctions.	(1 mark)
It is difficult for bidders to engage in bid-rigging in auctions for stalls at the Lunar New Year fair because the auctions have many bidders. Moreover, the bidders are not associated with each other. Thus, it is costly for bidders to gather information from each other and to collude at the auctions.	(3 marks)

questions.topic: B4 · Ch420 · Anti-competitive behaviours
questions.text:
Country A has only two supermarket chains, Supermart and Smarket. Suppose a new supermarket chain, Smart from Country B, plans to enter the market. How can the existing supermarket chains block the new entrant by a joint boycott? Explain.
	(4 marks)
questions.answerText:
Joint boycotts refer to an agreement between competitors not to deal with other competitors, suppliers or buyers.	(1 mark)
Supermart and Smarket may join together to urge suppliers not to supply products to Smart. They can threaten not to buy products from the suppliers if the suppliers sell products to Smart. To avoid losing business from them, suppliers may accede to their request. This will make it difficult for Smart to enter the market in Country A.
			(3 marks)

questions.topic: B4 · Ch420 · Anti-competitive behaviours
questions.text:
The following describes certain practices of a large supermarket chain. Which anti-competitive behaviours do these behaviours constitute? Explain how the behaviours could restrict competition.
(a)	When customers buy a certain six-pack of milk, they will also receive two low-fat yogurt packs as gifts.	(2 marks)
(b)	The supermarket signs contracts with local pig farms. The pig farms can only sell their pigs to the supermarket.	(2 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Bundling	(1 mark)
	This raises the cost of buying milk from other small retailers.	(1 mark)
(b)	Exclusive dealing	(1 mark)
	This makes it difficult for other small retailers to obtain pigs.	(1 mark)

questions.topic: B4 · Ch420 · Anti-competitive behaviours
questions.text:
State the names of the following anti-competitive behaviours and determine whether each is a vertical agreement or a horizontal agreement.
(a)	Dairy farms jointly agree on the total amount of milk to be produced each month.
	(2 marks)
(b)	Some dairy farms agree to sell their milk to only one baby formula producer, but not to other producers.	(2 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Output agreement	(1 mark)
	Horizontal agreement	(1 mark)
(b)	Exclusive dealing	(1 mark)
	Vertical agreement	(1 mark)

questions.topic: B4 · Ch420 · Anti-competitive behaviours
questions.text:
(a)	What is the difference between horizontal agreements and vertical agreements?
	(2 marks)
(b)	Identify the type of the following anti-competitive behaviours. Also, classify each case into a horizontal or vertical agreement.	
	(i)	Some banks provide jointly agreed currency exchange rates to their customers.	(2 marks)
	(ii)	A mobile phone manufacturer forces retailers to buy mobile phone accessories along with mobile phones.	(2 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Horizontal agreements are agreements among competitors in the same production stage,	(1 mark)
	while vertical agreements are agreements among producers in different production stages.	(1 mark)

(b)	(i)	Price-fixing	(1 mark)
		Horizontal agreement	(1 mark)
	(ii)	Tie-in sales	(1 mark)
		Vertical agreement	(1 mark)

questions.topic: B4 · Ch420 · Anti-competitive behaviours
questions.text:
(a)	Explain whether forming a cartel is a horizontal agreement or a vertical agreement.	(2 marks)
(b)	Explain why it is NOT common for vegetable stalls to form a cartel in Hong Kong.	(3 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	This is a horizontal agreement	(1 mark)
	because a cartel is formed by competitors in the same market.	(1 mark)
(b)	Hong Kong has many vegetable stalls. Most are small scale and usually not associated with each other. Even if some stalls form a cartel, their market power would not be enough to influence market prices.	(3 marks)

questions.topic: B4 · Ch420 · Anti-competitive behaviours
questions.text:
(a)	Distinguish between vertical agreements and horizontal agreements.	(2 marks)
(b)	List TWO kinds of vertical agreements and TWO kinds of horizontal agreements.	(4 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Vertical agreements are agreements among producers in different stages of production (i.e., not competitors), while horizontal agreements are agreements among competitors in the same market.	(2 marks)

(b)	Vertical agreements:
•	Exclusive dealing
•	Exclusive territory
•	Resale (or retail) price maintenance
•	Tie-in sales or bundling
(Any TWO of the above, 1 mark × 2 = 2 marks)
Horizontal agreements:
•	Price-fixing
•	Output agreement
•	Market allocation
•	Bid-rigging
•	Joint boycotts
(Any TWO of the above, 1 mark × 2 = 2 marks)

questions.topic: B4 · Ch420 · Anti-competitive behaviours
questions.text: It has been reported that singers who have signed contracts with Television Broadcast Ltd (TVB) in Hong Kong are prohibited from performing and agreeing to do interviews in Cantonese on other TV channels like ATV, Cable TV and now TV. If this were true, to what kind of anti-competitive behaviour does this belong? Give TWO reasons that explain why those singers accept contracts with such harsh terms.		(5 marks)
questions.answerText:
This is exclusive dealing.	(1 mark)
Reasons:
•	TVB's market share in Hong Kong is exceptionally large. Rejecting the contract from TVB will significantly decrease the singers' exposure.	(2 marks)
•	Besides the money reward from performing on TVB, exposure on TVB can help singers advertise their related products, such as albums and books, etc.	(2 marks)
(Accept other reasonable answers.)

questions.topic: B4 · Ch420 · Anti-competitive behaviours
questions.text:
(a)	What is the meaning of exclusive territory? How does it affect market 
competition? Give ONE example of exclusive territory in real life. 	(4 marks)
(b)	Why do some manufacturers prefer to market their products by exclusive 
territory? Give TWO reasons.	(4 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Under an exclusive territory agreement, a reseller is given the exclusive right to sell a supplier's products within a particular territory.	(1 mark)
The reseller becomes an artificial monopolist in the corresponding territory and need not face competition from other resellers in the market. This reduces market competition.	(1 mark)
It is common practice for car manufacturers to assign a sole agent the sole right to sell their products in a particular territory. (Accept other reasonable examples.)		(2 marks)
(b)	Reasons:
•	They want to avoid competition among retailers so that the sole agent has a greater incentive to promote their products and provide better services to customers.
•	They want to prevent their competitors from free riding on their investment in distribution, such as advertising, promotion and retailer training, etc.
•	They want to create an entry barrier. New entrants need a huge amount of capital to invest in their own distribution channels.
(Any TWO of the above, each 2 marks. Accept other reasonable answers.)

questions.topic: B4 · Ch420 · Anti-competitive behaviours
questions.text: What is the major difference between market allocation and exclusive territory? Illustrate with ONE example of EACH type.	(6 marks)
questions.answerText:
Market allocation involves a horizontal agreement among competitors in the same market to divide markets, while exclusive territory involves a vertical agreement between a supplier and a reseller - the supplier gives the reseller the exclusive right to sell its products within a particular territory.	(2 marks)
When car retailers in China form a cartel to divide the Chinese market into different territories, this is an example of market allocation. (Accept other reasonable answers.)	(2 marks)
When a foreign car manufacturer enters into an agreement to give a local retailer the sole right to sell its products in China, this is an example of exclusive territory. (Accept other reasonable answers.)	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B4 · Ch420 · Anti-competitive behaviours
questions.text:
In Country H, three airline companies dominate the airline industry. Recently, the three airline companies raised their ticket prices over a long holiday. Paula said, 'These airline companies must be colluding to raise prices together. This is an anti-competitive practice.' Suggest TWO possible arguments against her comment.
	(4 marks)
questions.answerText:
(	During long holidays, the demand for air tickets increases. This may lead to a rise in ticket prices.
(	In an oligopoly, when an oligopolist adjusts its prices, others may follow. The resulting increase in ticket prices may not be due to collusion.
(	The three companies may not have a price agreement.
(Any TWO of the above or other reasonable answers, 2 marks × 2 = 4 marks)

questions.topic: B4 · Ch420 · Anti-competitive behaviours
questions.text:
* The following is a conversation between Judy and Julia about the digital camera market in Hong Kong.
Judy says, 'If the sole agents of all brands of digital cameras strictly impose a retail price maintenance policy, there should be no price difference for the same model of a digital camera sold at different shops.'
Julia agrees, 'Yes. Such a practice will completely avoid competition among retailers. The information cost for buyers is zero.'
Comment on Judy and Julia's statements.	(6 marks)
questions.answerText:
Their statements are both wrong.
Under retail price maintenance, the manufacturer or the sole agent of a product may impose a minimum price on the product.	(1 mark)
Hence, although retail price maintenance is practised, the prices of digital cameras can be higher than the 'recommended prices' set by the sole agents. The price of the same model of a digital camera may be different at different shops in Hong Kong.	(2 marks)
There may be non-price competition among retailers, though price competition is avoided. For example, retailers offer gifts like memory cards and additional accessories to their customers. Hence, buyers may still have to gather information about the gifts offered by the retailers. 	(3 marks)
(Accept other reasonable answers.)

questions.topic: B4 · Ch420 · Anti-competitive behaviours
questions.text:
'Tie-in sales harm consumers.'
(a)	Give reasons to support this statement.	(2 marks)
(b)	Give reasons to argue against this statement.	(2 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Through the practice of tie-in sales, a supplier may extend its monopoly power from one product to another product. As a result, consumers have fewer choices and may effectively pay a higher price for the tied product.	(2 marks)
(b)	With tie-in sales, buyers may benefit from saving on the cost of searching for complementary products. Moreover, especially for some high-tech products (such as digital cameras), there is quality assurance when complementary products, such as batteries and lenses, are supplied by the original manufacturers.	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B4 · Ch420 · Anti-competitive behaviours
questions.text:
JTL is the leading jewellery producer in Country P. The jewellery market in 
Country P is oligopolistic. JTL is now planning to expand its business by the following mergers. Identify the type of each of the mergers and explain how they may be anti-competitive.
(a)	JTL acquires the second largest jewellery producer in Country P.	(4 marks)
(b)	JTL acquires a major diamond mine in Country P.	(4 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Horizontal merger	(1 mark)
	After the acquisition, the number of firms decreases and JTL's market share increases. Market competition may decrease. JTL may have greater market power to raise prices and earn a monopoly profit.	(3 marks)
(b)	Vertical (backward) merger	(1 mark)
	JTL may prevent its competitors from obtaining inputs from the diamond mine. Hence, JTL may face less competition. It can raise the prices of its jewellery and earn a monopoly profit.	(3 marks)

questions.topic: B4 · Ch420 · Anti-competitive behaviours
questions.text:
Suppose three beverage (飲料) companies in China merged into one single company.
(a)	Which type of anti-competitive practice could this be? Explain how the arrangement could restrain competition.	(3 marks)
(b)	Some say the arrangement does not necessarily harm consumers. Explain, giving ONE reason.	(3 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Horizontal merger	(1 mark)
	As the number of beverage companies in China decreases, competition in China's beverage market may decrease.	(2 marks)
(b)	If the three beverage companies were not large scale, the combined company may enjoy economies of scale. This may lower its production cost and raise its competitiveness. In this case, competition may be enhanced.	(3 marks)

questions.topic: B4 · Ch420 · Anti-competitive behaviours
questions.text: Suppose Sun Hung Kai Properties Ltd, Cheung Kong (Holdings) Ltd and Henderson Land Development Co Ltd merge. What type of merger is this? How will this affect consumers?	(4 marks)
questions.answerText:
This is a horizontal merger.	(1 mark)
This will reduce the number of firms in the market and thus reduce market competition.	(1 mark)
The combined firm may have greater market power to raise prices and to earn a monopoly profit. Also, it becomes easier for the remaining firms to collude as the number of firms decreases after the merger. As a result, consumers may have to pay higher prices.	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B4 · Ch420 · Anti-competitive behaviours
questions.text:
* Some restaurants only offer set meals on special days, such as Christmas and Easter holidays. Customers are not allowed to order à la carte (i.e., ordering dishes individually). 
(a)	Is this arrangement an example of tie-in sales? Why?	(2 marks)
(b)	Must this arrangement harm consumers? Give TWO reasons.	(4 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	This arrangement is an example of tie-in sales. This is because consumers who want to have one part of a set meal (say, the main course) are required to order all the other dishes in the same set (say, soup, salad and dessert).	(2 marks)
(b)	This arrangement does not necessarily harm consumers. Reasons:
•	Restaurants generally do not have sufficient market power and consumers have many choices. Consumers can choose to dine at restaurants that do not have such an arrangement. As a result, restaurants cannot effectively raise prices by this arrangement.
•	Because of the benefits of economies of scale, it is generally less costly to provide only set meals on peak days (such as Christmas and Easter holidays) than providing many different kinds of dishes. If the restaurants pass some of the cost savings on to consumers, consumers can benefit from lower prices.
•	Demand for a restaurant's services increases on peak days (such as Christmas and Easter holidays). Even if the prices of set meals increase on peak days, we cannot tell whether the price increase is due to an increase in demand or the arrangement. Hence, we cannot conclude that the arrangement must harm consumers.
(Any TWO of the above, each 2 marks. Accept other reasonable answers.)

questions.topic: B4 · Ch420 · Anti-competitive behaviours
questions.text:
Bazaar is the biggest supermarket chain in City Q. It has recently expanded into selling fresh meat and vegetables.
(a)	If Bazaar sells these products at prices lower than its costs, in what anti-competitive behaviour is Bazaar engaging?	(1 mark)
(b)	Why does Bazaar use the strategy in (a) even though it is losing money?		(3 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Predatory pricing	(1 mark)
(b)	This strategy can attract customers and may eventually drive other competitors out of the market. Afterward, Bazaar's market power increases, and it can increase prices to make more of a profit.	(3 marks)

questions.topic: B4 · Ch420 · Anti-competitive behaviours
questions.text:
T Company and S Company are two manufacturers of interchangeable lenses for major brands of digital single-lens reflex cameras (DSLRs). They have market shares totalling over 40%. The two companies decide to merge together in order to protect their market share. The new integrated company is called TS Company.
(a)	To what kind of merger does the merger of T and S belong?	(1 mark)
(b)	Are the following behaviours anti-competitive? Explain. If yes, to what kind of anti-competitive behaviours do they belong?
(i)	TS sells all of its lenses in a package with lens accessories, such as lens filters.	(2 marks)
(ii)	TS enters into an agreement with major DSLR manufacturers to adopt a technical standard for interchangeable lenses. This makes other manufacturers' lenses incompatible with major DSLRs in the market.
	(2 marks)
(iii)	TS enters into an agreement with a manufacturer of optical glass (an integral part of lenses). The manufacturer agrees to supply a newly developed optical glass solely to the company for three years.	(2 marks)
(iv)	TS slashes the prices of its lenses after the merger. The prices are still higher than the production costs.	(2 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Horizontal merger.	(1 mark)
(b)	(i)	Yes. It belongs to tie-in sales. Consumers who buy lenses from TS are required to buy lens accessories.	(2 marks)
(ii)	Yes. It belongs to discriminatory standards. The technical standard adopted by TS and major DSLR manufacturers makes it difficult for other lens manufacturers to compete with TS.	(2 marks)
(iii)	Yes. It belongs to exclusive dealing. The newly developed optical glass is solely supplied to TS and it is solely used on TS lenses.	(2 marks)
(iv)	It is not necessarily an anti-competitive behaviour. After the merger, TS may enjoy economies of scale as its scale of production becomes larger. It is possible that the company would slashes prices because of a decrease in its production costs.	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B4 · Ch420 · Anti-competitive behaviours
questions.text:
Hong Kong has passed the Competition Ordinance.
(a)	Briefly explain the first and second conduct rules of the Competition Ordinance.
	(4 marks)
(b)	Give ONE anti-competitive behaviour that EACH of the above conduct rules may regulate.	(2 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	First conduct rule: prohibits agreements, concerted practices and concerted decisions that prevent, restrict or distort competition in Hong Kong.	(2 marks)
	Second conduct rule: prohibits a firm with a substantial degree of market power from abusing that power to prevent, restrict or distort competition in Hong Kong.	(2 marks)
(b)	First conduct rule: price fixing / output agreement / market allocation / bid-rigging	(1 mark)
	Second conduct rule: predatory pricing / tie-in sales / cross-subsidisation / exclusive dealing	(1 mark)
	(Accept other reasonable answers.)

questions.topic: B4 · Ch420 · Anti-competitive behaviours
questions.text:
Hong Kong's jewellery gold prices are set by jewellers' and goldsmiths' associations. These prices are then followed by almost every jewellery shop in Hong Kong.
(a)	Which type of anti-competitive practice might this be? Explain.	(2 marks)
(b)	If the above case constitutes an anti-competitive behaviour, is it a horizontal agreement or a vertical agreement? Explain.	(2 marks)
(c)	Which conduct rule in Hong Kong's Competition Ordinance might the above practice violate? Explain.	(2 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Price fixing	(1 mark)
	Jewellery shops buy or sell jewellery gold at predetermined prices.	(1 mark)
(b)	Horizontal agreement	(1 mark)
	This is an agreement among competitors in the same market.	(1 mark)
(c)	First conduct rule	(1 mark)
	The first conduct rule prohibits agreements that prevent competition in Hong Kong, such as price-fixing agreements.	(1 mark)



Structured Questions

questions.topic: B4 · Ch420 · Anti-competitive behaviours
questions.text:
Refer to the following demand curve (D) faced by a monopolist and the monopolist's marginal cost curve (MC).

(a)	Indicate the consumer surplus under simple monopoly pricing on the above diagram. Briefly explain your answer.	(4 marks)
(b)	Suppose the demand curve and marginal cost curve does not change when the market becomes perfectly competitive. Use the same diagram in (a) to explain how a monopoly harms consumers.	(5 marks)
(c)	Suppose property developers in Hong Kong engage in the following practices. Classify the anti-competitive behaviours and state which conduct rule of the Competition Ordinance may regulate such behaviours.
	(i)	Some property developers predetermine the winner in land auctions.	(2 marks)
	(ii)	Some property developers jointly establish standard prices for newly built flats.	(2 marks)
	(iii)	Some property developers require flat buyers to use the interior design companies they recommend.	(2 marks)
(d)	State ONE objective of Hong Kong's Competition Ordinance.	(1 mark)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Indicate on the diagram:
	•	Correct marginal revenue (MR) curve	(1 mark)
	•	Consumer surplus (shaded area)	(1 mark)
	
Verbal elaboration:
The monopolist will produce where MR = MC. The profit-maximising price and quantity are PM and QM, respectively. The consumer surplus is the shaded area on the diagram.	(2 marks)


(b)	Indicate on the diagram:
	•	MC curve as the supply curve in a perfectly competitive market	(1 mark)
	•	Increase in consumer surplus (dotted area)	(1 mark)

	
	Verbal elaboration:
	Under a perfectly competitive market, the marginal cost curve is the market supply curve. The price decreases to PC while the quantity increases to QC. The consumer surplus increases as shown by the dotted area. This illustrates that a monopoly harms consumers because the consumer surplus is smaller in the case of a monopoly.	(3 marks)

(c)	(i)	Bid-rigging	(1 mark)
		First conduct rule	(1 mark)
	(ii)	Price fixing	(1 mark)
		First conduct rule	(1 mark)
	(iii)	Tie-in sales	(1 mark)
		Second conduct rule	(1 mark)

(d)	•	To prohibit and deter firms in all economic sectors from engaging in conduct that prevents, restricts or distorts competition in Hong Kong
	•	To prohibit mergers that substantially restrict competition in Hong Kong
	•	To establish a Competition Commission and a Competition Tribunal
	(Any ONE of the above, 1 mark)

questions.topic: B4 · Ch420 · Anti-competitive behaviours
questions.text:
HO is the sole printer producer on EP Island. HO also produces printer ink. HO faces the following demand curve for its printer ink.

(a)	Indicate the price, quantity and producer surplus under simply monopoly pricing.	(4 marks)
(b)	What is price discrimination?	(2 marks)
(c)	Determine whether each of the following HO practices necessarily constitutes price discrimination. Explain your answer.
(i)	HO provides a 'buy two, get one free' special offer for its ink cartridges.
	(3 marks)
(ii)	HO sells its own ink cartridges at higher prices on EP Island than in other countries.	(3 marks)
(d)	Suppose HO printers can only accept HO's ink cartridges. No compatible (代用) ink cartridges can be used.
(i)	Which anti-competitive behaviour is HO practicing? Explain how the practice can be 'anti-competitive'.	(2 marks)
(ii)	Which conduct rule of Hong Kong's Competition Ordinance can possibly regulate this kind of behaviour? Explain.	(2 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Indicate on the diagram:
	•	Correct marginal revenue (MR) curve	(1 mark)
	•	Profit-maximising output (QM)	(1 mark)
	•	Monopoly price (PM)	(1 mark)
	•	Producer surplus (shaded area)	(1 mark)
	

(b)	Price discrimination is the practice of charging different buyers different prices for the same good for reasons other than a difference in costs.	(2 marks)

(c)	(i)	Not necessarily.	(1 mark)
		All customers can enjoy the same discount.	(2 marks)
	(ii)	Not necessarily.	(1 mark)
		It may be due to price competition in other countries. 
OR: The costs of selling ink cartridges in other countries may be lower.
	(2 marks)

(d)	(i)	Unfair or discriminatory standards	(1 mark)
		Ink cartridges from other producers (compatible ink cartridges) cannot be used on HO printers. Therefore, HO will not face competition from other printer ink producers.	(1 mark)

	(ii)	Second conduct rule	(1 mark)
		This regulates the behaviour that extends monopoly power from one market (the printer market) to another (the printer ink market).	(1 mark)

questions.topic: B4 · Ch420 · Anti-competitive behaviours
questions.text:
* Rice is the major food and also agricultural product of Qinland. In the past, rice farmers in Qinland were small and not associated with each other. However, they all joined together recently to form a cartel and have entered into an output agreement.
(a)	Study the following diagram and answer the questions.
	
	Use the diagram above to:
	(i)	show the equilibrium price and quantity before the cartel was formed;
	(2 marks)
	(ii)	explain how the cartel set its output level and indicate the price it will set;
	(5 marks)
	(iii)	explain the loss of consumers due to the output agreement.	(3 marks)
(b)	Suppose several members leave the cartel and no longer follow the output agreement.
	(i)	What is the effect on the cartel?	(2 marks)
	(ii)	Suggest and describe ONE anti-competitive practice that the cartel may take to drive the members who have left out of the market.	(4 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)
	
	(i)	Indicate on the diagram:
Equilibrium price (Pc) and equilibrium quantity (Qc) in a perfectly competitive market (determined by the intersection between the MC and MB curves)
	(2 marks)
	(ii)	Indicate on the diagram:
(	Profit-maximising output level (Qm)	(1 mark)
(	Monopoly price (Pm)	(1 mark)
		Verbal elaboration:
		To maximise their profits, cartel members would determine the output level in the same way as a monopolist.	(1 mark)
		The output is set at a level where MR = MC.	(1 mark)
		The price at the corresponding output level is set according to the demand curve.	(1 mark)
	(iii)	Indicate on the diagram:
		The reduction in the consumer surplus	(1 mark)
		Verbal elaboration:
		Due to the output agreement, consumers enjoy less rice and pay a higher price. The reduction in the consumer surplus is equal to the shaded area.	(2 marks)

(b)	(i)	The total output in the market will be more than that under the output agreement. The market price will then fall below the monopoly price. So, the profit for the cartel will decrease.	(2 marks)

	(ii)	Joint boycott	(1 mark)
		The cartel may urge distributors not to distribute products from the members who have left. This would greatly affect those former members' revenues. They may suffer losses and eventually have to leave the market.	(3 marks)
		(Accept other reasonable answer with elaboration.)

questions.topic: B4 · Ch420 · Anti-competitive behaviours
questions.text:
In the New Territories, China Light & Power Company (CLP) is the only electricity supplier. 
(a)	With the help of two diagrams, compare the above situation and the situation when the electricity market becomes perfectly competitive in terms of the market price, output level, consumer surplus and efficiency. (Assume that the marginal cost curve of CLP is upward sloping, the demand and cost curves in both situations are the same, and there is no government regulation.)	(8 marks)
(b)	Suppose the HKSAR government invites new investors to enter the market. If CLP asked coal suppliers not to sell coal to the new entrant, discuss whether this would possibly violate Hong Kong's Competition Ordinance. If yes, which conduct rule(s) might be violated?	(3 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)

The current electricity market in the New Territories is a monopoly. The market price (Pm) will be higher and the output level (Qm) will be smaller than the situation under perfect competition.	(2 marks)
As a result, in a monopoly, the consumer surplus is smaller and resource allocation is inefficient.	(2 marks)

(b)	Yes. In this case, a firm which has a substantial degree of market power has possibly abused the power to restrict competition in Hong Kong.	(2 marks)
	This might violate the second conduct rule.	(1 mark)

questions.topic: B4 · Ch420 · Anti-competitive behaviours
questions.text:
The petroleum retailing industry in Liberty City is divided among RON, Terroil and Globe Oil. They also operate convenience stores at their gas stations. Some residents of Liberty City have accused the three companies of engaging in anti-competitive practices.
(a)	In the following, identify the types of anti-competitive practices and explain how the companies gain from those practices.
	(i)	RON stations are located in the northern and western part of Liberty City, while Terroil and Globe Oil stations are in the southern and eastern part of the City.	(3 marks)
	(ii)	They use the revenue earned from selling petrol to subsidise their convenience store business.	(3 marks)
(b)	RON's CEO said, 'Our practices may be anti-competitive, but consumers can benefit.' Of the practices stated in (a), give ONE reason for each to explain why consumers may benefit.	(4 marks)
(c)	How do anti-competitive behaviours harm consumers in general? List THREE effects.	(3 marks)
(d)	Suppose an oilfield was discovered recently in the countryside of Liberty City. The government auctions off the right to extract the oil. The three companies are the only bidders. Each has agreed that Terroil will win the bid.
	(i)	Identify the type of the above anti-competitive practice.	(1 mark)
	(ii)	How can the companies gain?	(2 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	(i)	Market allocation.	(1 mark)
		Each company becomes a monopolist in its assigned territory. The companies can raise prices and earn a monopoly profit in their own territories.	(2 marks)
	(ii)	Cross-subsidisation.	(1 mark)
		Petroleum retailers can set lower prices at their convenient stores. This can increase the competitiveness of their convenience stores.	(2 marks)

(b)	Market allocation provides the companies with incentives to advertise and promote new products. As they are the only seller in each territory, they can capture all the benefits from product promotions.	(2 marks)
	Under cross-subsidisation, prices at the petroleum retailers' convenience stores are lower. Consumers can enjoy larger consumer surpluses.	(2 marks)

(c)	Consumers will have fewer choices. They may have to pay higher prices but consume a smaller quantity. As a result, their consumer surpluses will decrease.
	(Any THREE of the above or other reasonable answers, 1 mark ( 3 = 3 marks)

(d)	(i)	Bid-rigging	(1 mark)
	(ii)	The bid price will be lower under collusion. Terroil can earn an extra profit. The three companies will then share the extra profit.	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B4 · Ch420 · Anti-competitive behaviours
questions.text:
(a)	What kind(s) of anti-competitive behaviour does each of the following involve?
(i)	A French winery asks retailers in Hong Kong to sell its wines at a price not lower than the recommended price.	(2 marks)
(ii)	A wine importer becomes the sole agent of an Australian brand of wine in Hong Kong.	(2 marks)
(iii)	Wine retailers in Hong Kong form a guild (同業公會) and ask suppliers not to supply goods to any non-members of the guild.	(2 marks)
(iv)	A French grape grower grows a new type of grape of exceptionally high quality. The grower will sell his grapes to only one buyer who accepts his harsh policies. A nearby winery agrees and signs a contract with him.
 	(2 marks)
(b)	'The practices described in (a)(i) and (a)(iv) harm consumers.' Evaluate this statement.	(6 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	(i)	It involves resale (or retail) price maintenance. Minimum prices for the wines are imposed by the winery.	(2 marks)
(ii)	It involves exclusive territory. The wine importer is given the sole right to sell the Australian brand of wine in Hong Kong.	(2 marks)
(iii)	It involves a joint boycott. The retailers enter into an agreement to request that suppliers not deal with other retailers. 	(2 marks)
(iv)	It involves exclusive dealing. The grape grower agrees to sell the grapes to one winery only.	(2 marks)
(b)	For case (a)(i)
	Resale price maintenance may harm consumers because the minimum price paid by consumers may be higher than the competitive one.	(3 marks)
	OR
	The practice may benefit consumers because it saves on the cost of searching for price information about the wines. If the cost is greater than the extra money consumers need to pay due to resale price maintenance, consumers gain from the practice. Hence, it is hard to say resale price maintenance harms consumers.
	(3 marks)
	For case (a)(iv)
	Exclusive dealing may harm consumers because competition among wineries can be avoided. The winery may charge a higher price and consumers may need to pay a higher price for the wines.	(3 marks)
	OR
	This may not harm consumers. The exclusive dealing provides a greater incentive for the winery to put more effort into developing new products with the new grapes. This may benefit consumers.	(3 marks)
(Accept other reasonable answers.)

questions.text:

questions.topic: B5 · Ch501 · What is economics?
questions.text:
Which of the following about gross domestic product (GDP) is correct?
A.	GDP includes the value of all unpaid household services.
B.	GDP represents the total amount of all transactions in an economy.
C.	The GDP of an economy represents the total value of final products produced by all resident producing units of the economy in a specified period.
D.	The total market value of Hang Seng Bank is included in Hong Kong's GDP.

questions.topic: B5 · Ch501 · What is economics?
questions.text:
Which of the following items is NOT included in Hong Kong's GDP?
A.	Government spending on civil servants' pay
B.	Government spending on old age allowances
C.	Commissions received by a property agent in a transaction
D.	Trading fees charged by HKEx for transactions through its stock exchange
questions.answerText:
Option A is included in the GDP as government consumption expenditure. Option B is a transfer payment and so is not included in the GDP.
Option D is the expenditure on services provided by the stock exchange and should be included in the GDP.

questions.topic: B5 · Ch501 · What is economics?
questions.text:
Which of the following items is included in the GDP?
A.	A businessman's donation to a political party for an election campaign
B.	A student's expense for a new dictionary
C.	The profits made from buying and selling bonds in Hong Kong
D.	The income gained from selling a used computer on the internet

questions.topic: B5 · Ch501 · What is economics?
questions.text:
Which of the following should be included in Hong Kong's GDP in the current year?
A.	The money received by a school-leaver who sold his old textbooks this year
B.	The value of banknotes issued by HSBC this year
C.	The value of unsold textbooks printed in Hong Kong this year
D.	The wages of the ground crew (地勤人員) employed by Cathay Pacific at the Beijing airport

questions.topic: B5 · Ch501 · What is economics?
questions.text:
Sharon is a Hong Kong resident. Which of the following items should be included in Hong Kong's GDP?
A.	Her revenue from reselling an unused iPhone to a mainlander
B.	The old age allowance she receives from the Government

D.	Her expenditure on her daughter's wedding jewellery

questions.topic: B5 · Ch501 · What is economics?
questions.text:
Amy is a Hong Kong resident and works in the mainland. Which of the following items should be included in Hong Kong's GDP?
A.	The commission she earns from a transaction involving a mainland property
B.	The money she receives from selling her second-hand handbag on a Hong Kong auction site
C.	Her expenditure from eating Cantonese dishes in the mainland
D.	Her expenditure on a flight from Hong Kong to Shanghai on a Hong Kong airline

questions.topic: B5 · Ch501 · What is economics?
questions.text:
Mark is a Hong Kong investor. At the beginning of this year, he bought stocks through a mainland company that were worth $10 million on the Shanghai stock market. At the end of this year, he sold the stocks for $18 million. Which of the following statements is correct?
A.	The commission he paid to the mainland company should be included in Hong Kong's GDP.
B.	The $8 million capital gain should be included in Hong Kong's GDP.
C.	The above event may make no contribution to Hong Kong's GDP.
D.	The $10 million spent should be included in Hong Kong's GDP as Mark provided factor services to the company.

questions.topic: B5 · Ch501 · What is economics?
questions.text:
In measuring current GDP, past inventories produced by resident producing units are
A.	included as they are produced by resident producing units.

questions.text:
Which of the following is/are NOT counted in Hong Kong's GDP this year?

	(2)	The value of a second-hand book sold this year in Mong Kok
	(3)	Capital gains from buying La Chapelle shares issued in Hong Kong this year
	(4)	The unpaid salary of a salesperson last year that was collected this year
A.	(1) only
B.	(1) and (2) only
C.	(2) and (3) only
D.	(2), (3) and (4) only
questions.answerText: Option (4) is not counted in GDP this year because the labour service was provided last year.

questions.topic: B5 · Ch501 · What is economics?

questions.topic: B5 · Ch501 · What is economics?

questions.topic: B5 · Ch501 · What is economics?
questions.text:
Tom is an economics tutor who works at a tutorial centre in Hong Kong. Which of the following situations will LEAST likely affect Hong Kong's GDP?
A.	He prepares a new set of study notes and sells them to his students.
B.	He makes illegal copies of textbooks and sells them to his students.
C.	He constructs an advanced economic model for his own enjoyment.
D.	He pays for his girlfriend's dinner.
questions.answerText: Option C is excluded from GDP because it is regarded as unpaid services for self-consumption.

questions.topic: B5 · Ch501 · What is economics?
questions.text:
A Hong Kong resident won a large amount of money betting on the World Cup Final. Which of the following statements is correct?
A.	The money should be included in Hong Kong's GDP as it represents an increase in the disposable income of the Hong Kong resident.
B.	The money should be included in Hong Kong's GDP as the Hong Kong resident has earned a profit by taking a risk.

questions.topic: B5 · Ch501 · What is economics?
questions.text:

questions.topic: B5 · Ch501 · What is economics?
questions.text:
A local film company used $1 million to advertise its new film, which was subsidised by the Film Development Fund (電影發展基金). The money ________ be counted in GDP because ________.

B.	should … it represents a corresponding service provided by resident producing units in Hong Kong

questions.topic: B5 · Ch501 · What is economics?
questions.text:
In measuring GDP, the scholarship received by a secondary student from a tutoring school is
A.	included as it involves a market transaction.
B.	excluded as it only represents an income transfer.
C.	excluded as it leads to the problem of double counting.
D.	excluded as it benefits only one individual.

questions.topic: B5 · Ch501 · What is economics?
questions.text:
* Which of the following about government financial assistance for university students is INCORRECT?
A.	Interest charged on government loans is included in GDP.
B.	A student's expenditure on a European tour financed by government loans is included in GDP.
C.	The government financial assistance should be included in GDP.
D.	When a student uses part of his government grant to buy shares, the money invested should not be included in GDP.
questions.answerText:
Option A is a correct statement. Interest on government loans represents the value of financial services provided by the government and is included in GDP.
Option B is a correct statement. Although transfer payments themselves are not counted in GDP, expenditure on final products supported by transfer payments is counted.
Option D is a correct statement. Purchases of financial assets are excluded from GDP.

questions.topic: B5 · Ch501 · What is economics?
questions.text:

C.	should not be … the student is not a resident producing unit of Hong Kong

questions.topic: B5 · Ch501 · What is economics?
questions.text:
Manchester United, a British football team, was invited by the Hong Kong Football Association (HKFA) to play a friendly game with the Hong Kong Team in Hong Kong. Hong Kong people's expenditure on the tickets was ________ in Hong Kong's GDP because ________.

questions.topic: B5 · Ch501 · What is economics?
questions.text:
The construction of a housing estate was completed in January 2014. In March 2014, Mr Kwan bought one of the flats for $20 million and sold it in December 2014 for $15 million. As a result, GDP in 2014 would
A.	decrease by $5 million to reflect Mr Kwan's capital loss.
B.	increase by $20 million to reflect the value of the first transaction on the flat.
C.	increase by $35 million to reflect the value of all transactions involved.
D.	All of the above are incorrect.

questions.topic: B5 · Ch501 · What is economics?
questions.text:
In 2014, Romeo gave his $50,000 used watch to Juliet as her birthday gift. Unfortunately, she was robbed of the watch on the same day. When she told Romeo, he gave her $10,000 as compensation. As a result of the above events, GDP this year
A.	increased by $50,000.
B.	increased by $60,000.
C.	remained unchanged as no production was involved.
D.	decreased by $50,000.
questions.answerText: The value of the second-hand watch from Romeo was not counted in GDP as it was not the value of current production; when the watch was robbed, its contribution to GDP was not lost as it was already zero. The compensation was not counted in GDP as it was only a transfer of money.

questions.topic: B5 · Ch501 · What is economics?
questions.text:
In 2014, May injured her legs. The related medical expense was $10,000, but she received $8,000 in compensation from her insurance company. As a result of the above events, the 2014 GDP
A.	increased by $18,000.
B.	increased by $10,000.
C.	increased by $2,000.
D.	remained unchanged.
questions.answerText: The $10,000 medical expense was counted in the 2014 GDP, but the $8,000 compensation from the insurance company represented only an income transfer, which was not counted in GDP.

questions.topic: B5 · Ch501 · What is economics?

* In 2014, a bicycle manufacturer produced bicycles whose value amounts to $100,000. However, it only sold 80% of the bicycles for $80,000 in 2014. Which of the following statements about the effect of this event is correct?

questions.answerText:

questions.topic: B5 · Ch501 · What is economics?
questions.text:
* Which of the following about the GDP computed under the production approach is correct?
A.	It does not include the value of exported goods and services.
B.	It is equal to the sum of the revenues of all resident producing units.
C.	It can be greater than the GDP computed under the expenditure approach.
D.	It does not include the value of semi-finished products.
questions.answerText:
Option B is incorrect. The revenue of a resident producing unit includes the value of intermediate consumption. Thus, the sum of the revenues of all resident producing units will lead to the problem of double counting.
Option D is incorrect. If semi-finished products are the current production of resident producing units, they are counted in GDP.

questions.topic: B5 · Ch501 · What is economics?

What is the above production chain's contribution to Hong Kong's GDP?

C.	$8,800

questions.answerText:

$4,800 + $4,000 - $1,200 - $2,000 = $5,600
Value-added approach:
Value-added of the Hong Kong beverage manufacturer + Value-added of the Hong Kong fast food chain
= [($4,000 + $3,500) - ($1,200 + $2,000)] + ($4,800 - $3,500)
= $4,300 + $1,300
= $5,600

questions.text:
The following table shows the financial statement of an electrical shop in City T in a particular year.
	$	$	
Sales revenue of electric appliances		480,000	
Less:	Rent	50,000		
	Wages	40,000		
	Electricity and water charges	10,000		
	Imported electric appliances	120,000		
	Profits tax	39,000	259,000	
Net profit			221,000	
What is the electrical shop's contribution to the GDP of City T?
A.	$221,000
B.	$260,000
C.	$300,000
D.	$360,000
questions.answerText:
The items 'rent', 'electricity and water charges' and 'imported electric appliances' are values of intermediate consumption and should be deducted from the sales revenue of the electrical shop when calculating its contribution to the GDP.
The electrical shop's contribution to the GDP
= Net profit + Wages + Profits tax
(= Sales revenue - Rent - Electricity and water charges - Imported electric appliances)
= $221,000 + $40,000 + $39,000
= $300,000

questions.topic: B5 · Ch501 · What is economics?

A.	increased by $2,000,000.
B.	increased by $2,700,000.
C.	increased by $3,000,000.
D.	did not change as the new diamond ring was just compensation.
questions.answerText: The loss of the old ring would not affect GDP in 2014. The value of the new ring would be counted as current production for the year but the materials imported should be deducted from the value of the ring to reflect the value-added of the jewellery shop.

questions.topic: B5 · Ch501 · What is economics?
questions.text:
Mr Lee wins a Mark Six Prize of $500,000. He uses the prize money to buy stocks. At the end of the year, Mr Chan sells his stocks through a local investment company and his capital gain is $1,000,000.
a.	Explain whether the following items should be included in Hong Kong's GDP:
i.	The prize money of $500,000	(2 marks)
