	(i)	a medium of exchange.	(3 marks)
	(ii)	a store of value.	(3 marks)
questions.answerText:

	(1 mark)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch608 · Ownership of firms
questions.text:
(a)	What is the monetary base?	(2 marks)
(b)	Is the monetary base included in the money supply? Explain.	(4 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	The monetary base (M0) is the total amount of currency issued in an economy at a certain moment. This is held either by the non-bank public as cash (CP) or by the banking system as reserves (R), i.e., M0 = CP + R.	(2 marks)
(b)	Only part of the monetary base, i.e., the currency held by the non-bank public, is included in the money supply. This is because only this part of the monetary base is available to serve as a medium of exchange.	(2 marks)
	The other part is held by banks as reserves and is not the currency in public circulation. Since it is not available for use, this part of the monetary base is not included in the money supply.	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch608 · Ownership of firms
questions.text:
* 'When M1 increases, M2 and M3 must also increase immediately.'
Is the statement true? Explain with ONE example.	(6 marks)
questions.answerText:
(	False.	(1 mark)
(	If the increase in M1 occurs because of changes in other M2 components which are not included in M1, then both M2 and M3 will remain unchanged.	(1 mark)
(	If the increase in M1 occurs because of changes in other M3 components which are not included in M2, then M2 will increase but M3 will remain unchanged.
	(1 mark)
(	Any well-reasoned example	(3 marks)
Example: When a person withdraws money from his savings account, M1 increases as the amount of currency held by the public increases. However, since savings deposits decrease by the same amount, M2 remains unchanged. As there are no changes in M2 and the other components of M3, M3 remains unchanged.

Do you agree? Explain.	(3 marks)
questions.answerText: Disagree. This is because M1, M2 and M3 include currency held by the public, instead of the total amount of currency issued. If the newly issued currency is held by the banking system, it will not be included in M1, M2 and M3; hence, M1, M2 and M3 will not increase.	(3 marks)

questions.text:
The required reserve ratio in Country Q is 70%. Suppose the central bank increases the amount of currency issued by $1,000 billion. 
(a)	Explain why the increase in M1 can be smaller than $1,000 billion immediately after the issuance of currency.	(3 marks)
(b)	Explain why the increase in M1 can be larger than $1,000 billion.	(3 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Although the central bank increases the monetary base, part of this may be kept by banks as reserves. As this part of the increase in currency is not available for use, the increase in M1 can be smaller than $1,000 billion.	(3 marks)
(b)	The public may deposit the newly issued currency as demand deposits. Since banks are required to keep 70% of the deposits as reserves, they can loan the excess reserves. This results in deposit creation, and thus the increase in M1 can be larger than $1,000 billion.	(3 marks)

questions.answerText:

questions.text:

	(1 mark)

questions.text:

questions.text:
The following is the balance sheet of a banking system.

Assets ($)	Liabilities ($)	
Reserves	1,000	Deposits	4,000	
Loans	3,000			

Assume the required reserve ratio is 20% and there is no cash leakage.
(a)	Calculate the amount of excess reserves held by banks.	(2 marks)
(b)	Calculate the increase in the amount of loans after excess reserves are loaned.
		(4 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Excess reserves = Actual reserves - Required reserves
= $1,000 - ($4,000 × 20%) = $200	(2 marks)
(b)	Since there is no cash leakage and all excess reserves are loaned, the actual increase in loans is equal to the maximum increase in loans.	(1 mark)
	The increase in loans
	= Excess reserves at the beginning × (1 / Required reserve ratio)	(1 mark)
	= $200 × (1 / 20%) = $1,000	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch608 · Ownership of firms
questions.text:
The following is the balance sheet of a banking system. Banks hold $8 billion in excess reserves.

Assets ($ billion)	Liabilities ($ billion)	
Reserves	25	Deposits	85	
Loans	60			

(a)	What is the legal reserve ratio in the above banking system?	(3 marks)
(b)	What is the maximum increase in deposits if the banks lend all excess reserves? Briefly explain the assumption for this increase in addition to the one given in the question.	(5 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Required reserves = $(25 - 8) billion = $17 billion	(1 mark)
	Legal reserve ratio = ($17 billion ( $85 billion) ( 100% = 20%	(2 marks)
(b)	The maximum increase in deposits
	= Excess reserves at the beginning × (1 / Legal reserve ratio)	(1 mark)
	= $[8 × (1 / 20%)] billion = $40 billion	(2 marks)
We have to assume there is no cash leakage, i.e., all the loans will be redeposited into the banking system, so that the banking system has the maximum amount of money for further lending.	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch608 · Ownership of firms
questions.text:
The following is the balance sheet of a banking system.

Assets ($)	Liabilities ($)	
Reserves	500	Deposits	1,500	
Loans	1,000			

Suppose the required reserve ratio of the banking system is 30%.
(a)	Calculate the actual banking multiplier and maximum banking multiplier of this banking system. Is the total amount of deposits in this banking system maximised? Explain with your calculation results.	(3 marks)
(b)	After Miss Chan deposits $100 cash into a bank, all banks lend all excess reserves. Calculate the maximum change in the money supply.	(5 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Actual banking multiplier = $1,500 ( $500 = 3	(1 mark)
	Maximum banking multiplier = 1 ( 30% = 3.33	(1 mark)
The total amount of deposits in the banking system is not maximised because the actual banking multiplier is smaller than the maximum banking multiplier.
	(1 mark)
(b)	After Miss Chan deposits $100 into the bank, the banking system has $600 in reserves.	(1 mark)
Since the required reserve ratio is 30%, a reserve amount equal to $600 can at most support a deposit amount of $2,000 [= $600 × (1 / 30%)].	(2 marks)
	Hence, the maximum change in the money supply
	= Change in cash held by the public + Maximum change in deposits
	= -$100 + $(2,000 - 1,500) = +$400	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch608 · Ownership of firms
questions.text:
The following is the balance sheet of a banking system. Suppose banks hold $10 billion in excess reserves and the public always holds $5 billion in cash.

Assets ($ billion)	Liabilities ($ billion)	
Reserves	70	Deposits	150	
Loans	80			

(a)	What is the required reserve ratio in the above banking system?	(2 marks)
(b)	What is the maximum possible amount of money supply in the economy?
		(4 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Required reserves = $(70 - 10) billion = $60 billion	(1 mark)
	Required reserve ratio = ($60 billion ( $150 billion) ( 100% = 40%	(1 mark)
(b)	The maximum possible amount of deposits in the banking system
	= $[70 × (1 / 40%)] billion = $175 billion	(2 marks)
	The maximum possible amount of money supply in the economy
	= Cash held by the public + Maximum possible amount of deposits
	= $5 billion + $175 billion = $180 billion	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch608 · Ownership of firms
questions.text: * In Banking System Y, the actual banking multiplier is 2, which is smaller than the maximum banking multiplier by 0.5. Moreover, the banking system has $400 billion in deposits. If banks lend all their excess reserves, what is the maximum change in money supply in the banking system? Explain.	(6 marks)
questions.answerText:
Actual reserves = Deposits ( Actual banking multiplier
= $400 billion ( 2 = $200 billion	(1 mark)
If banks lend all their excess reserves, the maximum amount of reserves in the banking system is exactly the current amount of reserves, i.e., $200 billion.	(1 mark)
The maximum banking multiplier = 2 + 0.5 = 2.5	(1 mark)
A reserve amount equal to $200 billion can at most support a deposit amount of 
$500 billion (= $200 billion × 2.5).	(1 mark)
The maximum increase in deposits = $500 billion - $400 billion = $100 billion
	(1 mark)
As there is no change in cash held by the public, the maximum increase in money supply is also $100 billion.	(1 mark)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch608 · Ownership of firms
questions.text:
The following is the balance sheet of a banking system.
Assets ($)	Liabilities ($)	
Reserves	2,000	Deposits	10,000	
Loans	8,000			

Assume the legal reserve ratio in this banking system is 20%. Mr Chan withdraws $500 from a bank.
(a)	Calculate the amount of reserves that the banking system falls short of after 
Mr Chan's withdrawal.	(2 marks)
(b)	Calculate the maximum amount of total deposits in the banking system after 
the withdrawal.	(3 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	The amount of reserves that the banking system falls short of
	= [$(10,000 - 500) × 20%] - $(2,000 - 500) = $400	(2 marks)
(b)	After the $500 withdrawal, there remains a reserve amount equal to $1,500 only.
	(1 mark)
Since the legal reserve ratio is 20%, a reserve amount equal to $1,500 can at most support a deposit amount of $7,500 [= $1,500 × (1 / 20%)].	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch608 · Ownership of firms
questions.text:
The following is the balance sheet of a banking system. The required reserve ratio is 25%.

Assets ($)	Liabilities ($)	
Reserves	300	Deposits	1,000	
Loans	700			

(a)	What is the amount of excess reserves in this banking system?	(2 marks)
(b)	If the public withdraws $200 from the banking system, what is the maximum change in loans?	(5 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Excess reserves = Actual reserves - Required reserves
= $300 - ($1,000 × 25%) = $50	(2 marks)
(b)	After the withdrawal of $200, the amount of reserves the banking system falls short of
	= [$(1,000 - 200) ( 25%] - $(300 - 200) = $100	(2 marks)
	Hence, the banking system has to call back $100 in loans.	(1 mark)
	The maximum change in loans = -$100 ( (1 / 25%) = -$400	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch608 · Ownership of firms
questions.text:
The following is the balance sheet of Banking System X.

Assets ($)	Liabilities ($)	
Reserves	400	Deposits	1,000	
Loans	600			

The required reserve ratio is 10%. Suppose $150 is withdrawn from Banking System X by the public.
(a)	Calculate the maximum possible amount of deposits in Banking System X after the withdrawal.	(3 marks)
(b)	Briefly describe the deposit creation/contraction process in (a).	(5 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	After the withdrawal of $150, the amount of reserves decreases to $250.	(1 mark)
The maximum possible amount of deposits in Banking System X
= $250 × (1 / 10%) = $2,500	(2 marks)
(b)	After the withdrawal of $150, the amount of required reserves is $85 
[= $(1,000 - 150) ( 10%]. Therefore, the banking system has $165 in excess reserves (= $250 - $85).	(2 marks)
Suppose banks do not keep excess reserves and there is enough borrowing. They will lend all their excess reserves. Assuming no cash leakage, the loan will be redeposited into the banking system. This creates new deposits and excess reserves for further lending. This deposit creation process continues until the banking system has no excess reserves.	(3 marks)


Structured Questions

questions.topic: B6 · Ch608 · Ownership of firms
questions.text:
The following is the balance sheet of a banking system.

Assets ($)	Liabilities ($)	
Reserves	1,000	Deposits	4,000	
Loans	3,000			

Suppose the required reserve ratio is 0.1 and the public holds $2,000 in cash.
(a)	(i)	Define the monetary base.	(2 marks)
	(ii)	Calculate the monetary base of the economy.	(1 mark)
(b)	Explain why the monetary base is NOT the money supply.	(2 marks)
(c)	(i)	Calculate the excess reserves held by the banking system.	(2 marks)
	(ii)	Suppose banks loan all of their excess reserves. Calculate the maximum change in deposits of the banking system.	(2 marks)
(d)	The public deposits $1,000 into the banking system. Calculate the maximum possible amount of money supply.	(4 marks)
(e)	Besides holding excess reserves, list TWO situations in which the actual amount of deposits would be lower than the maximum possible amount.	(2 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	(i)	Monetary base (M0) is the total amount of currency issued in an economy at a certain moment.	(2 marks)
	(ii)	M0 = Cash held by public + Reserves in the banking system
		= $2,000 + $1,000
		= $3,000	(1 mark)

(b)	Only currency held by the public is available for use. Reserves held by banks are not in public circulation. Hence, cash held by the public is a component of the money supply but reserves are not. Therefore, the monetary base is not the money supply.	(2 marks)

(c)	(i)	Required reserves = $4,000 × 0.1 = $400	(1 mark)
		Excess reserves = $1,000 - $400 = $600	(1 mark)
	(ii)	Maximum possible amount of deposits 
		= $1,000 × (1 / 0.1) = $10,000	(1 mark)
		Maximum change in deposits = $10,000 - $4,000 = $6,000	(1 mark)

(d)	After the public deposits the money, reserves increase to $2,000.	(1 mark)
	Maximum possible amount of deposits = $2,000 × (1 / 0.1) = $20,000	(1 mark)
	Maximum possible amount of money supply
= Maximum amount of deposits + Cash held by the public
= $20,000 + $1,000
= $21,000	(2 marks)

(e)	Not enough demand for loans	(1 mark)
	Cash leakage to the public	(1 mark)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch608 · Ownership of firms
questions.text:
The following shows the balance sheet of the banking system in Hana City.

Assets ($)	Liabilities ($)	
Reserves	300	Deposits	3,000	
Loans	2,700			

Suppose the banking system is fully loaned up and the public never holds cash. The central bank announces that it will increase the required reserve ratio to 15%.
(a)	(i)	Describe the process of change in the money supply.	(4 marks)
	(ii)	Calculate the maximum change in money supply.	(2 marks)
(b)	Explain whether the monetary base changes.	(2 marks)
(c)	Mr To deposits $10 into one of the banks in Hana City. If the $10 comes from Mr To's withdrawals from another bank in Hana City, explain the effect on Hana City's money supply.	(2 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	(i)	Initially, the banking system has no excess reserves. It cannot meet the reserve requirement after the central bank increases the required reserve ratio. Hence, banks have to call back loans. The public has to withdraw money to pay back the loans. The amount of deposits and the money supply decrease.	(2 marks)
		As long as the banking system is short of reserves, it needs to call back loans. This causes further withdrawals and a decrease in deposits. The process of money contraction continues until the actual reserves are equal to the required reserves.	(2 marks)
	(ii)	Maximum possible amount of deposits
		= $300 × (1 / 15%) = $2,000	(1 mark)
		Maximum change in money supply
		= $2,000 - $3,000 = -$1,000	(1 mark)

(b)	No.	(1 mark)
	The change in the required reserve ratio does not cause changes in reserves held by banks and cash held by the public. (OR: The amount of currency issued is not affected.)	(1 mark)

(c)	The money supply does not change.	(1 mark)
	This is because money creation from the deposit is offset by money contraction from the withdrawal.	(1 mark)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch608 · Ownership of firms
questions.text:
Study the following information about Economy X in a certain year.

Items	$ million	
Currency held by the public	100	
Currency held by the banking system	400	
Total issue of currency	500	
Demand deposits	800	
Savings deposits	1,000	
Time deposits with licensed banks	2,000	
Time deposits with restricted licence banks	600	
Negotiable certificates of deposit issued by licensed banks and held by the public	1,500	
Negotiable certificates of deposit issued by restricted licence banks and held by the public	300	

(a)	(i)	What is the monetary base? Find the monetary base in Economy X.	(3 marks)
	(ii)	Calculate M1 and M2.	(4 marks)
	(iii)	What additional information do we need to get M3?	(2 marks)
*(b)	Is the monetary base the same as M1? Why?	(6 marks)
*(c)	Suppose M3 is equal to $7,000 million. If people in Economy X change all their time deposits and negotiable certificates of deposit into savings deposits, how would this affect M1 and M2? Explain.	(4 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	(i)	The monetary base (M0) is the total amount of currency issued in an economy at a certain moment. It consists of currency in the hands of the non-bank public [called cash (CP)] and currency in the hands of banks [called reserves (R)], i.e., M0 = CP + R.	(2 marks)
		The monetary base in Economy X is $500 million.	(1 mark)
	(ii)	M1	= $(100 + 800) million = $900 million	(2 marks)
		M2	= $900 million + $(1,000 + 2,000 + 1,500) million = $5,400 million
				(2 marks)
	(iii)	(	Time deposits with deposit-taking companies	(1 mark)
		(	Negotiable certificates of deposit issued by deposit-taking companies and held by the public	(1 mark)

(b)	No. This is because the monetary base is the total amount of currency issued in an economy, while M1 measures the total amount of money available in an economy.	(2 marks)
	The monetary base includes bank reserves which are money but are not available for use. M1 includes demand deposits with banks which are not currency issued.
	(4 marks)

(c)	M1 is unaffected because it does not include savings deposits, time deposits and negotiable certificates of deposit.	(2 marks)
	M2 will increase to $7,000 million (i.e., increase by 1,600 million).	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch608 · Ownership of firms
questions.text:
Study the following information.

Money supply	$ billion	
M1	24.7	
M3	412.4	

(a)	(i)	Calculate the total deposits with all deposit-taking institutions, excluding demand deposits and negotiable certificates of deposit held by deposit-taking institutions.	(2 marks)
	(ii)	Are the reserves held by deposit-taking institutions included in the money supply? Explain.	(2 marks)
(b)	Suppose Mrs Chan uses $10,000 cash to buy gift coupons (in denominations of $100) issued by a department store. The department store deposits the money into its savings account.
	(i)	Explain why the gift coupons are NOT money.	(2 marks)
	(ii)	Do the gift coupons perform better than money as a store of value? Explain.
	(3 marks)
	(iii)	Calculate the immediate effects of the above transactions on money supply M1 and M2.	(4 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	(i)	The total deposits with all deposit-taking institutions, excluding demand deposits and negotiable certificates of deposit held by deposit-taking institutions = M3 - M1	(1 mark)
		= $(412.4 - 24.7) billion = $387.7 billion	(1 mark)
	(ii)	The reserves held by deposit-taking institutions are not included in the money supply because they are not in public circulation and thus are not available for public use.	(2 marks)

(b)	(i)	This is because the gift coupons are not generally accepted as a medium of exchange.	(2 marks)
	(ii)	No. As the denominations of the gift coupons are expressed by money, when there is inflation, the gift coupons can be exchanged for fewer goods than before. The fall in the purchasing power of the gift coupons will generally follow that of money.	(3 marks)
	(iii)	ΔM1 = ΔCP + ΔDL = -$10,000 + $0 = -$10,000	(2 marks)
		ΔM2 = ΔM1 + ΔSL + ΔTL + ΔNCDL
= -$10,000 + $10,000 + $0 + $0 = +$0	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch608 · Ownership of firms
questions.text:
Mr Chan has recently purchased a newly constructed apartment in Tai Po for $8,000,000. He has made a down payment (首期) of $2,400,000 to the property developer.
(a)	Give TWO reasons to explain why the above transaction raises Hong Kong's GDP by an amount smaller than $8,000,000.	(4 marks)
(b)	To make the down payment, Mr Chan withdrew $1,600,000 from a time deposit account with a deposit-taking company and sold his flat in Shenzhen for $800,000. Explain the immediate effects of the above asset transfers on Hong Kong's money supply M1, M2 and M3. Show your calculations.	(6 marks)
(c)	Besides the down payment, Mr Chan has obtained a mortgage loan from a bank to pay the remaining amount of the apartment. He has to repay the loan over the next 15 years in monthly instalments at a fixed interest rate.
	(i)	What function of money is performed in this case? Explain.	(2 marks)
	(ii)	Suppose there will be unexpected inflation in the next 15 years. Explain whether Mr Chan will gain or lose.	(3 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	The following are possible reasons why Hong Kong's GDP increases by an amount less than the price of the apartment:
	(	The value of the apartment has already included the value of imports. However, the value of imports is not counted in Hong Kong's GDP.	(2 marks)
	(	The construction work took more than one year. The value of the construction work completed in previous years is not counted in the current year's GDP.
						(2 marks)
	(Accept other reasonable answers)

(b)	As Mr Chan withdrew money and sold his flat, the cash he holds increases by $2,400,000. Since there is no change in demand deposits, M1 increases by $2,400,000.	(2 marks)
	As M1 increases by $2,400,000 while other components of M2 remain unchanged, M2 increases by $2,400,000.	(2 marks)
	Although M2 increases by $2,400,000, time deposits with deposit-taking companies decrease by $1,600,000. As a result, M3 increases by $800,000.
			(2 marks)

(c)	(i)	As a standard of deferred payments	(1 mark)
		This involves expressing future payments in terms of money.	(1 mark)
	(ii)	Mr Chan will gain.	(1 mark)
		As there will be unexpected inflation, the actual real interest rate he pays will be lower than the expected real interest rate / the purchasing power of the repayments will be less than expected.	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch608 · Ownership of firms
questions.text:
The following is the balance sheet of a banking system.

Assets ($)	Liabilities ($)	
Reserves	300	Deposits	1,000	
Loans	700			

Suppose the required reserve ratio is 25%.
(a)	Calculate the maximum banking multiplier, the actual reserve ratio and the amount of excess reserves. 	(3 marks)
(b)	Refer to the above balance sheet. Suppose Miss Lau withdraws $100 from a bank.
	(i)	Calculate the amount of reserves the banking system falls short of immediately after the withdrawal.	(2 marks)
	(ii)	If there is no cash injected into the banking system and the banks do not keep excess reserves, calculate the actual decrease in deposits. Explain your answer.	(3 marks)
	(iii)	Calculate the change in money supply.	(2 marks)
(c)	Is the actual banking multiplier necessarily the same as the maximum banking multiplier? Explain.	(3 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	The maximum banking multiplier = 1 / 25% = 4	(1 mark)
	The actual reserve ratio = ($300 ( $1,000) × 100% = 30%	(1 mark)
	Excess reserves = $300 - ($1,000 × 25%) = $50	(1 mark)

(b)	(i)	The amount of reserves the banking system falls short of
		= [$(1,000 - 100) × 25%] - $(300 - 100) = $25	(2 marks)
	(ii)	Since there is no cash injected into the banking system and the banks do not keep excess reserves, the actual decrease in deposits is equal to the maximum decrease in deposits.	(1 mark)
		Actual decrease in deposits = $100 + [$25 × (1 / 25%)] = $200	(2 marks)
	(iii)	Change in money supply
		= Change in cash held by the public + Change in deposits
		= +$100 + (-$200) = -$100	(2 marks)

(c)	No, the actual banking multiplier may be smaller than the maximum banking multiplier when: 	(1 mark)
	(	there is cash leakage; or	(1 mark)
	(	banks keep excess reserves.	(1 mark)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch608 · Ownership of firms
questions.text:
The following is the balance sheet of a banking system.
Assets ($ million)	Liabilities ($ million)	
Reserves	8	Deposits	10	
Loans	2			

(a)	Suppose the banks have loaned their maximum amount. The public deposits $0.5 million in cash into the banks.
	(i)	Calculate the maximum change in deposits in the banking system.	(3 marks)
	(ii)	Calculate the maximum change in money supply.	(2 marks)
(b)	Suppose there is a recession and people do not want to borrow money from the banks to invest or consume. How will this affect the deposit creation ability of the banking system?	(2 marks)
*(c)	Suppose Miss Cheung receives a remittance of $0.5 million from her sister who lives in the US. Miss Cheung deposits half the money as demand deposits into a deposit-taking institution and the other half as savings deposits into another deposit-taking institution.
	(i)	Which type(s) of institutions will accept Miss Cheung's deposits?	(2 marks)
	(ii)	Explain the immediate effects of the above event on M1, M2 and M3.
	(6 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	(i)	The required reserve ratio = $8 million ( $10 million ( 100% = 80%	(1 mark)
		The maximum change in deposits = $0.5 million × (1 / 80%) = $0.625 million
	(2 marks)
	(ii)	The maximum change in money supply
		= Change in cash held by the public + Maximum change in deposits
		= -$0.5 million + 0.625 million = +$0.125 million	(2 marks)

(b)	Since the demand for loans decreases, banks will very likely hold excess reserves. As a result, banks' deposit creation ability will weaken.	(2 marks)

(c)	(i)	Licensed banks will accept both demand deposits and savings deposits from Miss Cheung.	(2 marks)
	(ii)	M1:
		(	Demand deposits increase by $250,000 and there is no change in cash held by the public.	(1 mark)
		(	So M1 will increase by $250,000.	(1 mark)
		M2:
		(	Savings deposits increase by $250,000, M1 increases by $250,000, and there is no change in the rest of the M2 components.	(1 mark)
		(	So M2 will increase by $500,000.	(1 mark)
		M3:
		(	M2 increases by $500,000 and there is no change in the rest of the M3 components.	(1 mark)
		(	So M3 will increase by $500,000.	(1 mark)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch608 · Ownership of firms
questions.text:
The following is the balance sheet of Banking System X.

Assets ($)	Liabilities ($)	
Reserves	1,200	Deposits	3,000	
Loans	1,800			

Suppose the public has $800 in cash.
(a)	Calculate the money supply in this economy.	(2 marks)
(b)	Suppose the government lowers the required reserve ratio from 25% to 20%.
	(i)	Calculate the increase in excess reserves in the banking system after the decrease in the required reserve ratio.	(2 marks)
	(ii)	If the banks lend all their excess reserves, calculate the maximum changes in deposits and money supply.	(4 marks)
(c)	Suppose the required reserve ratio is 25% and the public deposits all its cash into banks. Calculate the maximum possible amounts of deposits, reserves, loans and money supply in this economy.	(10 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Money supply = Cash held by the public + Deposits = $800 + $3,000 = $3,800
				(2 marks)

(b)	(i)	The increase in excess reserves
		= ($1,200 - $3,000 × 20%) - ($1,200 - $3,000 × 25%) = $150	(2 marks)
	(ii)	The maximum change in deposits = +$600 × (1 / 20%) = +$3,000	(2 marks)
The maximum change in money supply = change in cash held by the public + the maximum change in deposits. Since cash held by the public does not change, the maximum change in money supply is equal to the maximum change in deposits, i.e., +$3,000.	(2 marks)

(c)	After the public deposited $800 cash into banks, reserves in the banking system
	= $1,200 + $800 = $2,000	(2 marks)
	The maximum possible amount of deposits that $2,000 in reserves can support
	= $2,000 × (1 / 25%) = $8,000	(2 marks)
	The maximum possible amount of reserves in the economy after the deposit creation process is equal to $2,000.	(2 marks)
	The maximum possible amount of loans in the economy
	= Maximum amount of deposits - Maximum amount of reserves
	= $8,000 - $2,000 = $6,000	(2 marks)
	Since the public does not hold cash, the maximum possible amount of money supply in the economy is exactly equal to the maximum possible amount of deposits, i.e., $8,000.	(2 marks)

questions.text:
Suppose online shopping becomes more popular and people use credit cards to make their online payments. Which of the following is the possible effect of this?
A.	A leftward shift in the money demand curve

As Winnie's salary increases, her wealth will increase. Therefore, her asset demand for money will increase.

questions.answerText: In the case of Country Z, banknotes cannot fulfill their functions as a medium of exchange and a store of value. Thus, both the transaction demand and asset demand for banknotes decrease.

questions.topic: B6 · Ch609 · Production and division of labour
questions.text:
Which of the following statements about the transaction demand for money and the asset demand for money is INCORRECT?
A.	Transaction demand for money refers to the total amount of money that an economy desires to hold as a medium of exchange while the asset demand for money refers to the total amount of money that an economy desires to hold as a store of value.
B.	When people expect a global financial crisis to occur, both transaction demand for money and asset demand for money will decrease.
C.	The transaction demand for money curve is vertical while the asset demand for money curve is downward sloping.
D.	When there is an increase in the nominal interest rate, both the transaction demand for money curve and the asset demand for money curve will remain unchanged.
questions.answerText: Option B is the answer. When people expect the risk of assets to rise, they may hold more money to avoid risk as money is the least risky asset. Thus, asset demand for money will increase.

questions.topic: B6 · Ch609 · Production and division of labour
questions.text:
Which of the following statements about the transaction demand for money curve and the asset demand for money curve is correct?
A.	When the nominal interest rate rises, the transaction demand for money curve will remain unchanged while the asset demand for money curve will shift leftwards.
B.	When there is an increase in actual income earned from income-earning assets, the transaction demand for money curve will remain unchanged while the asset demand for money curve will shift leftwards.
C.	When nominal GDP increases, the transaction demand for money curve will shift upwards while the asset demand for money curve will remain unchanged.
D.	None of the above
questions.answerText: When people earn more income, they will tend to consume more and so the transaction demand for money curve will shift rightwards. As actual income increases, savings may increase and so does wealth. The asset demand for money curve may shift rightwards.

questions.topic: B6 · Ch609 · Production and division of labour
questions.text:

A.	the risk of holding income-earning assets increases.
B.	the purchase price of income-earning assets increases.
C.	wealth increases.
D.	people expect bond prices to rise.
questions.answerText: When people expect bond prices to rise, it is more profitable for them to buy bonds now. Thus, they want to hold less money as a store of value.

questions.topic: B6 · Ch609 · Production and division of labour
questions.text:

A.	There is an increase in real investment demand.
B.	There is an increase in the nominal interest rate.
C.	There is an increase in real consumption expenditure.
D.	There is an increase in wealth.
questions.answerText: When there is an increase in wealth (other things being equal), people will consume more and want to hold more money to conduct transactions. As a result, the transaction demand for money will increase. At the same time, people will also desire to hold more money to store wealth. The asset demand for money will also increase.

questions.text:
If the central bank raises the required reserve ratio and the nominal income level decreases, the nominal interest rate will
A.	increase.
B.	decrease.
C.	remain unchanged.
D.	Insufficient information to answer
questions.answerText: The increase in the required reserve ratio will decrease the money supply. The decrease in the nominal income level will decrease the money demand. Without knowing the extent of the changes, we cannot determine the change in the nominal interest rate.

questions.topic: B6 · Ch609 · Production and division of labour
questions.text:
* Other factors being constant, which of the following will cause a decrease in the nominal interest rate?
	(1)	The central bank lowers the required reserve ratio.
	(2)	People expect gold prices to increase.
	(3)	More people engage in barter.
A.	(1) and (2) only
B.	(1) and (3) only
C.	(2) and (3) only
D.	(1), (2) and (3)
questions.answerText:
Option (1) is correct. When the required reserve ratio decreases, money supply increases. Therefore, the nominal interest rate will decrease.
Option (2) is correct. When people expect gold prices to increase, they tend to hold more gold to store wealth. The asset demand for money decreases. Hence, the nominal interest rate will decrease.
Option (3) is correct. When more people engage in barter, less money is used as a medium of exchange. The transaction demand for money decreases. Therefore, the nominal interest rate will decrease.

questions.text:
* Study the diagram below.

Which of the following can help explain the movement from Point A to Point B when the money supply curve shifts from MS1 to MS2?
(1)	The demand for income-earning assets increases.
(2)	The supply of income-earning assets decreases.
(3)	After the shift of the money supply curve, there is an excess supply of money at n1.
A.	(3) only
B.	(1) and (3) only
C.	(2) and (3) only
D.	None of the above
questions.answerText: Options (1) and (3) are the answers. At Point A, with the same interest rate, the increase in money supply will lead to an excess supply of money. People will invest their excess money balance in income-earning assets. Thus, the demand for income-earning assets will increase and so their prices will rise. The nominal interest rate will continue to fall until there is no excess money supply, and the new equilibrium at Point B is achieved.

questions.text:
* Which of the following would lead to a rightward shift in the transaction money demand curve?
A.	The Octopus card offers a new function that enables fund transfers between users.
B.	Buying and selling shares become easier using smartphone apps.
C.	More and more people quit their jobs and travel for extended periods.
D.	The property market becomes riskier.
questions.answerText:
Option A is not correct. Transaction demand for money would decrease because there will be fewer cash transactions.
Option B is not correct. Asset demand for money would decrease when it is easier to sell shares.
Option D is not correct. This would lead to an increase in asset demand for money, without affecting transaction demand.
Option C is correct. As people travel for extended periods without income from regular jobs, they need a larger sum of money to finance their trips. Therefore, transaction demand for money would increase.

B.	3% … 4% … -3%
C.	5% … 2% … 0%
D.	5% … 4% … -3%

questions.topic: B6 · Ch609 · Production and division of labour
questions.text:

A.	3% … 0% … 7%
B.	3% … 10% … -3%
C.	4% … 0% … -3%
D.	4% … 10% … 7%

questions.topic: B6 · Ch609 · Production and division of labour
questions.text:
* Harold bought a one-year bond with a fixed nominal interest rate. He expected the inflation rate to be 2%. His expected real interest rate from the bond was 5%. Suppose the actual inflation rate was 4%. The actual real interest rate would be __________ and the cost of holding cash would be __________.
A.	2% … 0%
B.	2% … 7%
C.	3% … 0%
D.	3% … 7%
questions.answerText:
The cost of holding cash is the nominal interest rate.
The nominal interest rate of the bond
= Expected real interest rate + Expected inflation rate = 5% + 2% = 7%
The actual real interest rate
= Nominal interest rate - Actual inflation rate = 7% - 4% = 3%

questions.topic: B6 · Ch609 · Production and division of labour
questions.text: Briefly explain how TWO of the functions of money are related to the demand for money.	(6 marks)
questions.answerText:
As a medium of exchange:	(1 mark)
As money is used to settle payments, people desire to hold money as a medium of exchange to conduct transactions.	(2 marks)
As a store of value:	(1 mark)
Since money can preserve purchasing power, people want to hold money as an asset to store wealth.	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch609 · Production and division of labour
questions.text:
Explain how the following events affect the transaction demand for money.
(a)	The government grants transfer payments to recipients weekly instead of monthly.
	(3 marks)
(b)	Christmas is coming.	(3 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	The transaction demand for money decreases.	(1 mark)
	To the recipients, the time interval between two successive income receipts becomes shorter, so fewer transactions have to be settled within the reduced time interval. Hence, less money is needed for transactions.	(2 marks)
(b)	The transaction demand for money increases.	(1 mark)
	As Christmas is coming, people have to spend more to buy gifts and celebrate. Hence, the value of transactions increases and more money is needed.	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch609 · Production and division of labour
questions.text:
In Country A, some shops do not accept money with a certain face value for payments, while some shops do not accept cash at all.
If a currency's function as a medium of exchange is restricted, how would the nominal interest rate be affected? Explain with the aid of a diagram.	(5 marks)
questions.answerText:
Indicate on the diagram:
(	Leftward shift of money demand curve	(1 mark)
(	Decrease in nominal interest rate	(1 mark)

Verbal elaboration:
If the function as a medium of exchange is restricted, the transaction demand for money decreases.	(1 mark)
Therefore, money demand decreases from Md1 to Md2.	(1 mark)
As a result, the nominal interest rate decreases from n1 to n2.	(1 mark)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch609 · Production and division of labour
questions.text:
The following table shows data for Economy Q in a certain year.

Real GDP growth rate	Deflation rate	
1%	2%	

Based on the data, explain how money demand changes.	(4 marks)
questions.answerText:
The growth rate of nominal GDP 
= Real GDP growth rate + Inflation rate = 1% + (-2%) = -1%	(1 mark)
Since nominal national income decreases, people's consumption expenditure decreases. The value of transactions decreases.	(1 mark)
Less money is needed to conduct transactions. The transaction demand for money and the money demand decrease.	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch609 · Production and division of labour
questions.text:
Explain how the following events affect the transaction demand for money.
(a)	More shops offer discounts for payments with credit cards.	(2 marks)
(b)	More employers pay their workers' salaries bi-monthly instead of monthly.
	(2 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Due to the discounts, consumers tend to pay with credit cards more frequently. The number of cashless transactions increases.	(1 mark)
	Therefore, the transaction demand for money will decrease.	(1 mark)
(b)	Due to the change, the time interval between two successive income receipts increases.	(1 mark)
	More money is needed for transactions within the extended time interval. Hence, the transaction demand for money increases.	(1 mark)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch609 · Production and division of labour
questions.text:
(a)	What is transaction demand for money?	(2 marks)
(b)	Brief explain with TWO reasons why there is transaction demand for money.
	(4 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Transaction demand for money is the total amount of money that an economy desires to hold as a medium of exchange to conduct transactions.	(2 marks)
(b)	Reasons behind transaction demand for money:
(	There is non-synchronisation between money receipts and expenditures. Thus, to settle payments between two successive receipts of income, people need to hold money.	(2 marks)
(	Money is a medium of exchange. People can use money to settle payments immediately.	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch609 · Production and division of labour
questions.text:
In Country A, to stimulate economic growth, the government increases transfer payments.
(a)	With the aid of a diagram, explain how the above event affects real GDP and the price level in the short run.	(5 marks)
(b)	Based on the result in (a), other things being equal, explain how the above event affects the transaction demand for money.	(3 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	If the government raises transfer payments, people's disposable income will increase. Hence, private consumption expenditure increases.	(1 mark)
	The aggregate demand curve shifts rightwards from AD1 to AD2.	(1 mark)
Both the real GDP and the price level rise.	(1 mark)
	(2 marks)
(b)	When both real GDP and the price level increase, nominal GDP increases.
	(1 mark)
	The value of transactions increases. Thus, more money is needed to conduct transactions.	(1 mark)
As a result, other things being equal, the transaction demand for money will increase.	(1 mark)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch609 · Production and division of labour
questions.text: State TWO determinants of transaction demand for money and briefly explain how they are related to transaction demand for money.	(4 marks)
questions.answerText:
(	Nominal national income: This is positively related to transaction demand for money.
(	Desire to save: This is negatively related to transaction demand for money.
(	Time interval between two successive receipts of income: This is positively related to transaction demand for money.
(	The advancement of payment technology: This can be negatively related to transaction demand for money.
(Any TWO of the above or other reasonable answers, 2 marks × 2 = 4 marks)

	(1 mark)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch609 · Production and division of labour
questions.text:
Cherie, who lives in Hong Kong, bought some euros and sold them later for a profit.
(a)	To Cherie, are the euros money or are they an income-earning asset? Explain.
	(3 marks)
(b)	Briefly explain TWO factors affecting asset demand for money.	(4 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Income-earning asset	(1 mark)
Cherie could not use the euros as a medium of exchange in Hong Kong and she bought the euros for capital gains only.	(2 marks)
(Accept other reasonable answers.)
(b)	The factors affecting asset demand for money are as follows:
(	Nominal interest rate - The higher the nominal interest rate, the higher the cost of holding money and the smaller the asset demand for money.
(	Risk of holding income-earning assets - Since most people dislike risk, the higher the risk of holding income-earning assets, the greater the asset demand for money.
(	The purchase price of income-earning assets - The higher the purchase price of income-earning assets, the lower the nominal rates of returns of holding those assets and the larger the asset demand for money.
(	Wealth - The larger the amount of wealth one possesses, the larger the asset demand for money.
(	Cost of transacting assets - The higher the cost involved in transacting income-earning assets, the lower the net returns on the assets and the larger the asset demand for money.
(Any TWO of the above or other reasonable answers. 2 marks × 2 = 4 marks)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch609 · Production and division of labour
questions.text: Plot the asset demand for money curve. Explain its shape.	(4 marks)
questions.answerText:
Indicate on the diagram:
(	A downward sloping asset demand for money curve	(1 mark)

Verbal elaboration:
The nominal interest rate is the cost of holding money.	(1 mark)
When the nominal interest rate increases, people tend to hold less money.	(1 mark)
Hence, the nominal interest rate is negatively related to the asset demand for money.
	(1 mark)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch609 · Production and division of labour
questions.text:
(a)	Define asset demand for money.	(2 marks)
(b)	Brief explain with TWO reasons why there is asset demand for money.	(4 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Asset demand for money is the total amount of money that an economy desires to hold as an asset to store wealth.	(2 marks)
(b)	Reasons behind asset demand for money:
(	Money is the least risky asset. The nominal return on money is certain to be zero while the nominal returns on income-earning assets may be negative.
	(2 marks)
(	Liquidating assets can be costly and time-consuming. Hence, people keep money (the most liquid asset) to take advantage of timely investment opportunities.	(2 marks)
(Accept any other reasonable answers.)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch609 · Production and division of labour
questions.text:
(a)	What is the cost of holding money?	(1 mark)
(b)	Suppose the inflation rate is 10%. What are the actual nominal rate of return and actual real rate of return on money?	(2 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	The cost of holding money is the nominal interest rate.	(1 mark)
(b)	The actual nominal rate of return on money = 0%	(1 mark)
	The actual real rate of return on money = 0% - 10% = -10%	(1 mark)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch609 · Production and division of labour
questions.text:
Suppose Ming can only choose to hold cash or fixed deposits (with a 10% nominal interest rate) and the inflation rate is 3%.
(a)	Calculate the real rate of return on cash and fixed deposits, respectively.	(2 marks)
(b)	What is the cost of holding cash (in percentage)?	(1 mark)
*(c)	Use the result in (a) to find the difference between the real rate of return on fixed deposits and the real rate of return on cash. In this case, must it be the same as the cost of holding cash? Explain.	(4 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	The real rate of return on cash = 0 - 3% = -3%	(1 mark)
The real rate of return on fixed deposits = 10% - 3% = 7%	(1 mark)
(b)	The cost of holding cash (in percentage) = Nominal interest rate of fixed deposits = 10%	(1 mark)
(c)	Real rate of return on fixed deposits - Real rate of return on cash 
= 7% - (-3%) = 10%	(1 mark)
Real rate of return on fixed deposits - Real rate of return on cash 
= (Nominal rate of return on fixed deposits - Inflation rate) 
	- (Nominal rate of return on cash - Inflation rate) 
= Nominal rate of return on fixed deposits - Nominal rate of return on cash
	(1 mark)
As the nominal rate of return on cash is zero, the difference between the real rate of return on fixed deposits and the real rate of return on cash must be equal to the nominal rate of return on fixed deposits, which, in this case, is the cost of holding cash.	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch609 · Production and division of labour
questions.text: Use TWO characteristics of cash to explain why people may prefer to hold some of their wealth in cash, instead of holding wealth only in the form of income-earning assets.	(6 marks)
questions.answerText:
(	Money is the least risky asset.	(1 mark)
Since most people dislike uncertainty, other things being equal, the lower the risk (the uncertainty) of an asset, the more desirable it is. Thus, people may desire to hold some cash to lower the risk of their portfolio.	(2 marks)
(	Money is the most liquid asset. It can be used to settle payments immediately without the need for conversion.	(1 mark)
Since people prefer liquidity, other things being equal, the higher the liquidity of an asset, the more desirable it is. Thus, people may desire to hold some cash to increase the liquidity of their portfolio.	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch609 · Production and division of labour
questions.text: State TWO determinants of asset demand for money other than the interest rate and explain how they can lead to an increase in asset demand for money.	(4 marks)
questions.answerText:
(	Risk of holding income-earning assets: Since most people dislike risk, the higher the risk of holding income-earning assets, the greater the amount of money they would desire to hold as a store of wealth.
(	Cost of transacting assets: The higher the cost involved in transacting income-earning assets, the lower the net returns on the assets and the greater the asset demand for money.
(	Wealth: The greater one's wealth, the greater the amount of various assets held. Since money is also an asset for storing wealth, the asset demand for money will increase too.
(Any TWO of the above or other reasonable answers, 2 marks × 2 = 4 marks)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch609 · Production and division of labour
questions.text:
(a)	Explain the relationship between the asset demand for money and the nominal interest rate.	(2 marks)
(b)	What is the shape of a money demand curve? Use the answer in (a) to explain.
	(4 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	By holding money, a person gives up the nominal return generated by holding income-earning assets. Therefore, the nominal interest rate is the cost of holding money.	(1 mark)
The nominal interest rate and asset demand for money are negatively related.
	(1 mark)
(b)	The money demand curve is equal to the horizontal summation of the transaction and asset demand for money curves.	(1 mark)
The transaction demand for money curve is vertical.	(1 mark)
Based on the answer in (a), the asset demand for money curve is downward sloping.	(1 mark)
As a result, the money demand curve is downward sloping.	(1 mark)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch609 · Production and division of labour
questions.text:
Recently, some low-risk income-earning assets have been introduced in the market. At the same time, banks loan larger portions of their excess reserves. With the aid of a diagram, explain the effects of the above events on the nominal interest rate.
	(6 marks)
questions.answerText:
Indicate on the diagram:
(	Leftward shift in money demand curve	(1 mark)
(	Rightward shift in money supply curve	(1 mark)
(	Decrease in nominal interest rate	(1 mark)

Verbal elaboration:
As there are more low-risk income-earning assets, money demand decreases from Md1 to Md2.	(1 mark)
When banks loan more of their excess reserves, money supply increases from MS1 to MS2.	(1 mark)
As a result, the nominal interest rate decreases from n1 to n2.	(1 mark)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch609 · Production and division of labour
questions.text: With the aid of a diagram, explain how the equilibrium nominal interest rate changes when people desire to save more.	(6 marks)
questions.answerText:
(	When people desire to save more, they will consume less. This reduces the value of transactions and the transaction demand for money.	(2 marks)
(	Money demand will decrease and the money demand curve will shift leftwards from Md1 to Md2.	(1 mark)
(	As a result, the nominal interest rate will decrease.	(1 mark)
	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch609 · Production and division of labour
questions.text:
An economist believes the price of US government bonds would increase after the United Kingdom voted to leave the European Union.
(a)	What is the opportunity cost of holding US dollars instead of holding US government bonds?	(2 marks)
(b)	Explain how an increase in the price of US government bonds would affect the demand for US dollars.	(3 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	The opportunity cost is the nominal interest rates of US government bonds.
	(2 marks)
(b)	The increase in the price of US government bonds lowers the (expected) nominal rate of return of investing in US government bonds.	(1 mark)
	This raises the asset demand for money,	(1 mark)
	and thus the demand for money.	(1 mark)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch609 · Production and division of labour
questions.text:
(a)	What is the opportunity cost of holding cash instead of holding bonds?	(2 marks)
(b)	Suppose the costs of bond transaction decrease due to financial innovation. With the aid of a diagram, explain the effect on the interest rate in the money market.
	(5 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	The opportunity cost is the nominal interest rates of the bonds.	(2 marks)
(b)	Indicate on the diagram:
•	Leftward shift in money demand curve	(1 mark)
•	Decrease in interest rate	(1 mark)

Verbal elaboration:
Lower transaction costs imply a higher net return from investing in bonds.
	(1 mark)
Asset demand for money decreases.	(1 mark)
This will lower the money demand, and thus the interest rate.	(1 mark)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch609 · Production and division of labour
questions.text:
Refer to the following information in Country H.
Year	Consumer price index	
2015	103	
2016	107	
(a)	Explain how the above change in the consumer price index would affect the transaction demand for money.	(2 marks)
(b)	Suppose the nominal interest rate of the bonds in Country H is linked with the inflation rate or a minimum rate of 2%.
	Explain the effect on the asset demand for money as a result of the above change in the consumer price index. 	(3 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	As the general price level increases, more money is needed to conduct transactions.	(1 mark)
	The transaction demand for money increases.	(1 mark)
(b)	With an increase in the consumer price index, the nominal interest rate of the bonds increases accordingly.	(1 mark)
	The cost of holding money is the nominal interest rate of the bonds.	(1 mark)
	As the cost of holding money increases, asset demand for money will decrease.
	(1 mark)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch609 · Production and division of labour
questions.text:
Study the following information.
	Nominal interest rate	
Year 1	5%	
Year 2	3%	
Suppose people expect a 1% inflation rate in Year 2, but it turns out to be 2%.
(a)	Calculate the expected real interest rate in Year 2.	(2 marks)
(b)	Explain how the cost of holding money would change in Year 2.	(3 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Expected real interest rate 
	= Nominal interest rate - Expected inflation rate	(1 mark)
	= 3% − 1% = 2%	(1 mark)
(b)	The cost of holding money decreases from 5% to 3%	(1 mark)
	The cost of holding money is equal to the nominal interest rate because when people hold money, they forgo the opportunity of earning interest from holding an interest-earning asset.	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch609 · Production and division of labour
questions.text:
Mr Chan can choose to buy a one-year bond or hold money.
(a)	Explain under what condition the expected real rate of return is greater than the nominal rate of return of holding a bond.	(2 marks)
(b)	How is the real rate of return on money calculated? Explain.	(3 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Real rate of return = Nominal rate of return - Expected inflation rate	(1 mark)
	When the expected inflation rate is negative (i.e., deflation), the expected real rate of return is greater than the nominal rate of return.	(1 mark)
(b)	The real rate of return on money is the negative of the inflation rate.	(1 mark)
	The nominal rate of return on money is 0% because holding money earns zero nominal income. Therefore, the real rate of return = 0% − inflation rate.	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch609 · Production and division of labour
questions.text:
'The economic situation is getting worse. The nominal values of most of my assets keep decreasing. I have decided to hold more cash,' Wayne said.
'However, you cannot gain by holding cash,' Kent said.
(a)	What is the nominal rate of return of holding cash? Explain your answer briefly.
	(2 marks)
(b)	Explain under what circumstance Kent would be incorrect with reference to the real rate of return of holding cash.	(4 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	The nominal rate of return of holding cash is 0% because holding cash earns zero nominal income.	(2 marks)
(b)	The real rate of return of holding cash is equal to the negative of the inflation rate (= 0% − inflation rate).	(2 marks)
	If the inflation rate is negative (i.e., deflation), the real rate of return of holding cash will be positive. In this case, cash holders would gain.	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch609 · Production and division of labour
questions.text:
Jason is a secondary school student who does not have any savings. Every day, his mother gives him $50 for his daily transport and meal expenses. Study the following conversation and answer the questions.
Jason's mother: Due to inflation, the prices of all goods are increasing. But your father has not received a pay rise. Thus, I am so sorry to have to reduce your pocket money.
Jason: No! As there is inflation, you should raise my pocket money instead.
(a)	What is inflation? Explain whether Jason's mother's comment about inflation is correct.	(5 marks)
(b)	Give ONE reason to support Jason. Explain your answer.	(2 marks)
(c)	Define the type of Jason's demand for money.	(2 marks)
(d)	Use ONE diagram to explain the change in Jason's demand for money in (c) if Jason's mother changes Jason's pocket money payment to a monthly payment and the monthly amount of Jason's pocket money is the same as before.	(3 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Inflation is the phenomenon of a persistent increase in the general price level.
	(2 marks)
She is not correct.	(1 mark)
The general price level is the weighted average of prices of all goods and services in an economy at a certain moment. Its increase does not imply that the prices of all goods have increased. The prices of some goods may decrease during inflation.	(2 marks)

(b)	(	During inflation, the cost of living rises and the purchasing power of money drops. Jason may not have enough money to cover his daily expenses. To maintain the purchasing power of Jason's pocket money, Jason's mother should increase his pocket money.

questions.topic: B6 · Ch610 · Factors of production
questions.text:
* Which of the following are possible effects of raising the discount rate?
(1)	The cost of holding money increases.
(2)	Private banks' cost of borrowing from the central bank increases.
(3)	The real return on money decreases.
A.	(1) and (2) only
B.	(1) and (3) only
C.	(2) and (3) only
D.	(1), (2) and (3)
questions.answerText:
The discount rate is the interest rate that the central bank charges when it lends money to private banks. Option (2) is correct.
When there is an increase in the discount rate, money supply will decrease and so the nominal interest rate (i.e., the cost of holding money) will increase. Hence, Option (1) is correct.
The decrease in aggregate demand will lead to a decrease in the price level. As the real return on money (in percentage) = - inflation rate, the real return on money will increase. Therefore, Option (3) is incorrect.

* When the central bank lowers the discount rate, the money supply curve will

B.	shift rightwards only if there is no cash leakage.
C.	shift leftwards because banks will borrow less from other banks.
D.	remain unchanged if people do not borrow money from banks.
questions.answerText:
Option B is incorrect. The assumption of 'no cash leakage' is needed only in the case of maximum creation of money. Even if there is cash leakage, money creation may still take place if some loans are redeposited into the banking system.
Option D is correct. If people do not borrow money from banks, banks cannot create new loans. Thus, the money supply curve will not change.

questions.topic: B6 · Ch610 · Factors of production
questions.text:
Suppose Country D is facing the risk of recession. To avoid serious unemployment, the central bank lowers the required reserve ratio to change the money supply.
(a)	Briefly describe how the decrease in the required reserve ratio affects the money supply. Does the monetary base change at the same time? Explain.	(5 marks)
(b)	Explain briefly how a change in the money supply can avoid serious unemployment in the country.	(4 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	When the central bank lowers the required reserve ratio, banks need to keep less in required reserves.	(1 mark)
	Thus, they have more excess reserves to lend for profit.	(1 mark)
	Through the process of money creation, the money supply increases further.
	(1 mark)
	The monetary base does not change because the total amount of cash held by the public and bank reserves are not affected.	(2 marks)
(b)	Due to an increase in the money supply, nominal interest rates and hence real interest rates fall.	(1 mark)
	The fall in real interest rates raises both private consumption expenditure and gross investment expenditure.	(1 mark)
	Hence, aggregate demand increases.	(1 mark)
	The increase in aggregate demand raises aggregate output and the employment level. Hence, serious unemployment can be avoided.	(1 mark)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch610 · Factors of production
questions.text:
Suppose the central bank of Country Z keeps printing more money to pay for government expenditure.

(b)	With the aid of an AS-AD diagram, explain how the price level and output level are affected by the policy in the short run.	(7 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Indicate on the diagram:
	(	Rightward shift in the money supply curve	(1 mark)
	(	Decrease in the nominal interest rate	(1 mark)
	
	Verbal elaboration:
	When the central bank prints more money, the money supply increases from MS1 to MS2.	(1 mark)
	As a result, nominal interest rates decrease from n1 to n2.	(1 mark)
(b)	Indicate on the diagram:
	(	Rightward shift in the aggregate demand curve	(1 mark)
	(	Increase in the price level	(1 mark)
	(	Increase in the output level	(1 mark)
	
	Verbal elaboration:
	When nominal interest rates decrease, real interest rates decrease too.	(1 mark)
	The fall in real interest rates raises both private consumption expenditure and gross investment expenditure.	(1 mark)
	Hence, aggregate demand increases.	(1 mark)
	The increase in aggregate demand raises both the output level and the price level.
	(1 mark)

This will increase the money supply.	(1 mark)

	The money supply increases as cash held by public increases and banks have more reserves to create money.	(1 mark)
	As a result, nominal interest rates decrease.	(1 mark)
(b)	As nominal interest rates decrease, real interest rates also decrease.	(1 mark)
	Hence, both private consumption expenditure and gross investment expenditure increase.	(1 mark)
	Aggregate demand increases.	(1 mark)
	As a result, their price levels increase. Their inflation rates will be higher.
	(1 mark)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch610 · Factors of production
questions.text:
There are four common tools of monetary policy: open market operations, adjusting the discount rate, adjusting the required reserve ratio and printing money. 
Briefly explain which of the tools will affect the monetary base and which will affect the maximum banking multiplier.	(6 marks)
questions.answerText:
(	Open market operations
As there are transactions of bonds between the central bank and the public or private banks, currency held by the public or private banks will change and so will the monetary base.	(2 marks)
(	Adjusting the discount rate
As the cost of borrowing from the central bank changes, private banks will borrow more / less from the central bank. The reserves of private banks will change and so will the monetary base.	(2 marks)
(	Adjusting the required reserve ratio
When the central bank changes the required reserve ratio, the maximum banking multiplier will change.	(1 mark)
(	Printing money
Printing money will increase the amount of currency issued. Thus, the monetary base will increase.	(1 mark)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch610 · Factors of production
questions.text: Explain how open market sales of government bonds affect the market nominal interest rate and draw ONE diagram to show your answer.	(7 marks)
questions.answerText:
When the central bank sells government bonds to the market, less money circulates. The cash held by non-bank public decreases, and some people withdraw money from banks.	(2 marks)
Some banks may lack reserves and need to call back loans. Multiple contraction of money results.	(1 mark)
Thus, the money supply decreases and the money supply curve shifts leftwards.
	(1 mark)
As a result, the nominal interest rate will increase from n1 to n2.	(1 mark)
	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch610 · Factors of production
questions.text: Explain how an increase in the discount rate affects the equilibrium nominal interest rate and draw ONE diagram to show your answer.	(7 marks)
questions.answerText:
When the central bank raises the discount rate, the cost of borrowing from the central bank increases.	(1 mark)
Banks will reduce their loans from the central bank. Some banks may call back loans to repay loans from the central bank. The monetary base will decrease. This results in multiple contraction of money.	(2 marks)
Hence, the money supply decreases and the money supply curve shifts leftwards.
 	(1 mark)
As a result, the nominal interest rate will increase from n1 to n2.	(1 mark)
	(2 marks)

If private banks lend their excess reserves, the money supply increases further through the money creation process.	(3 marks)

	(2 marks)
(b)	As the money supply increases, the nominal interest rate will decrease from n2 to n1. This can stabilise the nominal interest rate.	(1 mark)
	(1 mark)

Assets ($ billion)	Liabilities ($ billion)
