Loans	350			

(a)	Suppose banks do not keep excess reserves. What is the value of the required reserve ratio?	(1 mark)
(b)	Suppose the central bank lowers the required reserve ratio by 5%. Calculate the maximum change in the money supply.	(3 marks)
(c)	Suggest ONE example to explain why lowering the required reserve ratio may NOT be an effective monetary policy.	(2 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Required reserve ratio = $150 billion / $500 billion = 30% or 0.3	(1 mark)
(b)	New required reserve ratio = 30% - 5% = 25%	(1 mark)
	New maximum amount of money supply = $150 billion / 25% = $600 billion
	(1 mark)
	Maximum change in money supply = $(600 - 500) billion = $100 billion	(1 mark)
(c)	Even if the central bank lowers the required reserve ratio, the amount of deposits will not increase if banks do not loan out their excess reserves. Hence, the money supply may not increase.	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch610 · Factors of production
questions.text:
Country A is an agricultural economy. The harvest has been poor this year because of a serious drought.
(a)	With the aid of a diagram, briefly explain the effect of the serious drought on Country A's real GDP and the price level in the short run.	(5 marks)
(b)	How can an expansionary monetary policy help stabilise real GDP? Explain with the aid of the diagram drawn in (a). Also explain how the policy will affect the price level.	(9 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Indicate on the diagram:
	(	Short run aggregate supply curve shifts leftwards.	(1 mark)
	(	Real GDP decreases and the price level increases.	(1 mark)
	
Verbal elaboration:
(	The serious drought lowers the short run aggregate supply in Country A.
	(1 mark)
(	Therefore, real GDP decreases and the price level increases in the short run.
	(2 marks)
(b)	Indicate on the diagram:
	(	The aggregate demand curve shifts rightwards.	(1 mark)
	(	Real GDP is restored to the original level.	(1 mark)
	(	The price level increases further.	(1 mark)
	
Verbal elaboration:
(	An expansionary monetary policy will lower the nominal interest rate and also the real interest rate.	(1 mark)
(	A fall in the real interest rate increases both private consumption expenditure and gross investment expenditure.	(2 marks)
(	Hence, the aggregate demand curve shifts rightwards.	(1 mark)
(	As a result, real GDP can be restored to its original level Y1, but the price level increases further to P3.	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch610 · Factors of production
questions.text: How can the discount rate be adjusted to solve the problem of unemployment in the short run? Explain your answer with the aid of an AS-AD diagram.	(10 marks)
questions.answerText:
Indicate on the diagram:
(	The original short run equilibrium real GDP is smaller than the full employment real GDP.	(1 mark)
(	The aggregate demand curve shifts rightwards.	(1 mark)
(	Real GDP is restored to its full employment level.	(1 mark)

Verbal elaboration:
(	Lowering the discount rate can reduce banks' cost of borrowing from the central bank.	(1 mark)
(	Therefore, it is profitable for banks to borrow more from the central bank and issue more loans.	(1 mark)
(	Money supply will increase. So, the real interest rate decreases.	(2 marks)
(	Both private consumption expenditure and gross investment expenditure will increase. Hence, the aggregate demand curve shifts rightwards.	(2 marks)
(	As a result, real GDP is restored to its full employment level.	(1 mark)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch610 · Factors of production
questions.text:
(a)	Explain with the aid of a diagram how a decrease in the required reserve ratio affects the nominal interest rate.	(6 marks)
(b)	Use the result in (a) to explain how a decrease in the required reserve ratio affects real GDP.	(4 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Indicate on the diagram:
(	The money supply curve shifts rightwards.	(1 mark)
(	The nominal interest rate decreases.	(1 mark)

Verbal elaboration:
(	When the required reserve ratio decreases, banks can keep less required reserves. So they have more excess reserves to loan out and create money. The money supply increases.	(3 marks)
(	As a result, the nominal interest rate decreases from n1 to n2.	(1 mark)
(b)	(	Other things being equal, when the nominal interest rate decreases, the real interest rate decreases too.	(1 mark)
(	This increases both private consumption expenditure and gross investment expenditure. Hence, aggregate demand increases.	(2 marks)
(	As a result, real GDP increases.	(1 mark)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch610 · Factors of production
questions.text: With the aid of an AS-AD diagram, explain how an expansionary monetary policy can solve the problem of unemployment.	(7 marks)
questions.answerText:
Unemployment exists when the aggregate output (Y1) is below the full employment level (Yf).	(1 mark)
When the central bank adopts an expansionary monetary policy, the real interest rate will decrease.	(1 mark)
The fall in the real interest rate increases both private consumption expenditure and gross investment expenditure. Hence, the aggregate demand curve shifts rightwards.
	(2 marks)
The increase in aggregate demand from the expansionary monetary policy can increase output to the full employment level.	(1 mark)
	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch610 · Factors of production
questions.text:
* The government in Country H has a huge fiscal surplus this year. To 'give wealth to people' (藏富於民), the government decides to offer an income tax rebate (退回).
(a)	Suppose the economy is originally at long run equilibrium. With the aid of a diagram, briefly explain how the tax rebate will affect output and the price level in the short run.	(6 marks)
(b)	Based on the answer in (a), what will the change in output be in the long run?
	(1 mark)
(c)	Based on the answer in (a), can the central bank stabilise the price level with a monetary policy? Can the central bank also stimulate short run economic growth with this type of monetary policy? Briefly explain.	(2 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Suppose the economy is originally at Point A. The tax rebate will stimulate consumption. Aggregate demand increases and the aggregate demand curve shifts rightwards from AD1 to AD2.	(2 marks)
Output increases from Yf to Y2.	(1 mark)
The price level increases from P1 to P2.	(1 mark)
	(2 marks)
(b)	Output will remain at its original full employment level (Yf).	(1 mark)
(c)	The central bank can stabilise the price level with a contractionary monetary policy, which will lead to a decrease in aggregate demand and offset the increase in aggregate demand in (a).	(1 mark)
However, the central bank cannot stimulate economic growth at the same time because the monetary policy to stabilise the price level is contractionary.	(1 mark)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch610 · Factors of production
questions.text:
(a)	What is overheating? Is there a deflationary gap or inflationary gap when overheating occurs?	(3 marks)
(b)	With the aid of an AS-AD diagram, briefly explain how a contractionary monetary policy can solve the problem of overheating.	(6 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Overheating of an economy occurs when the production capacity of the economy cannot keep pace with the growing aggregate demand.	(2 marks)
When overheating occurs, the short run equilibrium output level will be greater than the full employment output level. Thus, there is an inflationary gap.	(1 mark)
(b)	A contractionary monetary policy will lower the money supply or directly raise interest rates.	(1 mark)
This will reduce both private consumption expenditure and gross investment expenditure.	(1 mark)
Hence, aggregate demand decreases from AD1 to AD2.	(1 mark)
The decrease in aggregate demand from the contractionary monetary policy can reduce output to the full employment level (Yf).	(1 mark)
	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch610 · Factors of production
questions.text:
In Country A, the aggregate demand curve is downward sloping due to the interest rate effect.
(a)	Briefly explain how the interest rate effect mentioned above works when there is an increase in the price level.	(4 marks)
*(b)	Can we use the interest rate effect mentioned above to explain the effects of an expansionary monetary policy in the short run? Explain.	(5 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	The nominal amount of money supply does not change with the price level. When the price level rises, households and firms need more money to finance their transactions.	(1 mark)
	Thus, some save less and some borrow more from banks. Both will push up real interest rates.	(1 mark)
	The rise in real interest rates discourages consumption and investment. Consequently, aggregate output demanded falls.	(1 mark)
	Thus, the price level and aggregate output demanded are negatively related. This explains why the aggregate demand curve is downward sloping.	(1 mark)
(b)	No, because	(1 mark)
the interest rate effect mentioned in the question assumes that the nominal money supply remains unchanged. In this case, the real interest rate changes due to the change in the price level. There is movement along the aggregate demand curve.
	(2 marks)
In the case of using an expansionary monetary policy, the real interest rate changes due to factors other than a change in the price level. Thus, there is a shift of the aggregate demand curve.	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch610 · Factors of production
questions.text: * Suppose Country Q was initially at the long run equilibrium. A large oilfield has been recently discovered in Country Q. Compare the effects on the price level of doing nothing or carrying out an expansionary monetary policy. Explain your answer with the aid of a diagram. (Assume that the discovery of the oilfield does not affect the economy in the short run.)	(10 marks)
questions.answerText:
Indicate on the diagram:
(	Deflationary gap due to rightward shift in the long run aggregate supply curve
	(1 mark)
Effects of doing nothing:
(	Rightward shift in the short run aggregate supply curve	(1 mark)
(	Decrease in the price level	(1 mark)
Effects of an expansionary monetary policy:
(	Rightward shift in the aggregate demand curve	(1 mark)
(	Increase in the price level	(1 mark)

Verbal elaboration:
When a new oilfield is discovered, the long run aggregate supply increases from LRAS1 to LRAS2, and thus a deflationary gap exists.	(1 mark)
If nothing is done, the excess supply of inputs will cause the short run aggregate supply to increase from SRAS1 to SRAS2.	(1 mark)
Hence, the price level will decrease from P0 to P1.	(1 mark)
If an expansionary monetary policy is carried out, the aggregate demand will increase from AD1 to AD2.	(1 mark)
The price level will increase from P0 to P2.	(1 mark)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch610 · Factors of production
questions.text:
(a)	State the equation of exchange.	(2 marks)
(b)	Suppose the central bank carries out an expansionary monetary policy. In the short run, the real national income and price level increase by 3% and 4%, respectively.
	(i)	What is the percentage change in money supply? Show your calculations.
	(2 marks)
	(ii)	What is the percentage change in the price level in the long run? Briefly explain your answer.	(3 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	MV ≡ PY, where M = money stock / nominal money supply, 
V = velocity of circulation of money, 
P = general price level and 
Y = real output / real national income.	(2 marks)
(b)	(i)	%Δ in money supply
		= %Δ in real national income + %Δ in price level	(1 mark)
		= 3% + 4% = 7%	(1 mark)
	(ii)	In the long run, the real national income is constant at the full employment level.	(1 mark)
		Hence, the change in money supply only causes the same percentage change in the price level.	(1 mark)
		As a result, the price level will increase by 7% in the long run.	(1 mark)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch610 · Factors of production
questions.text:
(a)	State the equation of exchange.	(2 marks)
(b)	What are the assumptions of the quantity theory of money?	(2 marks)
(c)	How do the assumptions lead to predictions of the quantity theory of money?
	(4 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	MV ≡ PY, where M = money stock / nominal money supply, 
V = velocity of circulation of money, 
P = general price level and 
Y = real output / real national income.	(2 marks)
(b)	The velocity of circulation of money is assumed to be constant.	(1 mark)
	Real national income is assumed to be constant at the full employment level in the long run.	(1 mark)
(c)	As V is assumed to be constant, the quantity theory of money predicts that a change in nominal money supply (M) will cause a proportional change in nominal national income (PY).	(2 marks)
	Since Y is assumed to be constant in the long run, the quantity theory of money predicts that a change in money supply will only lead to a proportional change in the price level in the long run.	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch610 · Factors of production
questions.text:
In Country X, the public never hold cash and banks never hold excess reserves. The required reserve ratio of the banking system is 10% and the total amount of reserves is $1,000.
(a)	Calculate the money supply.	(2 marks)
(b)	Suppose the central bank lowers the required reserve ratio by 2%. Calculate the change in the money supply.	(2 marks)
(c)	According to the quantity theory of money, predict the change in the price level in the long run.	(4 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Total amount of deposits 
	= $1,000 ÷ 10% = $10,000	(1 mark)
	Money supply
	= Deposits + Cash held by the public = $10,000 + 0 = $10,000	(1 mark)
(b)	Change in deposits
	= $1,000 ÷ (10% − 2%) − $10,000 = $2,500	(1 mark)
	Change in money supply
	= Change in deposits + Change in cash held by the public
	= +$2,500 + 0 = +$2,500	(1 mark)
(c)	According to the quantity theory of money, a change in money supply will lead to the same proportional change in the price level in the long run.	(2 marks)
	Percentage change in money supply = Percentage change in the price level
	= +$2,500 / $10,000 × 100% = +25%	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch610 · Factors of production
questions.text:
Refer to the following balance sheet of a banking system which accepts only demand deposits. Suppose the public does not hold any cash and there is no excess reserve.

Assets ($)	Liabilities ($)	
Reserves	150	Deposits	750	
Loans	600			

(a)	Calculate the required reserve ratio.	(1 mark)
(b)	Suppose $100 in money is issued and banks are fully loaned up.
(i)	What is the maximum change in money supply? Show your calculations.
	(2 marks)
(ii)	According to the quantity theory of money, what is the percentage change in the price level in the long run?	(5 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Required reserve ratio = $150 / $750 = 20% or 0.2	(1 mark)
(b)	(i)	The maximum change in money supply = +$100 × (1 / 0.2) = +$500	(2 marks)
(ii)	(	The equation of exchange is MV ( PY.	(1 mark)
(	The quantity theory of money assumes that the velocity of circulation of money (V) is constant.	(1 mark)
(	The theory also assumes that, in the long run, the output level (Y) remains constant at the full employment level.	(1 mark)
	(	So, 
		Percentage change in price level = Percentage change in money supply 
= (+$500 / $750) × 100% = +66.7%	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch610 · Factors of production
questions.text:
'Money is neutral in the long run.' Illustrate this statement with
(a)	the quantity theory of money;	(4 marks)
(b)	the AS-AD model (you may only discuss the case of an expansionary monetary policy).	(7 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	(	The equation of exchange is MV ( PY.	(1 mark)
	(	The quantity theory of money assumes that the velocity of circulation of money (V) is constant.	(1 mark)
	(	The theory also assumes that real GDP (Y) is constant in the long run.
	(1 mark)
	(	Therefore, changes in nominal money supply (M) can only affect nominal values (e.g., P - the general price level), but not real values (e.g., real GDP).
	(1 mark)
(b)	Indicate on the diagram:
	(	Vertical long run aggregate supply curve	(1 mark)
	(	Aggregate demand curve shifts rightwards.	(1 mark)
	(	Real GDP stays at the full employment level in the long run.	(1 mark)

Verbal elaboration:
(	Suppose an expansionary monetary policy is imposed by increasing the money supply. In this case, the nominal interest rate falls and aggregate demand increases.	(2 marks)
(	However, in the long run, real GDP remains unchanged at its full employment level.	(1 mark)
(	So, money is neutral, in the sense that changes in money supply do not affect real values (e.g., real GDP).	(1 mark)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch610 · Factors of production
questions.text: Issuing money without controls is regarded as one of the causes of the collapse of several ancient dynasties. With the aid of an AS-AD diagram, explain how excessive issuance of money will increase people's cost of living in the short run and long run.	(12 marks)
questions.answerText:
Indicate on the diagram:
(	Aggregate demand curve shifts rightwards.	(1 mark)
(	Short run situation: Price level increases.	(1 mark)
(	Short run aggregate supply curve shifts upwards.	(1 mark)
(	Long run situation: Price level increases further.	(1 mark)

Verbal elaboration:
(	Excessive issuance of money will greatly increase the money supply and so lower the nominal interest rate and real interest rate.	(1 mark)
(	This increases both private consumption expenditure and gross investment expenditure. Hence, aggregate demand increases.	(2 marks)
(	The price level increases to PS2 in the short run.	(1 mark)
(	There is an inflationary gap. The excess demand for resources will raise input prices. The short run aggregate supply curve shifts upwards until the inflationary gap is closed.	(2 marks)
(	As a result, the price level increases further to PL2 in the long run.	(1 mark)
(	Therefore, people's cost of living, as reflected by the price level, increases in both the short run and long run.	(1 mark)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch610 · Factors of production
questions.text:
(a)	What is the equation of exchange? Briefly describe the components of the equation.	(2 marks)
(b)	What is the assumption of the quantity theory of money on the velocity of circulation of money?	(1 mark)
(c)	According to the quantity theory of money, explain the effect of a 10% increase in the money supply on the general price level
(i)	in the short run;	(2 marks)
(ii)	in the long run.	(2 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	The equation of exchange is MV ( PY. M is the nominal money supply, V is the velocity of circulation of money, P is the general price level, and Y is the real 
GDP.	(2 marks)
(b)	The velocity of circulation of money is assumed to be constant.	(1 mark)
(c)	(i)	The general price level may increase by less than 10% as the real GDP may also increase at the same time..	(2 marks)
(ii)	The general price level will increase by 10% as the real GDP is assumed to remain unchanged in the long run.	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch610 · Factors of production
questions.text:
(a)	State the assumptions of the quantity theory of money.	(2 marks)
(b)	Briefly explain the predicted outcomes of the quantity theory of money in the long run.	(2 marks)
(c)	Use the answer in (b) to describe the neutrality of money.	(3 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	(	The velocity of circulation of money is stable and is assumed to be constant.
	(1 mark)
(	The real national income may vary in the short run but remains constant at the full employment level in the long run.	(1 mark)
(b)	In the long run, a change in the nominal money supply will cause a proportional change in the price level.	(2 marks)
(c)	As predicted by the quantity theory of money, a change in M will lead to a proportional change in P and the nominal national income (PY) in the long run but not the real national income (Y). Thus, changes in the nominal money supply can affect nominal values only. They cannot affect real values. This phenomenon is the neutrality of money.	(3 marks)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch610 · Factors of production
questions.text:
(a)	List TWO common tools of expansionary monetary policy.	(2 marks)
(b)	'In the long run, it is better for the government to do nothing rather than intervene in the economy with an expansionary monetary policy.' Based on the following items, explain why this statement can be true.
(i)	The quantity theory of money	(2 marks)
(ii)	AS-AD model	(2 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	(	Open market purchase of government bonds
(	Lowering the discount rate
(	Lowering the required reserve ratio
(	Printing money
(Any TWO of the above, 1 mark × 2 = 2 marks)
(b)	(i)	According to the quantity theory of money, an expansionary monetary policy will only lead to an increase in the general price level in the long run, but will not raise the real GDP. Thus, it is better for the government to do nothing.
	(2 marks)
(ii)	Suppose an economy is originally at long run equilibrium. If an expansionary monetary policy only affects aggregate demand, although real GDP will increase in the short run, it will return to its original long run equilibrium in the long run. However, the policy will raise the price level in the long run. Thus, it is better for the government to do nothing.	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch610 · Factors of production
questions.text:
Refer to the following data about Country B.

Year	Nominal money supply ($ billion)	Nominal GDP 
($ billion)	
1	100	110	
2	150	140	

(a)	Define the velocity of circulation of money (V) and show the definition by an equation.	(3 marks)
(b)	Explain whether the above data are consistent with the assumption of the quantity theory of money on V.	(4 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Velocity of circulation of money is the average number of times that money has to change hands in order to complete transactions of final products in a year.
	(2 marks)
It is the ratio of the nominal GDP (PY) to the nominal money supply (M) as shown below:
	(1 mark)
(b)	V in Year 1 = 110 / 100 = 1.1	(1 mark)
V in Year 2 = 140 / 150 = 0.93 (corr. to 2 decimal places)	(1 mark)
The quantity theory of money assumes that V is a constant.	(1 mark)
As there is a decrease in V during the period, the data are not consistent with the assumption.	(1 mark)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch610 · Factors of production
questions.text:
To finance its expenditure in building Olympic Games facilities, the Brazilian government had to reduce its expenditures on public hospitals, schools and the police force.
(a)	Explain ONE possible undesirable consequence on the economy of cutting the above expenditures.	(2 marks)
(b)	Construction of the facilities might have been financed by printing money instead. Briefly explain ONE advantage and ONE disadvantage of printing money, compared with reducing the above expenditures.	(4 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	(	Cutting expenditure on public services will reduce social transfers to low income groups. This tends to widen the income gap and cause social problems.
	(	Cutting expenditure on schools may reduce labour productivity in the future. Long run aggregate supply and thus aggregate output decrease.
	(Any ONE of the above or other reasonable answers. 2 marks)
(b)	Advantage:
	Printing money can lower interest rates and stimulate investment. Aggregate demand will increase, resulting in an increase in the output level and employment level (in the short run).	(2 marks)
	Disadvantage:
	Printing money will raise the price level, which may cause/worsen the problem of inflation.	(2 marks)
	(Accept other reasonable answers.)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch610 · Factors of production
questions.text:
The government has considered stimulating the economy by one of the following measures:
Measure 1: Lowering the required reserve ratio
Measure 2: Providing production subsidies to firms
(a)	Explain how the above measures can stimulate the economy.	(4 marks)
(b)	Discuss ONE possible undesirable effect of EACH measure.	(4 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Lowering the required reserve ratio increases money supply, resulting in a decrease in interest rates and an increase in investment expenditure. Aggregate demand will increase and so will aggregate output.	(2 marks)
	Providing production subsidies to firms reduces production costs. Short run aggregate supply will increase and so will aggregate output.	(2 marks)
(b)	Measure 1 will increase the price level, which may worsen the problem of inflation.	(2 marks)
	Measure 2 will impose a financial burden on the government, which may increase the fiscal deficit or reduce the fiscal surplus.	(2 marks)
	(Accept other reasonable answers.)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch610 · Factors of production
questions.text:
Country J is facing an enormous fiscal deficit. As a result, the central bank decides to reduce the discount rate.
(a)	Explain the effect that reducing the discount rate would have on the fiscal deficit.	(4 marks)
(b)	Increasing tax rates may also help relieve the fiscal deficit. State ONE advantage and ONE disadvantage of reducing the discount rate over increasing tax rates.
	(4 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	When the discount rate decreases, banks borrow more from the central bank to make more loans. Therefore, money supply increases and the market interest rate falls.	(2 marks)
	Aggregate demand increases, leading to an increase in real output. Therefore, tax revenue increases and the fiscal deficit decreases.	(2 marks)
(b)	Advantage:
	Reducing the discount rate leads to an increase in real output while increasing tax rates leads to a decrease in real output.	(2 marks)
	(Accept other reasonable answer.)
	Disadvantage:
	Reducing the discount rate causes the price level to increase while increasing tax rates suppresses the price level.	(2 marks)
	(Accept other reasonable answer.)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch610 · Factors of production
questions.text: In 2015, Taiwan faced the problems of unemployment and deflation. To increase the employment level and the price level, the Central Bank of Taiwan lowered the discount rate by 0.125%. With the aid of a diagram, explain whether the unemployment and deflation problems could be solved by lowering the discount rate.	(6 marks)
questions.answerText:
Indicate on the diagram:
(	Aggregate demand curve shifts rightwards.	(1 mark)
(	Output and price levels increase.	(1 mark)

Verbal elaboration:
Yes.
Lowering the discount rate will increase money supply, resulting in a decrease in the interest rate.	(1 mark)
Consumption and investment expenditures will increase and so will aggregate demand.	(1 mark)
Therefore, output increases, leading to an increase in the employment level.	(1 mark)
Also, the price level will increase from P1 to P2.	(1 mark)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch610 · Factors of production
questions.text:
The People's Bank of China has lowered the required reserve ratio several times.
(a)	With the aid of an AS-AD diagram, explain the short run effect of the above policy on price and output levels in China.	(7 marks)
(b)	An economist commented that the effect on the output level is limited due to the revaluation of the renminbi against its trading partners' currencies. Explain his statement.	(3 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Indicate on the diagram:
(	Aggregate demand curve shifts rightwards.	(1 mark)
(	Price and output levels increase.	(1 mark)

Verbal elaboration:
Lowering the required reserve ratio will increase money supply.	(1 mark)
This will lower the interest rate.	(1 mark)
Gross investment expenditure and consumption expenditure increase.	(1 mark)
Aggregate demand increases.	(1 mark)
Both output and price levels increase in the short run.	(1 mark)
(b)	When the renminbi is revaluated against foreign currencies, China's volume of exports will decrease and its volume of imports will increase.	(2 marks)
	As a result, aggregate demand decreases, which offsets the effect on the output level of lowering the required reserve ratio.	(1 mark)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch610 · Factors of production
questions.text:
On March 1, 2016, the People's Bank of China cut the required reserve ratio by 0.5%.
(a)	Explain the effect of lowering the required reserve ratio on the real interest rate in China.	(4 marks)
(b)	With the aid of an AS-AD diagram, explain the effects of the above event on China's price and output levels in the short run.	(5 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	When the central bank lowers the required reserve ratio, banks need to keep less in required reserves.	(1 mark)
	Thus, they have more excess reserves to lend for profit.	(1 mark)
	Through the process of money creation, the money supply increases further.
	(1 mark)
	Due to the increase in money supply, the nominal interest rate and the real interest rate fall.	(1 mark)
(b)	Indicate on the diagram:
	(	Rightward shift in the aggregate demand curve	(1 mark)
	(	Increase in price level and output level	(1 mark)
	
	Verbal elaboration:
	The fall in the real interest rate raises both private consumption expenditure and gross investment expenditure.	(1 mark)
	Hence, aggregate demand increases.	(1 mark)
	The increase in aggregate demand raises both output level and the price level.
	(1 mark)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch610 · Factors of production
questions.text:
Country H plans to expand its airport.
(a)	With the aid of a diagram, explain the effect of the airport expansion on Country H's output and price levels in the short run.	(4 marks)
(b)	Explain, giving ONE example, how monetary policy could reduce the effect of the airport expansion on the price level in the short run.	(4 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Indicate on the diagram:
(	Aggregate demand curve shifts rightwards.	(1 mark)
(	Output level and price level increase.	(1 mark)

Verbal elaboration:
Expanding the airport increases investment expenditure, leading to growth in aggregate demand.	(1 mark)
Price and output levels will increase to P2 and Y2, respectively.	(1 mark)
(b)	Contractionary monetary policies:
(	The central bank's sale of government bonds on the open market
(	Raising the discount rate
(	Raising the required reserve ratio
	(Any ONE of the above. 1 mark)
	The contractionary monetary policy reduces money supply, resulting in an increase in interest rates.	(1 mark)
	This will lower private consumption expenditure and gross investment expenditure, and thus aggregate demand.	(1 mark)
	The price level will decrease in the short run, reducing the effect of the airport expansion.	(1 mark)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch610 · Factors of production
questions.text:
An earthquake in Country E has led to severe unemployment. As a result, the central bank decides to buy government bonds from the market. With the aid of an AS-AD diagram, explain how the above policy can help relieve the unemployment problem.
	(8 marks)
questions.answerText:
Indicate on the diagram:
(	Unemployment exists (Y1 < Yf).	(1 mark)
(	Rightward shift in aggregate demand curve	(1 mark)
(	Increase in output level	(1 mark)


Verbal elaboration:
When the central bank buys government bonds, money supply increases.	(1 mark)
This causes a decrease in the interest rate.	(1 mark)
As a result, private consumption expenditure and gross investment expenditure increase.	(1 mark)
Aggregate demand increases from AD1 to AD2.	(1 mark)
Output level increases from Y1 to full employment output level Yf. Unemployment can be relieved.	(1 mark)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch610 · Factors of production
questions.text:
An economy faces the problem of unemployment. To tackle the problem, the central bank purchases government bonds from the market.
(a)	With the aid of a diagram, explain how the above measure can help the economy solve the problem.	(6 marks)
(b)	Even without the help of the central bank, discuss how market forces can also solve the problem.	(3 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Indicate on the diagram:
(	Unemployment exists (Y1 < Yf).	(1 mark)
(	Aggregate demand curve shifts rightwards.	(1 mark)
(	Output level increases.	(1 mark)

Verbal elaboration:
When the central bank purchases government bonds, money supply increases. This will lower the interest rate.	(1 mark)
As a result, gross investment expenditure increases, and so does the aggregate demand.	(1 mark)
Aggregate output increases to the full employment output level. The unemployment problem is solved.	(1 mark)
(b)	The economy faces a deflationary gap.	(1 mark)
	The excess supply of inputs will lower input prices. The short run aggregate supply will increase until the aggregate output reaches the full employment output level in the long run.	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch610 · Factors of production
questions.text:
Country X is initially at long run equilibrium. Suppose imports of oil are interrupted by heavy snowstorm.
(a)	With the aid of an AS-AD diagram, explain the short run effects of the snowstorm on Country X's price and output levels.	(4 marks)
(b)	To relieve the economic shock, Country X's central bank decides to lower the discount rate. With the aid of the same diagram, explain the effects of this monetary measure on Country X's price and output levels.	(6 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Indicate on the diagram:
	(	Leftward shift in short run aggregate supply curve	(1 mark)
	(	Increase in price level and decrease in output level in the short run	(1 mark)
	Verbal elaboration:
	As the supply of a factor input (i.e., oil) is interrupted, the short run aggregate supply decreases from SRAS1 to SRAS2.	(1 mark)
	In the short run, the price level increases from P1 to PS2 and the output level decreases from Yf to Y2.	(1 mark)
(b)	Indicate on the diagram:
	(	Rightward shift in aggregate demand curve	(1 mark)
	(	Further increase in price level and increase in output level	(1 mark)
	Verbal elaboration:
	As the central bank reduces the discount rate, money supply increases and interest rates decrease.	(1 mark)
	Therefore, consumption and investment expenditures increase.	(1 mark)
	Aggregate demand increases from AD1 to AD2.	(1 mark)
	As a result, the price level further increases to PL2 while the output level is restored to Yf.	(1 mark)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch610 · Factors of production
questions.text:
Country C is originally at long run equilibrium. Suppose the government excessively invests in infrastructure throughout the country.
(a)	With the aid of an AS-AD diagram, explain the economic phenomenon caused by excessive government investment in the short run.	(5 marks)
(b)	Explain ONE possible measure that the central bank can take to solve the problem in (a).	(5 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Indicate on the diagram:
	(	Rightward shift in aggregate demand curve	(1 mark)
	(	Increases in output level and price level	(1 mark)
	Verbal elaboration:
	Excessive government investment increases aggregate demand from AD1 to AD2.	(1 mark)
	Both output level and the price level increase.	(1 mark)
	As the output level is higher than the full employment level (Yf), the economy has overheated.	(1 mark)
(b)	The central bank may
	(	sell government bonds on the market.
	(	increase the required reserve ratio.
	(	increase the discount rate.
	(Any ONE of the above, 1 mark)
	Money supply decreases, resulting in an increase in interest rates.	(1 mark)
	Therefore, consumption and investment expenditures decrease.	(1 mark)
	Aggregate demand decreases.	(1 mark)
	The output level and price level are restored to the original level. The economy stops overheating.	(1 mark)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch610 · Factors of production
questions.text:
Country U has been accused of excessively printing money.
(a)	With the aid of an AS-AD diagram, explain the effect of printing money on the price level in the long run.	(6 marks)
(b)	'An increase in money supply will have no effect on nominal national income.' Using the quantity theory of money, explain whether you agree with this statement.
	(4 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Indicate on the diagram:
(	Aggregate demand curve shifts rightwards.	(1 mark)
(	Vertical LRAS	(1 mark)
(	Price level increases.	(1 mark)

Verbal elaboration:
Printing money increases the money supply, resulting in a decrease in the interest rate.	(1 mark)
Gross investment expenditure and consumption expenditure increase and so does aggregate demand.	(1 mark)
The price level increases in the long run.	(1 mark)
(b)	Disagree.	(1 mark)
	According to the quantity theory of money, MV = PY, where M, V, P, and Y are money stock, velocity of circulation of money, general price level, and real output, respectively. V is assumed to be constant.	(2 marks)
	An increase in money supply will lead to an increase in nominal national income by the same percentage.	(1 mark)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch610 · Factors of production
questions.text:
The following table shows a banking system's balance sheet.

Assets ($ million)	Liabilities ($ million)	
Reserves	200	Deposits	1,000	
Loans	800			

Suppose the public does not hold cash, and the banking system has no excess reserves.
(a)	Find the required reserve ratio. Show your calculations.	(2 marks)
(b)	Suppose $200 million newly printed banknotes are injected into the banking system.
	(i)	If the banking system lends all of its excess reserves, what is the new money supply? Show your calculations.	(2 marks)
	(ii)	With the aid of a diagram, explain the long run effect of the change in money supply on output and price levels.	(7 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Required reserve ratio = $200 million ÷ $1,000 million = 0.2	(2 marks)
(b)	(i)	New money supply = $(200 + 200) million × (1/0.2) = $2,000 million
	(2 marks)
	(ii)	Indicate on the diagram:
(	Rightward shift in aggregate demand curve	(1 mark)
(	Vertical LRAS	(1 mark)
(	Increase in price level	(1 mark)

	Verbal elaboration:
As money supply increases, interest rates decrease.	(1 mark)
Therefore, gross investment expenditure increases,	(1 mark)
and thus aggregate demand increases.	(1 mark)
In the long run, the change in money supply does not have an impact on the output level. Only the price level increases in the long run.	(1 mark)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch610 · Factors of production
questions.text:
The following shows a banking system's balance sheet.

Assets ($ billion)	Liabilities ($ billion)	
Reserves	100	Deposits	500	
Loans	400			

Suppose the public never holds cash and banks never hold excess reserves. The central bank conducts open market sales of bonds worth $20 billion.
(a)	Calculate the change in monetary base and money supply.	(4 marks)
(b)	Suppose the economy initially overheats. With the aid of an AS-AD diagram, explain how the above change in money supply can solve the problem.	(7 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	As $20 billion in bonds are sold on the market, the bank's reserves decrease by $20 billion. Hence, the monetary base decreases by $20 billion.	(2 marks)
	Required reserve ratio = $100 billion ÷ $500 billion = 0.2	(1 mark)
	Change in money supply = 0 + (-$20 billion ÷ 0.2) = -$100 billion	(1 mark)
(b)	Indicate on the diagram:
	(	Initial output level > Long run output level	(1 mark)
	(	Leftward shift in aggregate demand curve	(1 mark)
	(	Decrease in output level	(1 mark)
	
	Verbal elaboration:
	The decrease in money supply causes an increase in the interest rate.	(1 mark)
	As a result, private consumption expenditure and gross investment expenditure decrease.	(1 mark)
	Aggregate demand decreases from AD1 to AD2.	(1 mark)
	Hence, output level decreases from Y1 to the full employment output level Yf. The problem of overheating can be solved.	(1 mark)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch610 · Factors of production
questions.text:
The balance sheet of Country C's banking system is shown as follows:

Assets ($)	Liabilities ($)	
Reserves	300	Deposits	3,000	
Loans	2,700			

Suppose the public holds $100 cash, and the banking system has no excess reserves.
(a)	Calculate the money supply. Show your calculations.	(2 marks)
(b)	Suppose the public deposits the $100 cash into the banking system, and the banking system lends all of its excess reserves.
	(i)	Calculate the change in money supply. Show your calculations.	(3 marks)
	(ii)	Based on the quantity theory of money, predict the effect of the change in money supply in (b)(i) on the price level. State the assumptions needed to reach your conclusion.	(4 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Money supply = $100 + $3,000 = $3,100	(2 marks)
(b)	(i)	Money supply = Cash in circulation + Deposits
		= $0 + ($400 × 1/0.1)
		= $4,000	(2 marks)
		Change in money supply = $4,000 - $3,100 = $900	(1 mark)
	(ii)	According to the quantity theory of money, MV = PY, where M, V, P, and Y are money stock, velocity of circulation of money, general price level, and real output, respectively. V is assumed to be constant.	(2 marks)
		The increase in M leads to an increase in P in the short run if Y increases by a smaller percentage than M.	(2 marks)
		OR
		The increase in M leads to an increase in P by the same percentage when Y remains unchanged.	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch610 · Factors of production
questions.text:
The following table shows a banking system's balance sheet.

Assets ($)	Liabilities ($)	
Reserves	1,000	Deposits	20,000	
Loans	19,000			

Suppose the public does not hold cash and the banking system has no excess reserves.
(a)	Find the money supply. Show your calculations.	(2 marks)
(b)	Suppose the central bank lowers the required reserve ratio by 1%.
	(i)	Find the change in money supply. Show your calculations.	(3 marks)
	(ii)	Based on the quantity theory of money, predict the long run effect of the change in money supply in (b)(i) on the price level. State the assumptions needed to reach your conclusion.	(4 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Money supply = $0 + $20,000 = $20,000	(2 marks)
(b)	(i)	The new required reserve ratio is 4%.	(1 mark)
		Change in money supply = ($1,000 × 1/0.04) - $20,000 = $5,000	(2 marks)
	(ii)	According to the quantity theory of money, MV = PY, where M, V, P, and Y are money stock, velocity of circulation of money, general price level, and real output, respectively.	(1 mark)
		In the long run, both V and Y are assumed to be constant.	(1 mark)
		The increase in M leads to an increase in P by the same percentage (25%) in the long run.	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch610 · Factors of production
questions.text:
The following is a banking system's balance sheet.

Assets ($ billion)	Liabilities ($ billion)	
Reserves	300	Deposits	1,200	
Loans	900			

Suppose the public never holds cash and banks never hold excess reserves. The central bank lowers the required reserve ratio by 5%.
(a)	Calculate the percentage change in money supply.	(4 marks)
(b)	(i)	State the equation of exchange.	(2 marks)
	(ii)	With reference to your answer in (a), compare the percentage change in the price level in the short run and long run, respectively.	(4 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Original required reserve ratio 
= ($300 billion ÷ $1,200 billion) × 100% = 25%	(1 mark)
	New required reserve ratio = 25% − 5% = 20%	(1 mark)
	New amount of deposits = $300 billion ÷ 20% = $1,500 billion	(1 mark)
	Percentage change in money supply 
	= $(1,500 - 1,200) billion ÷ $1,200 billion × 100% = 25%	(1 mark)
(b)	(i)	MV ≡ PY, where M = money stock / nominal money supply, 
V = velocity of circulation of money, 
P = general price level and 
Y = real output / real national income.	(2 marks)
	(ii)	In the short run, only V is a constant. Both P and Y are variables. Therefore, a 25% increase in the money supply may lead to an increase of less than 25% in the price level.	(2 marks)
		In the long run, both V and Y are constants. Therefore, a 25% increase in the money supply will cause a 25% increase in the price level.	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch610 · Factors of production
questions.text: Explain whether a persistent increase in money supply can create long run real output growth, according to the classical quantity theory of money. State the assumption(s) of the theory in order to reach your conclusion.	(5 marks)
questions.answerText:
No.	(1 mark)
According to the classical quantity theory of money, an increase in money supply only causes the same proportional increase in the price level without affecting real output in the long run.	(2 marks)
Assumptions:
Velocity of circulation of money is constant.	(1 mark)
Real output is constant in the long run.	(1 mark)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch610 · Factors of production
questions.text:
In Country Z, the money supply has recently increased by 100%. The president thinks that this can boost production in the economy.
(a)	State the equation of exchange.	(2 marks)
(b)	Explain whether the president's goal can be achieved in the short run and the long run, respectively.	(4 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	MV ≡ PY, where M = money stock / nominal money supply, 
V = velocity of circulation of money, 
P = general price level and 
Y = real output / real national income.	(2 marks)
(b)	In the short run, only V is a constant. Both P and Y are variables. Therefore, an increase in money supply may lead to an increase in production.	(2 marks)
	In the long run, both V and Y are constants. Therefore, a 100% increase in money supply will only cause a 100% increase in the price level, without affecting production.	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch610 · Factors of production
questions.text: The Zimbabwean government issued money without restraint to finance its military expenses from a war in the 2000s. With reference to the quantity theory of money, explain the economic phenomenon that would likely occur in the long run.	(5 marks)
questions.answerText:
According to the quantity theory of money, the velocity of circulation of money and real output are constant in the long run. Hence, the price level changes positively with money supply in the long run.	(2 marks)
As money supply was increased without restraint, the price level would increase at an extremely high rate.	(2 marks)
Hence, hyperinflation (or extreme inflation) occurred.	(1 mark)


Structured Questions

questions.topic: B6 · Ch610 · Factors of production
questions.text:
City A was originally in long run equilibrium. Suppose the government begins construction of the new airport.
(a)	With the aid of an AS-AD diagram, explain the short run and long run effects of the above policy on the price level.	(10 marks)
(b)	Suggest ONE monetary tool that the central bank can use to offset the change in the price level in the long run. Briefly explain how it works.	(4 marks)
(c)	After the completion of the project, some economists predict that the economy will slow down. Due to this prediction, some politicians suggest that the central bank should increase the money supply to raise real national income. Explain the effectiveness of this suggestion in both the short run and the long run, according to the predictions of the quantity theory of money.	(5 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Indicate on the diagram:
	(	Rightward shift in the aggregate demand curve	(1 mark)
	(	Increase in the price level in the short run	(1 mark)
	(	Leftward shift in the short run aggregate supply curve	(1 mark)
	(	Further increase in the price level in the long run	(1 mark)
	
	Verbal elaboration:
	Government investment expenditure increases due to the construction of the new airport.	(1 mark)
	Hence, aggregate demand increases from AD1 to AD2.	(1 mark)
	In the short run, the price level increases from P1 to PS2.	(1 mark)
	As there is an inflationary gap, the excess demand for inputs raises input prices.
	(1 mark)
	The short run aggregate supply decreases from SRAS1 to SRAS2.	(1 mark)
	In the long run, the price level further increases to PL2.	(1 mark)

(b)	The central bank can
	(	sell government bonds to the market.
	(	raise the discount rate.
	(	raise the required reserve ratio.
	(Any ONE of the above, 1 mark)
	The money supply will decrease.	(1 mark)
	Aggregate demand will then decrease.	(1 mark)
	Hence, the price level can be brought down.	(1 mark)

(c)	The quantity theory of money predicts that a change in nominal money supply will cause the same percentage change in nominal national income.	(1 mark)
	In the short run, the expansionary monetary policy may be effective. Both the price level and real national income may increase.	(2 marks)
	In the long run, the policy will not be effective as real national income is fixed at the full employment level. The increase in money supply will only cause the same percentage increase in the price level.	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch610 · Factors of production
questions.text:
To reduce the impact of inflation, the government of Region H has issued inflation-linked bonds (iBonds). Many of the iBonds are sold from the central bank to the public.
(a)	What are the effects of inflation? State TWO of them.	(2 marks)
(b)	Suppose there is unexpected inflation after people buy iBonds. Explain whether these bondholders would gain or lose from the unexpected inflation.	(3 marks)
(c)	With the aid of a diagram, explain the effect of issuing iBonds on the cost of holding money.	(5 marks)
(d)	What is the effect of issuing iBonds on the price level in the short run? Briefly explain with the aid of a diagram.	(5 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Effects include:
	(	Income redistribution
	(	Increase in the cost of living
	(	Possible decrease in the standard of living
	(	Resource reallocation
	(	Decrease in net exports
(Any TWO of the above or other reasonable answers. 1 mark × 2 = 2 marks)

(b)	(	Those bondholders would neither gain nor lose from the unexpected inflation.	(1 mark)
(	Their interest income from iBonds is indexed to the inflation rate.	(1 mark)
(	Therefore, the purchasing power of their interest income does not change.
	(1 mark)

(c)	Indicate on the diagram:
	(	Leftward shift of money supply curve	(1 mark)
	(	Increase in nominal interest rate	(1 mark)
	
Verbal elaboration:
(	As the central bank sells iBonds to the public, the money supply decreases.
	(1 mark)
(	The nominal interest rate, which is the cost of holding money, increases.
	(2 marks)

(d)	Indicate on the diagram:
	(	Aggregate demand curve shifts leftwards.	(1 mark)
	(	The price level decreases in the short run.	(1 mark)

Verbal elaboration:
(	Other things being equal, the increase in the nominal interest rate implies an increase in the real interest rate. As a result, aggregate demand decreases.
	(2 marks)
(	The price level decreases in the short run.	(1 mark)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch610 · Factors of production
questions.text:
Country A's government has distributed $10,000 to each citizen. The policy is financed by printing money.
(a)	John is a citizen in Country A and has received the $10,000 grant. Given constant market prices, how will this affect John's consumption of luxury goods? Explain with a well-labelled diagram.	(4 marks)
(b)	Briefly explain how the above policy will affect Country A's output level and price level in the long run with
(i)	the AS-AD model;	(7 marks)
(ii)	the quantity theory of money.	(4 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Indicate on the diagram:
	(	John's demand for luxury goods increases.	(1 mark)
	(	John's consumption of luxury goods increases.	(1 mark)

Verbal elaboration:
(	The increase in John's wealth will lead to an increase in his demand for luxury goods.	(1 mark)
(	As a result, his consumption increases from Q1 to Q2.	(1 mark)

(b)	(i)	Indicate on the diagram:
(	Aggregate demand curve shifts rightwards.	(1 mark)
(	Vertical long run aggregate supply curve	(1 mark)
(	Output stays at its full employment level and the price level increases.
	(1 mark)

Verbal elaboration:
(	When everyone in Country A has more wealth, their private consumption expenditure will increase. Thus, aggregate demand will increase.	(2 marks)
(	In the long run, the output level will remain unchanged.	(1 mark)
(	The price level will increase.	(1 mark)
(ii)	(	The equation of exchange is MV ( PY.	(1 mark)
(	The quantity theory of money assumes that the velocity of circulation of money (V) is constant.	(1 mark)
(	The theory also assumes that, in the long run, the output level (Y) remains constant at the full employment level.	(1 mark)
(	Hence, in the long run, the increase in money supply (M) will bring a proportional change in the price level (P) only.	(1 mark)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch610 · Factors of production
questions.text:
Suppose an economy faces the problem of unemployment caused by a decrease in the short run aggregate supply. The government decides to solve the problem by printing more money. Some free-market economists claim that it is better for the government to do nothing than printing more money.
(a)	Use an AS-AD diagram to explain how the market achieves long run equilibrium without government intervention. Show the change in the general price level.
	(5 marks)
(b)	Use an AS-AD diagram to explain the effect of the above policy on the general price level in the long run.	(7 marks)
*(c)	Evaluate the claim of free-market economists, based on the stability of the general price level.	(3 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	When there is a problem of unemployment, the real GDP will be smaller than the full employment level (or long run equilibrium level) in the short run. A deflationary gap exists.	(1 mark)
In the long run, excess supply of resources would lower input prices. The short run aggregate supply curve shifts downwards from SRAS1 to SRAS2.	(1 mark)
The deflationary gap is closed and the general price level decreases from P1 to P2.	(1 mark)
	(2 marks)
(b)	The policy will increase the money supply.	(1 mark)
As the money supply increases, the real interest rate will fall.	(1 mark)
A fall in the real interest rate increases both private consumption expenditure and gross investment expenditure.	(1 mark)
The aggregate demand increases and the aggregate demand curve shifts rightwards from AD1 to AD2.	(1 mark)
The general price level will increase from P1 to P2.	(1 mark)
	(2 marks)
(c)	The problem of unemployment is caused by a decrease in short run aggregate supply. Thus, initially, there is an increase in the general price level. If the government increases the money supply, the general price level will increase further.	(1 mark)
However, if the government does nothing, the economy can adjust itself and achieve long run equilibrium without an increase in the general price level.
	(1 mark)
Thus, if the government wants to stabilise the general price level at the same time, it may be better for the government to do nothing rather than printing money.
	(1 mark)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch610 · Factors of production
questions.text:
Suppose Country A is now facing the problem of unemployment. To deal with the problem, the central bank lowers the discount rate.
(a)	Explain the effect of the decrease in the discount rate on the money supply.
	(3 marks)
(b)	With the aid of a diagram, explain how the policy can solve the unemployment problem.	(6 marks)
(c)	Some people claim that the policy can be used to boost economic growth in the long run. Explain whether this claim is true in light of the quantity theory of money.	(3 marks)
(d)	Suggest TWO policies that can stimulate long run economic growth.	(2 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	When the central bank lowers the discount rate, banks' cost of borrowing from the central bank drops.	(1 mark)
	It is profitable for banks to borrow more from the central bank to make more 
loans.	(1 mark)
	Through the money creation process, the money supply increase further.	(1 mark)

(b)	Indicate on the diagram:
	(	Unemployment	(1 mark)
	(	Rightward shift in the aggregate demand curve	(1 mark)
	(	Increase in aggregate output	(1 mark)
	
	Verbal elaboration:
	When the money supply increases, both nominal and real interest rates decrease.
	(1 mark)
	Both consumption expenditure and gross investment expenditure increase. 
Hence, aggregate demand increases from AD1 to AD2.	(1 mark)
	The increase in aggregate demand raises aggregate output back to the full employment level.	(1 mark)

(c)	According to the quantity theory of money, an increase in the money supply cannot raise real national income in the long run. This will only cause inflation in the long run.	(2 marks)
	Hence, the claim is not true.	(1 mark)

(d)	(	Increasing government expenditure on education
	(	Increasing government expenditure on medical care
	(	Increasing government expenditure on infrastructure
	(Any TWO of the above or other reasonable answers. 1 mark × 2 = 2 marks)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch610 · Factors of production
questions.text:
Venezuela has suffered from severe inflation in recent years.
(a)	To relieve people's burden, the Venezuelan government imposed price ceilings on daily necessities.
	Briefly explain whether the price ceilings necessarily benefit consumers in terms of consumer surplus.	(4 marks)
(b)	Recently, the Venezuelan government opened its border with Colombia. As a result, Venezuelan citizens have rushed to Colombia for daily necessities.
	(i)	With the aid of a diagram, explain the short run effect of opening the border on Colombia's output and price levels.	(5 marks)
	(ii)	Explain, with ONE example, what measure the central bank of Colombia can take to reduce the effects that you stated in (b)(i).	(3 marks)
(c)	Venezuela's money supply has increased by several times in recent years. Based on the quantity theory of money, explain the effect of the increase in money supply on the price level. State the assumptions needed to reach your conclusion.
	(4 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	No.	(1 mark)
	Under price ceilings, both the price and quantity transacted decrease.	(1 mark)
	If the gain in consumer surplus that results from a falling price is smaller than the loss in consumer surplus from a drop in quantity transacted, consumers will enjoy less of a consumer surplus.	(2 marks)
(b)	(i)	Indicate on the diagram:
		(	Increase in aggregate demand	(1 mark)
		(	Increase in output level and price level	(1 mark)
		
	Verbal elaboration:
	As Venezuelans can now buy daily necessities from Colombia, Colombia's net exports increase.	(1 mark)
	Aggregate demand increases,	(1 mark)
	leading to an increase in Colombia's output and price levels in the short run.		(1 mark)
	(ii)	Selling government bonds on the market / Raising the discount rate / Raising the required reserve ratio	(1 mark)
		The measure can reduce money supply, leading to an increase in the interest rate and a decrease in gross investment expenditure.	(1 mark)
		Aggregate demand will decrease, resulting in a decrease in output and price levels.	(1 mark)
(c)	According to the quantity theory of money, MV = PY, where M, V, P, and Y are money stock, velocity of circulation of money, general price level, and real output, respectively. V is assumed to be constant.	(2 marks)
	The increase in M leads to an increase in P in the short run, if Y increases by a smaller percentage than M.	(2 marks)
	OR

questions.topic: B6 · Ch611 · Production in the short run and long run
questions.text:

	Abalone		Mangoes	
Australia	10 units	OR	2 units	
Thailand	4 units	OR	32 units	

Suppose the original terms of trade is 1 unit of mangoes : 0.18 units of abalone. Now, the terms of trade changes to 1 unit of mangoes : 0.1 units of abalone. Thailand's unit gains from trading mangoes will
A.	increase by 0.08 units of abalone.
B.	decrease by 0.08 units of abalone.
C.	remain unchanged.
D.	None of the above
questions.answerText:
Opportunity cost of producing mangoes in Thailand = 4 ÷ 32 = 0.125 units of abalone
Opportunity cost of producing mangoes in Australia = 10 ÷ 2 = 5 units of abalone
As the new terms of trade is lower than both countries' cost of producing mangoes, there will be no trade.

questions.topic: B6 · Ch611 · Production in the short run and long run
questions.text:
* The following table shows the production and consumption information of 
Country Y.

	Milk (units)		Bread (units)	
Total production without trade	40	AND	60	
Total production with complete specialisation	0	AND	180	
Total consumption with trade	80	AND	100	

Which of the following statements are correct?
(1)	The cost of producing 1 unit of milk in Country Y is 1.5 units of bread.
(2)	The terms of trade is 1 unit of milk : 1 unit of bread.
(3)	The gain from trading 1 unit of milk is 2 units of bread
A.	(2) only
B.	(1) and (3) only
C.	(2) and (3) only
D.	(1), (2) and (3)
questions.answerText:
Country Y has to forgo 40 units of milk in order to produce extra 120 units of bread. Hence, the cost of producing 1 unit of milk is 3 units of bread. Option (1) is not correct.
Country Y exports 80 units of bread in exchange for 80 units of milk. Option (2) is correct.
Gain from trading 1 unit of milk
= Cost of producing 1 unit of milk - Cost of importing 1 unit of milk
= 3 - 1 = 2 units of bread
Option (3) is correct.

questions.topic: B6 · Ch611 · Production in the short run and long run
questions.text:
* Before trading, Country A and Country B use half of their resources to produce wheat and the other half to produce machines. The following table gives information about the two countries before and after they trade according to the principle of comparative advantage.

		Wheat (units)		Machines (units)	
Country A	Production combinations before trade	50	AND	80	
	Consumption combinations after trade	60	AND	90	
Country B	Production combinations before trade	90	AND	45	
	Consumption combinations after trade	120	AND	X	

Suppose Country A does not keep any stock of machines. From the data above, which of the following conclusions can be drawn?
A.	The total gains from trade for the two countries are 40 units of wheat.
B.	The terms of trade is 1 unit of wheat : 1 unit of machines.
C.	The value of X is 70.
D.	There is insufficient information to determine.
questions.answerText:
Option A is incorrect. In this case, total production is equal to total consumption. To find the total gains from trade, we need to compare the total production (consumption) before trade and the total production (consumption) after trade. The total production of wheat before trade is 140 units while the total production of wheat after trade is 180 units. The total production of machines before trade is 125 units while the total production after trade is 160 units. Thus, the total gains from trade are 40 units of wheat and 35 units of machines.
Option C is correct. When Country A specialises in producing machines, it can produce 160 units of machines. As Country A consumes 90 units of machines after trade, Country B can only consume 70 units of machines.

questions.topic: B6 · Ch611 · Production in the short run and long run
questions.text:
* Suppose the marginal costs of producing wheat and machines are constant. Before trading, Country A and Country B use half of their resources to produce wheat and the other half to produce machines. The following table gives information about the two countries before and after they trade according to the principle of comparative advantage.

		Wheat (units)		Machines (units)	
Country A	Production combinations before trade	50	AND	80	
	Consumption combinations after trade	X	AND	100	
Country B	Production combinations before trade	90	AND	45

Suppose both countries keep no inventory. The values of X and Y are _________ and _________, respectively.
A.	60 … 60
B.	40 … 70
C.	70 … 50
D.	Insufficient information to answer.
questions.answerText:
After complete specialisation, the total production of wheat is 180 units while the total production of machines is 160 units. These are the maximum amounts of goods that the two countries can consume. Hence,
X + 2X = 180 ( X = 60
100 + Y = 160 ( Y = 60

questions.topic: B6 · Ch611 · Production in the short run and long run
questions.text:
(a)	'When a country has an absolute advantage over another country in producing Good X, it must have a comparative advantage over the other country in producing Good X.' Do you agree? Explain.	(3 marks)
(b)	'When a country has a comparative advantage over another country in producing Good Y, it must have an absolute advantage over the other country in producing Good Y.' Do you agree? Explain.	(3 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	No.	(1 mark)
Even if a country has a higher productivity in producing Good X than the other country, it may have a higher cost (i.e., forgoing a larger amount of another good) of producing Good X than the other country.	(2 marks)
(b)	No.	(1 mark)
Even if a country has a lower cost (i.e., forgoing a smaller amount of another good) of producing Good Y than the other country, it may have lower productivity in producing Good Y than the other country.	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch611 · Production in the short run and long run
questions.text:
(a)	What is absolute advantage?	(2 marks)
(b)	'It is impossible for a country to have absolute disadvantages in producing all goods.' Do you agree? Briefly explain.	(2 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	A country has an absolute advantage over another country in the production of a good if it can produce a larger amount of the good than the other country with the same amount of resources.	(2 marks)
(b)	No.	(1 mark)
It is possible for a country to have lower productivity than the other country in producing all goods.	(1 mark)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch611 · Production in the short run and long run
questions.text:
(a)	What is the meaning of absolute advantage?	(2 marks)
(b)	Suppose the amount of resources in Country A is double that of Country B, and the two countries can produce the same amount of Good X and Good Y with all of their resources. Explain which country has the absolute advantages in producing these two goods.	(2 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	A country has an absolute advantage over another country in the production of a good if it can produce a larger amount of the good than the other country with the same amount of resources.	(2 marks)
(b)	Country B will have absolute advantages in producing both Good X and Good Y as it can use a smaller amount of resources than Country A to produce the same amount of the two goods.	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch611 · Production in the short run and long run
questions.text:
(a)	What is comparative advantage?	(2 marks)
(b)	'Suppose there are two goods: Good X and Good Y. If Country A can use a smaller amount of resources than Country B to produce the same amount of 
Good X and Good Y, it will have comparative advantages in producing both 
Good X and Good Y.' Is this statement correct? Explain.	(3 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	A country has a comparative advantage over another country in the production of a good if it can produce the good at a lower opportunity cost than the other country.	(2 marks)
(b)	Incorrect.	(1 mark)
It is impossible for Country A to have comparative advantages in producing all goods.	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch611 · Production in the short run and long run
questions.text:
(a)	State the principle of comparative advantage.	(2 marks)
(b)	Suppose on Planet X all countries have the same production technology in all goods: the amount of output produced is the same for a given amount of resources in all countries. Explain whether the total output will increase if two countries trade according to the principle of comparative advantage.	(2 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	The principle of comparative advantage states that if each country specialises in producing the good in which it has a comparative advantage, total world output will increase.	(2 marks)
(b)	As production costs are the same in the countries, no country has comparative advantages in producing the goods. No cost can be saved by reallocating the production of a good. Thus, total output will remain unchanged.	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch611 · Production in the short run and long run
questions.text:
The following table shows the amount of goods that each unit of resources can produce in Country X and Country Y. Both countries only produce paper and cheese.

	Paper (units)		Cheese (units)	
Country X	10	OR	40	
Country Y	25	OR	50	

(a)	Determine which country has a comparative advantage in producing each of the goods.	(6 marks)
(b)	Suppose both countries have 10 units of resources, and employ 6 units in producing paper while 4 units are employed in producing cheese before trade. Explain whether this case can illustrate the principle of comparative advantage if both countries engage in complete specialisation.	(6 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Cost of producing paper in Country X
	= 40 ÷ 10 = 4 units of cheese	(1 mark)
	Cost of producing paper in Country Y
	= 50 ÷ 25 = 2 units of cheese	(1 mark)
	As Country Y can produce paper at a lower cost, it has a comparative advantage in producing paper.	(1 mark)
	Cost of producing cheese in Country X
	= 10 ÷ 40 = 0.25 units of paper	(1 mark)
	Cost of producing cheese in Country Y
	= 25 ÷ 50 = 0.5 units of paper	(1 mark)
	As Country X can produce cheese at a lower cost, it has a comparative advantage in producing cheese.	(1 mark)
(b)	Total production of paper before trade
	= 10 × 6 + 25 × 6 = 210 units	(1 mark)
	Total production of cheese before trade
	= 40 × 4 + 50 × 4 = 360 units	(1 mark)
	Total production of paper after complete specialisation
	= 25 × 10 = 250 units	(1 mark)
	Total production of cheese after complete specialisation
	= 40 × 10 = 400 units	(1 mark)
	The case can illustrate the principle of comparative advantage because the total output of all countries increases.	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch611 · Production in the short run and long run
questions.text:
Suppose Country A and Country B produce only peanuts and almonds. The following table shows the amount of peanuts or almonds produced per unit of resources.

	Peanuts (units)	Almonds (units)	
Country A	15	12	
Country B	20	16	

(a)	Which country has an absolute advantage in producing peanuts? Which country has a comparative advantage in producing almonds? Explain.	(4 marks)
(b)	Explain whether Country A and Country B will trade peanuts with each other.
	(2 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Country B can produce a larger amount of peanuts per unit of input. Thus, it has an absolute advantage in producing peanuts.	(2 marks)
Country A's opportunity cost of producing 1 unit of almonds is 1.25 (= 15 / 12) units of peanuts. Country B's opportunity cost of producing 1 unit of almonds is also 1.25 (= 20 / 16) units of peanuts. As both countries have the same cost in producing almonds, no country has a comparative advantage in producing almonds.	(2 marks)
(b)	Country A's opportunity cost of producing 1 unit of peanuts is 0.75 (= 12 / 15) units of almonds while Country B's opportunity cost of producing 1 unit of peanuts is also 0.75 (= 16 / 20) units of almonds. 
(Or: Since their opportunity costs of producing almonds are the same, their opportunity cost of producing peanuts are also the same.)	(1 mark)
Since their opportunity costs of producing peanuts are the same, they will not trade with each other.	(1 mark)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch611 · Production in the short run and long run
questions.text:
The following table shows the number of working hours required to produce 1 unit of apple juice or orange juice in two countries.

	Apple juice	Orange juice	
Country A	2 hours	4 hours	
Country B	3 hours	12 hours	

Explain the direction of trade between them according to the principle of comparative advantage.	(6 marks)
questions.answerText:
•	The following table shows the opportunity costs in the two countries.

	Apple juice	Orange juice	
Country A	0.5 units of orange juice	2 units of apple juice	
Country B	0.25 units of orange juice	4 units of apple juice	
		(2 marks)
•	Country A has a comparative advantage in producing orange juice since its cost of producing orange juice is lower. Therefore, Country A should export orange juice to Country B.	(2 marks)
•	Country B has a comparative advantage in producing apple juice since its cost of producing apple juice is lower. Therefore, Country B should export apple juice to Country A.	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch611 · Production in the short run and long run
questions.text:
* Country A uses an equal amount of resources to produce food and machines; Country B uses 40% of its resources to produce food and 60% of its resources to produce machines. The following table shows their production combinations.

	Food (units)		Machines (units)	
Country A	50	AND	100
