Explain the pattern of trade between the two countries according to the principle of comparative advantage.	(7 marks)
questions.answerText:
•	The following table shows the amount of goods that can be produced with all the resources in each country:

	Food (units)		Machines (units)	
Country A	100	OR	200	
Country B	100	OR	100	
		(1 mark)
•	The following table shows the opportunity costs of producing 1 unit of goods in the two countries:

	Food	Machines	
Country A	2 units of machines	0.5 units of food	
Country B	1 unit of machines	1 unit of food	
		(2 marks)
•	Since Country A's cost of producing machines is lower, Country A has a comparative advantage in producing machines. Therefore, Country A should export machines to Country B.	(2 marks)
•	Since Country B's cost of producing food is lower, Country B has a comparative advantage in producing food. Therefore, Country B should export food to 
Country A.	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch611 · Production in the short run and long run
questions.text:
Country A can produce 1 unit of Good X or 2 units of Good Y with 1 unit of inputs, while Country B can produce 2 units of Good X or 3 units of Good Y with the same amount of inputs.
(a)	Which country has an absolute advantage in producing Good X? Explain.
	(2 marks)
(b)	Which country has a comparative advantage in producing Good X? Explain.
	(2 marks)
(c)	What is the range in the terms of trade that allows both countries to gain from trade? Explain your answer briefly.	(2 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Country B has an absolute advantage in producing Good X.	(1 mark)
With 1 unit of inputs, Country B's output (2 units of Good X) is greater than Country A's (1 unit of Good X).	(1 mark)
(b)	Country B has a comparative advantage in producing Good X.	(1 mark)
To produce 1 unit of Good X, Country B's cost (1.5 units of Good Y) is lower than that of Country A (2 units of Good Y).	(1 mark)
(c)	The terms of trade should lie between their unit costs,	(1 mark)
	i.e., 1.5Y < 1X < 2Y (or 0.5X < 1Y < 0.67X).	(1 mark)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch611 · Production in the short run and long run
questions.text:
The following shows the amount of paper or pencils that two countries can produce with 1 unit of resources.

	Paper (units)		Pencils (units)	
Country A	20	OR	22	
Country B	16	OR	24	

Suppose each country has 10 units of resources.
(a)	If both countries completely specialise in producing the good in which they have a comparative advantage, find the total output of the two goods.	(6 marks)
(b)	If 1 unit of paper can be exchanged by one country for the other country's 1.2 units of pencils, find the two countries' gain from each unit of paper exchanged,
respectively.	(4 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Country A's cost of producing 1 unit of paper 
	= 22 ÷ 20 = 1.1 units of pencils	(1 mark)
	Country B's cost of producing 1 unit of paper
	= 24 ÷ 16 = 1.5 units of pencils	(1 mark)
	Hence, Country A has a comparative advantage in producing paper while 
Country B has a comparative advantage in producing pencils.	(2 marks)
	Total output of paper = 10 × 20 = 200 units of paper	(1 mark)
	Total output of pencils = 10 × 24 = 240 units of pencils	(1 mark)
(b)	Country A's gain from each unit of paper exported
= 1.2 - 1.1 = 0.1 units of pencils	(2 marks)
Country B's gain from each unit of paper imported
= 1.5 - 1.2 = 0.3 units of pencils	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch611 · Production in the short run and long run
questions.text:
The following shows the amount of inputs needed to produce 1 unit of cotton or wool in two countries.

	Cotton	Wool	
Country A	5 units	4 units	
Country B	6 units	8 units	

(a)	Which country has a comparative advantage in producing cotton? Explain.
	(3 marks)
(b)	If the gain from trade is shared equally among the countries, what is the terms of trade? Explain your answer briefly.	(2 marks)
(c)	Suppose there is a transaction cost for each unit of cotton traded. What is the minimum amount of the transaction cost that makes trading not mutually beneficial?	(2 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Country A's cost of producing 1 unit of cotton
= 5 ÷ 4 = 1.25 units of wool	(1 mark)
Country B's cost of producing 1 unit of cotton
= 6 ÷ 8 = 0.75 units of wool	(1 mark)
Therefore, Country B has a comparative advantage in producing cotton.	(1 mark)
(b)	As the gain from trade is shared equally, the terms of trade must be the average of the two countries' production costs.	(1 mark)
	Terms of trade:
	1 unit of cotton = (1.25 + 0.75) ÷ 2 = 1 unit of wool	(1 mark)
(c)	If the transaction cost is greater than or equal to the total gain from trade, trade will not be mutually beneficial.	(1 mark)
	Minimum amount = Total gain from trade = 1.25 - 0.75 = 0.5 units of wool
	(1 mark)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch611 · Production in the short run and long run
questions.text:
The following table shows the amount of resources required to produce 1 unit of ham or 1 unit of eggs in Country E and Country F.

	Ham	Eggs	
Country E	12	8	
Country F	30	15	

(a)	Which country has a comparative advantage in producing ham? Explain your answer briefly.	(3 marks)
(b)	Suppose the terms of trade is 1 unit of ham = 1.9 units of eggs, and the transaction cost of each unit of ham is 0.3 units of eggs. If each of the countries pays half of the transaction cost, explain whether the countries would trade with each other.
	(2 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Country E's cost of producing 1 unit of ham = 12 ÷ 8 = 1.5 units of eggs	(1 mark)
	Country F's cost of producing 1 unit of ham = 30 ÷15 = 2 units of eggs	(1 mark)
	As Country E can produce ham at a lower cost, it has a comparative advantage in producing ham.	(1 mark)
(b)	Country F's gain from importing each unit of ham
	= 2 - 1.9 - 0.15 = -0.05 units of eggs	(1 mark)
	As Country F cannot gain from trade, it will not trade with Country E.	(1 mark)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch611 · Production in the short run and long run
questions.text:
The following table shows the amount of two goods that 1 unit of resources can produce in Country A and Country B.

	Pears (units)		Books (units)	
Country A	3	OR	6	
Country B	2	OR	8	

(a)		Suppose 1 unit of pears can be exchanged for 3 units of books. Based on the above information, explain why the trade between the two countries is mutually beneficial.	(4 marks)
(b)	Give ONE economic reason why the two countries may NOT trade.	(1 mark)
questions.answerText:
(a)	The cost of producing 1 unit of a good for both countries:

	Pears (P)	Books (B)	
Country A	2B	0.5P	
Country B	4B	0.25P	
	(2 marks)
The terms of trade is 1 unit of pears for 3 units of books. By exporting 1 unit of pears, Country A can gain 1 (= 3 - 2) unit of books. By importing 1 unit of pears, Country B can gain 1 (= 4 - 3) unit of books. Both countries will gain from trade and so the trade is mutually beneficial.	(2 marks)
(b)	They will not trade with each other if the gains from trade are smaller than the transport costs and transaction costs.	(1 mark)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch611 · Production in the short run and long run
questions.text:
The following table shows the amount of goods that can be produced with 1 unit of resources.

	Beer (units)		Potato chips (units)	
US	1,100	OR	550	
Canada	700	OR	420	

Suppose there is no transaction cost. According to the above table, calculate the range of the terms of trade (for 1 unit of beer) that is mutually beneficial to the two 
countries.	(3 marks)
questions.answerText:
The US's cost of producing 1 unit of beer
= 550 ÷ 1,100 = 0.5 units of potato chips	(1 mark)
Canada's cost of producing 1 unit of beer
= 420 ÷ 700 = 0.6 units of potato chips	(1 mark)
Hence, the terms of trade for 1 unit of beer should lie between 0.5 units of potato chips and 0.6 units of potato chips.	(1 mark)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch611 · Production in the short run and long run
questions.text:
Suppose there are only two goods: electronic watches and toys. The cost of producing 1 unit of electronic watches in Hong Kong is 5 units of toys.
(a)	Calculate the cost of producing 1 unit of toys in Hong Kong.	(1 mark)
(b)	Explain if Hong Kong has a comparative advantage in producing watches or toys based on the information provided and your answer in (a).	(3 marks)
(c)	Suppose the terms of trade is 1 unit of electronic watches : 6 units of toys. If there are no transport costs and transaction costs, explain which goods will be exported by Hong Kong. Calculate Hong Kong's unit gain from exports.	(2 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	0.2 (= 1 / 5) units of electronic watches	(1 mark)
(b)	We cannot determine whether Hong Kong has a comparative advantage in producing either of the goods.	(1 mark)
	Comparative advantage is the comparison in costs of producing a good between two or more countries. But we only have the information for Hong Kong.
	(2 marks)
(c)	Hong Kong will export electronic watches as its cost is smaller than the terms of trade.	(1 mark)
	It can gain 1 unit of toys from each electronic watch exported.	(1 mark)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch611 · Production in the short run and long run
questions.text:
The following table shows the amount of cakes (C) and mangoes (M) that one unit of resources can produce in Country X and Country Y.

	Cakes (units)	Mangoes (units)	
Country X	20	5	
Country Y	32	4	

(a)	Which country has a comparative advantage in producing cakes? Explain your answer briefly.	(3 marks)
(b)	Explain whether the following are possible terms of trade for the trade between Country X and Country Y.
	(i)	1C = 1M	(2 marks)
	(ii)	1C = 0.1M	(2 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Opportunity cost of producing 1 unit of cakes in Country X (in terms of mangoes) = 5 ÷ 20 = 0.25 units of mangoes	(1 mark)
	Opportunity cost of producing 1 unit of cakes in Country Y (in terms of mangoes) = 4 ÷ 32 = 0.125 units of mangoes	(1 mark)
	Country Y has a comparative advantage in producing cakes since it can produce at a lower cost than Country X.	(1 mark)
(b)	(i)	No, Country X would not import cakes because its cost of producing cakes is lower than the terms of trade.	(2 marks)
		OR
		No, Country X would not export mangoes as its cost of producing mangoes is higher than the terms of trade.	(2 marks)
	(ii)	No, Country Y would not export cakes as its cost of producing cakes is higher than the terms of trade.	(2 marks)
		OR
		No, Country Y would not import mangoes as its cost of producing mangoes is lower than the terms of trade.	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch611 · Production in the short run and long run
questions.text:
The following table shows the output per unit of resources in each of the two countries.

	Fashions (units)		Hamburgers (units)	
US	6	OR	12	
France	12	OR	9	

(a)	Which country has a comparative advantage in producing fashions? Show your steps.	(3 marks)
(b)	Suppose 4 units of fashions can be exchanged for 5 units of hamburgers. Calculate the US's gain from trading 1 unit of fashions if 
(i)	there are no other costs involved in the trade between them;	(2 marks)
(ii)	the US has to pay an insurance cost of 0.75 units of hamburgers per unit of fashions traded.	(2 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	The opportunity cost of producing 1 unit of fashions in the US 
	= 12 ÷ 6 = 2 units of hamburgers	(1 mark)
	The opportunity cost of producing 1 unit of fashions in France
	= 9 ÷ 12 = 0.75 units of hamburgers	(1 mark)
	Since France has a lower opportunity cost of producing 1 unit of fashions, it has a comparative advantage in producing fashions.	(1 mark)
(b)	(i)	For each unit of fashions imported, the US's gain
= Domestic cost of producing 1 unit of fashions - Cost of obtaining 1 unit of fashions from trade
	= (2 - 1.25) units of hamburgers	(1 mark)
	= 0.75 units of hamburgers	(1 mark)
(ii)	For each unit of fashions imported, the US's gain
= Domestic cost of producing 1 unit of fashions - Cost of obtaining 1 unit of fashions from trade - Per-unit insurance cost
= (2 - 1.25 - 0.75) unit of hamburgers	(1 mark)
= 0 units of hamburgers	(1 mark)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch611 · Production in the short run and long run
questions.text:
The following table shows the amount of resources required to produce 1 unit of clothes or food in two countries.

	Clothes	Food	
Greece	20 units of resources	50 units of resources	
Russia	40 units of resources	80 units of resources	

(a)	Which country has a comparative advantage in producing food? Show your steps.	(3 marks)
(b)	Calculate the minimum transaction cost per unit of food which will make the two countries stop trading. Briefly explain your answer.	(3 marks)
(c)	Suppose 1 unit of food can be exchanged for 2.2 units of clothes. Under a situation where there is no transaction cost, calculate the gains from trade for Greece by importing 1 unit of goods.	(3 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	The opportunity cost of producing 1 unit of food in Greece is 2.5 (= 50 / 20) units of clothes.	(1 mark)
	The opportunity cost of producing 1 unit of food in Russia is 2 (= 80 / 40) units of clothes.	(1 mark)
	Since Russia's cost of producing 1 unit of food is lower, it has a comparative advantage in producing food.	(1 mark)
(b)	When the total transaction cost is higher than the total gains from trade for the two countries, they will stop trading.	(1 mark)
	The total gains from trade are equal to the difference in the two countries' opportunity costs. Therefore, the minimum transaction cost per unit of food which will make the two countries stop trading 
	= (2.5 - 2) units of clothes	(1 mark)
	= 0.5 units of clothes	(1 mark)
(c)	Since Greece's cost of producing food is higher than Russia's, Greece will import food from Russia.	(1 mark)
	The gains from trade for Greece by importing 1 unit of food
	= Domestic cost - The cost of getting 1 unit of food from trade
	= (2.5 - 2.2) units of clothes	(1 mark)
	= 0.3 units of clothes	(1 mark)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch611 · Production in the short run and long run
questions.text:
The following table shows the amount of resources required to produce 1 unit of Good X or Good Y in two countries.

	Good X	Good Y	
Country A	15 units of resources	30 units of resources	
Country B	25 units of resources	40 units of resources	

(a)	Which country has an absolute disadvantage in both goods? Explain.	(2 marks)
(b)	Explain which country has the comparative advantage in Good Y.	(3 marks)
(c)	Based on the results in (a) and (b), is the possession of absolute advantage necessary for comparative advantage in a good? Briefly explain you answer.
	(3 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Country B because	(1 mark)
it has to use a greater amount of resources to produce the same amount of the two goods.	(1 mark)
(b)	Opportunity cost of producing 1 unit of Good Y in Country A
	= 30 ÷ 15 = 2 units of Good X	(1 mark)
	Opportunity cost of producing 1 unit of Good Y in Country B
	= 40 ÷ 25 = 1.6 units of Good X	(1 mark)
Since Country B has a lower opportunity cost, it has a comparative advantage over Country A in producing Good Y.	(1 mark)
(c)	Although Country B has an absolute disadvantage in both goods, it has a comparative advantage in Good Y.	(1 mark)
	Therefore, having an absolute advantage is not necessary for a comparative advantage in a good.	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch611 · Production in the short run and long run
questions.text:
The following table shows the pre-trade production combinations in the US and Hong Kong. Suppose the marginal costs of producing both goods are constant.

	Food (units)		Computers (units)	
US	16	AND	20	
Hong Kong	16	AND	32	

The US employs 8 units of resources while Hong Kong employs 6 units of resources. Their resources are divided equally to produce food and computers.
(a)	Which region has an absolute advantage in producing each good? Which region has a comparative advantage in producing each good?	(7 marks)
(b)	If the US consumes 12 units of food and 30 units of computers after specialisation, find the consumption combination of Hong Kong and the terms of trade between the two regions.	(4 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	The amount of the two goods that 1 unit of resources can produce:

	Food (units)		Computers (units)	
US	4	OR	5	
Hong Kong	5.33	OR	10.67	
	(1 mark)
(Note: To determine which region has an absolute advantage, we need to compare the amounts of output produced by the same amount of resources.)

Hong Kong can produce a larger amount of food and computers than the US per unit of resources. Therefore, Hong Kong has absolute advantages in producing both food and computers.	(2 marks)

The opportunity costs in the two regions are:

	Food (F)	Computers (C)	
US	1.25C (= 20C / 16)	0.8F (= 16F / 20)	
Hong Kong	2C (= 32C / 16)	0.5F (=16F / 32)	
	(2 marks)
(Note: As both regions use an equal division of resources to produce food and computers, we can simply use the table in the question to find the opportunity costs. If the amount of resources used in producing food is not equal to the amount of resources used in producing computers, we need to find the amount of output with the same amount of resources before calculating the opportunity costs.)

Hong Kong has a comparative advantage in producing computers since its cost (0.5F) is lower.	(1 mark)
The US has a comparative advantage in producing food since its cost (1.25C) is lower.	(1 mark)

(b)	The production combinations after specialisation:

	Food (units)		Computers (units)	
US	32	AND	0	
Hong Kong	0	AND	64	
		(1 mark)
	The final consumption combination of Hong Kong is 20 (= 32 - 12) units of food and 34 (= 64 - 30) units of computers.	(1 mark)
This implies the US exports 20 units of food for 30 units of computers. Therefore, the terms of trade is 1 unit of food for 1.5 units of computers (or 1 unit of computers for 0.67 units of food).	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch611 · Production in the short run and long run
questions.text:
Both Hong Kong and Macau have 2 units of resources. They use an equal division of resources to produce biscuits and cakes.

	Biscuits (units)		Cakes (units)	
Hong Kong	75	AND	25	
Macau	40	AND	20	

(a)	Explain which region has a comparative advantage in producing biscuits.
		(2 marks)
(b)	The two regions trade according to the principle of comparative advantage. The consumption combinations after trade in Hong Kong are 100 units of biscuits and 20 units of cakes. Find the final production combinations of Hong Kong and Macau. Calculate the terms of trade between the two regions and the gains from trade for Hong Kong in importing goods from Macau.	(7 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	•	Hong Kong's cost of producing 1 unit of biscuits is 0.33 (= 25 / 75) units of cakes; Macau's cost of producing 1 unit of biscuits is 0.5 (= 20 / 40) units of cakes.	(1 mark)
•	Hong Kong has a comparative advantage in producing biscuits since its cost is lower.	(1 mark)
(b)	•	Opportunity costs in the two regions:

	Biscuits	Cakes	
Hong Kong	0.33 units of cakes	3 units of biscuits	
Macau	0.5 units of cakes	2 units of biscuits	
(1 mark for opportunity costs of producing cakes)
•	According to the principle of comparative advantage, Hong Kong should specialise in producing biscuits while Macau should specialise in producing cakes. The production combinations of the two regions after specialisation are as below:

	Biscuits (units)		Cakes (units)	
Hong Kong	150	AND	0	
Macau	0	AND	40	
	(2 marks)
•	Hong Kong's consumption combinations after trade are 100 units of biscuits and 20 units of cakes. This implies Hong Kong imports 20 units of cakes with 50 (= 150 - 100) units of biscuits, so the terms of trade is 1 unit of cakes for 2.5 units of biscuits.	(2 marks)
•	Hong Kong's cost of producing 1 unit of cakes is 3 units of biscuits. By importing 1 unit of cakes, it needs to pay 2.5 units of biscuits. Therefore, the gain from trade for Hong Kong in importing 1 unit of cakes is 0.5 units of biscuits.	(1 mark)
•	The gains from trade for Hong Kong in importing 20 units of cakes are 10
(= 0.5 × 20) units of biscuits.	(1 mark)

Structured Questions

questions.topic: B6 · Ch611 · Production in the short run and long run
questions.text:
The following table shows the amount of goods that can be produced by two countries in 100 man-hours.

	Ships (units)		Planes (units)	
Country J	40	OR	100	
Country U	60	OR	30	

(a)	Which country has a comparative advantage in producing planes? Explain.
	(3 marks)
(b)	Find the range of the terms of trade that makes trading between the two countries mutually beneficial.	(2 marks)
(c)	Suppose each country evenly allocates 2,000 man-hours to produce both goods before trade. Recently, Country J and Country U have produced and traded according to the principle of comparative advantage.
(i)	State the principle of comparative advantage.	(2 marks)
*(ii)	Can the above case illustrate the principle of comparative advantage? Explain your answer with calculation.	(6 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Country J's cost of producing 1 unit of planes
	= 40 ÷ 100 = 0.4 units of ships	(1 mark)
	Country U's cost of producing 1 unit of planes
	= 60 ÷ 30 = 2 units of ships	(1 mark)
	Therefore, Country J has a comparative advantage in producing planes.	(1 mark)
(b)	2 units of ships > 1 unit of planes > 0.4 units of ships	(2 marks)
(c)	(i)	The principle of comparative advantage states that if each country specialises in producing the good in which it has a comparative advantage, the total output of all countries can increase.	(2 marks)
	(ii)	Total production of ships before trade
		= 40 × 10 + 60 × 10 = 1,000 units	(1 mark)
		Total production of planes before trade
		= 100 × 10 + 30 × 10 = 1,300 units	(1 mark)
		According to the principle, Country J will completely specialise in producing planes while Country U will completely specialise in producing ships.
	(1 mark)
		Total production of ships after trade
		= 60 × 20 = 1,200 units	(1 mark)
		Total production of planes after trade
		= 100 × 20 = 2,000 units	(1 mark)
		As the outputs of both goods increase after trade, the principle of comparative advantage can be illustrated.	(1 mark)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch611 · Production in the short run and long run
questions.text:
The following shows the amount of inputs needed to produce 1 unit of rice or 1 unit of flowers.

	Rice	Flowers	
Country A	4 units	8 units	
Country B	8 units	12 units	

(a)	(i)	Complete the following table.	(4 marks)
	
	Cost of producing 
1 unit of rice	Cost of producing 
1 unit of flowers	
Country A	_______ units of flowers	_______ units of rice	
Country B	_______ units of flowers	_______ units of rice	

(ii)	Explain which country will export rice.	(2 marks)
(b)	Suppose the rainfall in Country A decreases. As a result, the production of 1 unit of rice now requires 8 units of inputs.
	(i)	Explain which country will export rice.	(3 marks)
(ii)	Suppose the terms of trade is 1 unit of rice for 0.6 units of flowers.
(I)	Can Country B gain from trading rice before the change? Explain.
	(2 marks)
(II)	Can Country B gain from trading rice after the change? Explain.	(2 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	(i)	
	Cost of producing 
1 unit of rice	Cost of producing 
1 unit of flowers	
Country A	0.5 units of flower	2 units of rice	
Country B	0.67 units of flower	1.25 units of rice	
			(4 marks)
(ii)	Country A will export rice	(1 mark)
because Country A has a lower cost of producing rice.	(1 mark)
(b)	(i)	Country B will export rice.	(1 mark)
Country A's cost of producing 1 unit of rice becomes 1 unit of flowers.
	(1 mark)
Therefore, Country B has a lower cost in producing rice.	(1 mark)
	(ii)	(I)	Country B can gain from importing rice before the change.	(1 mark)
The gain is 0.07 units of flowers for each unit of rice imported.	(1 mark)
(II)	Country B cannot gain from exporting rice after the change.	(1 mark)
Because Country B's production cost is higher than the terms of trade.
	(1 mark)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch611 · Production in the short run and long run
questions.text:
The following table shows the amount of two goods that 1 unit of resources can produce in two countries:

	Good X (units)		Good Y (units)	
Country A	3	OR	12	
Country B	4	OR	6	

(a)	Calculate a range for the terms of trade (for 1 unit of Good X) which is mutually beneficial to both countries.	(3 marks)
(b)	Suppose there is technological progress in producing Good Y in Country B and that it now can produce 20 units of Good Y with 1 unit of resources.
(i)	Explain which country has a comparative advantage in producing Good Y.
	(3 marks)
(ii)	Suppose the terms of trade is 4.5 units of Good Y for 1 unit of Good X.
(I)	Calculate and explain the gains from trade to both countries from exporting 1 unit of a good.	(6 marks)
(II)	If Country B has to pay 1 unit of Good Y as a transport cost for every unit of imported goods, explain whether Country B can benefit from imports.
	(4 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	The costs of producing 1 unit of Good X in both countries are:
Country A: 1 unit of Good X = 4 units of Good Y	(1 mark)
Country B: 1 unit of Good X = 1.5 units of Good Y	(1 mark)
Therefore, the terms of trade should lie within this range:
1.5 units of Good Y < 1 unit of Good X < 4 units of Good Y	(1 mark)

(b)	(i)	Opportunity cost of producing 1 unit of Good Y in Country A
		= 3 ÷ 12 = 0.25 units of Good X	(1 mark)
		Opportunity cost of producing 1 unit of Good Y in Country B
		= 4 ÷ 20 = 0.2 units of Good X	(1 mark)
	The cost of producing Good Y in Country B is lower than that in Country A. Therefore, Country B has a comparative advantage in producing Good Y.
	(1 mark)
(ii)	(I)	According to the principle of comparative advantage, Country A should specialise in the production of Good X while Country B should specialise in the production of Good Y.
The terms of trade is 4.5 units of Good Y for 1 unit of Good X, i.e.,
1 unit of Good X = 4.5 units of Good Y or
1 unit of Good Y = 0.22 units of Good X	(2 marks)
The cost of producing 1 unit of Good X in Country A is 4 units of Good Y. Country A can receive 4.5 units of Good Y by exporting 1 unit of Good X. So, it gains 0.5 (= 4.5 - 4) units of Good Y.	(2 marks)
The cost of producing 1 unit of Good Y in Country B is 0.2 units of 
Good X. Country B can receive 0.22 units of Good X by exporting 1 unit of Good Y. So, it gains 0.02 (= 0.22 - 0.2) units of Good X.	(2 marks)
(II)	The cost of producing 1 unit of Good X in Country B is 5 units of Good Y. The price of importing 1 unit of Good X is 4.5 units of Good Y. Without the transport cost, the unit gain from importing Good X is 0.5 units of Good Y.	(2 marks)
However, Country B has to pay 1 unit of Good Y for every unit of imported good (Good X) as a transport cost. Because the unit transport cost is greater than the unit gain from importing Good X, Country B cannot benefit from imports.	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch611 · Production in the short run and long run
questions.text:
The following table shows the amount of resources (R) required for producing 1 unit of goods in Country A and Country B.

	Wheat	Hot dogs	
Country A	20R	30R	
Country B	25R	20R	

(a)	(i)	Calculate the opportunity costs of producing both goods in both countries.
	(4 marks)
(ii)	Explain which country has a comparative advantage in producing wheat.
	(1 mark)
(iii)	Based on the principle of comparative advantage, explain the direction of trade between the two countries.	(2 marks)
(b)	Suppose the cost of transporting 1 unit of wheat is 0.3 units of hot dogs.
	(i)	Explain whether trade is possible between Country A and Country B.
	(3 marks)
(ii)	If the terms of trade is 1 unit of wheat = 0.9 units of hot dogs, explain whether trade would be possible when the transportation cost is completely paid by
	(I)	Country A.	(3 marks)
	(II)	Country B.	(3 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	(i)	The opportunity cost of producing wheat in Country A
		= 20 ÷ 30 = 0.67 units of hot dogs	(1 mark)
		The opportunity cost of producing hot dogs in Country A
		= 30 ÷ 20 = 1.5 units of wheat	(1 mark)
		The opportunity cost of producing wheat in Country B
		= 25 ÷ 20 = 1.25 units of hot dogs	(1 mark)
		The opportunity cost of producing hot dogs in Country B
		= 20 ÷ 25 = 0.8 units of wheat	(1 mark)
(ii)	Country A has a comparative advantage in producing wheat as its opportunity cost is lower.	(1 mark)
(iii)	As Country A has a comparative advantage in producing wheat, it will specialise in producing wheat and export wheat to Country B.	(1 mark)
	Country B has a comparative advantage in producing hot dogs. So, it will specialise in producing hot dogs and export hot dogs to Country A.	(1 mark)

(b)	(i)	The total gain from trading 1 unit of wheat
		= 1.25 - 0.67 = 0.58 units of hot dogs	(1 mark)
		As the total gain from trade is greater than the transportation cost, trade is possible between the two countries.	(2 marks)
(ii)	(I)	Country A's gain from trading 1 unit of wheat
		= 0.9 - 0.67 - 0.3 = -0.07 units of hot dogs	(1 mark)
		As Country A cannot gain from trade, it would not export wheat and trade would not be possible.	(2 marks)
	(II)	Country B's gain from trading 1 unit of wheat
		= 1.25 - 0.9 - 0.3 = 0.05 units of hot dogs	(1 mark)
		As Country B can gain from trade, it would import wheat. Country A can also gain from exporting wheat (= 0.9 - 0.67 = 0.23 units of hot dogs). Thus, trade would be possible.	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch611 · Production in the short run and long run
questions.text:
The following table shows the actual output of Country J and Country K. Each uses 20% of the resources to produce computers and the other 80% to produce clothing.

	Computers (units)	Clothing (units)	
Country J	20	100	
Country K	10	400	

(a)	Can we conclude that Country J has an absolute advantage in producing computers and Country K has an absolute advantage in producing clothing? Explain your answers.	(4 marks)
(b)	Calculate the opportunity cost of producing 1 unit of computers for each country. If they trade, explain which country will export computers. Show your steps.
	(6 marks)
(c)	Calculate the minimum transportation cost per unit of computers which would lead to a total stoppage of trade between the two countries. Explain your answer.
	(4 marks)
(d)	Suppose after a catastrophic earthquake, Country J's outputs of both goods decline to 20% of what they were before the earthquake. What will the new pattern of trade between the two countries be? Explain.	(4 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	No. Absolute advantage means that a country can produce more goods given the same amount of resources.	(2 marks)
	Since we do not know the amount of resources in the two countries, we cannot tell whether the actual outputs given are produced by the same amount of resources. Thus, there is insufficient information to draw that conclusion.	(2 marks)

(b)	Country J can produce 100 (= 20 / 0.2) units of computers or 125 (= 100 / 0.8) units of clothing with all of its resources.	(1 mark)
	Therefore, the opportunity cost of producing 1 unit of computers for Country J is 1.25 (= 125 / 100) units of clothing.	(1 mark)
	Country K can produce 50 (= 10 / 0.2) units of computers or 500 (= 400 / 0.8) units of clothing with all of its resources.	(1 mark)
	Therefore, the opportunity cost of producing 1 unit of computers for Country K is 10 (= 500 / 50) units of clothing.	(1 mark)
	Thus, Country J has a comparative advantage in producing computers.	(1 mark)
	Country J should export computers.	(1 mark)

(c)	Whenever the total gain from trade is smaller than the transportation cost per unit of computers, trade will stop.	(2 marks)
	Therefore, the minimum transportation cost per unit of computers 
	= (10 - 1.25) units of clothing	(1 mark)
	= 8.75 units of clothing	(1 mark)

(d)	After the earthquake, Country J could produce 20 units (100 units × 20%) of computers or 25 units (125 units × 20%) of clothing with all of its resources.
	(1 mark)
	The opportunity costs of producing computers and clothing are the same as before.	(1 mark)
	Since the opportunity costs of producing the two goods in the two countries remain unchanged, the pattern of comparative advantages in the two goods is the same as before.	(1 mark)
	Therefore, the pattern of trade will be the same as it was.	(1 mark)

(3)	Domestic consumers of Good X will lose.

questions.answerText: The tariff only reduces the effects of opening the economy. Thus, compared with a situation when there is no trade, after opening the economy and imposing a tariff, both the domestic price and domestic production will decrease, while domestic consumption will increase. questions.answerText: Option D is correct. When Country B imposes a tariff on Good X, the quantity of Country A's exports will decrease. free)	(2 marks)

World price: Pw    Price with a quota: Pq

Thus, domestic consumers will suffer.	(1 mark)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch612 · Expansion of firms
questions.text: Briefly explain how the imposition of quotas affects the quality of imports.	(3 marks)
questions.answerText: Importers have to pay a cost to compete for quotas. After the addition of a unit quota-cost, the money prices of higher quality imports rise by a smaller percentage than the money prices of lower quality imports. In other words, the relative prices of higher quality imports drop. By the law of demand, the importing country will import a greater proportion of higher quality goods. Hence, the average quality of imports improves.	(3 marks)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch612 · Expansion of firms
questions.text:
(a)	What are an import quota and a tariff?	(2 marks)
(b)	Suppose a country's demand for imported goods is not perfectly inelastic.
(i)	'A decrease in the amount of import quotas must decrease the volume of imports.' Evaluate this statement. 	(2 marks)
(ii)	'An increase in tariffs must decrease the volume of imports.' Evaluate this statement.	(4 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	•	An import quota refers to the maximum limit imposed on the quantity of imports.	(1 mark)
•	A tariff is a tax imposed on imports.	(1 mark)
(b)	(i)	•	The statement is incorrect. A decrease in the amount of import quotas may not decrease the volume of imports.	(1 mark)
•	Suppose the original quotas are ineffective. After the decrease in the amount of import quotas, if the quotas are still ineffective, the volume of imports will remain unchanged.	(1 mark)
(ii)	•	The statement is correct.	(1 mark)
•	Before the increase in tariffs, the domestic prices of imports must be lower than the domestic autarkic equilibrium prices of the goods (otherwise, the country will not import the goods).	(1 mark)
•	After the increase in tariffs, the domestic prices of imports will increase. Domestic consumers will buy fewer imports and the volume of imports will decrease.	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch612 · Expansion of firms
questions.text:
* Country A is a small open economy. Suppose the government in Country A decides to impose either a tariff or a quota to limit the amount of imported cars.
(a)	With the aid of a diagram, briefly explain under what situation a tariff will be ineffective in reducing the amount of imported cars. What is the change in the domestic price of imported cars?	(5 marks)
(b)	With the aid of a diagram, explain under what situation a quota will be ineffective in reducing the amount of imported cars. What is the change in the domestic price of imported cars?	(5 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	•	A tariff cannot reduce the import volume if there is no domestic supply (i.e., no domestic substitutes) and the demand is perfectly inelastic (i.e., the quantity demanded remains unchanged even when the price increases).	(2 marks)
•	The domestic price of imported cars will increase by the amount of the tariff (t).	(1 mark)
	(2 marks)
(Accept other reasonable answers.)
(b)	•	A quota cannot reduce the import volume if the amount of the quota is greater than the original quantity imported.	(2 marks)
•	The domestic price of imported cars will remain unchanged at Pw.	(1 mark)
	(2 marks)

Suppose Country A is a small open economy and the demand for beer is perfectly inelastic. The government decides to implement one of the following measures:

questions.topic: B6 · Ch612 · Expansion of firms
questions.text:
Country H is a small open economy. The following are its demand and supply schedules for vegetables under autarky.

Unit price ($)	Quantity demanded (units)	Quantity supplied (units)	
0	900	0	
100	750	75	
200	600	150	
300	450	225	
400	300	300	
500	150	375	
600	0	450	

(a)	Under autarky, what are the equilibrium price and equilibrium quantity?	(2 marks)
(b)	Suppose the world price of vegetables is $200/unit.
	(i)	How many units of vegetables will Country H consume? How many units of vegetables will Country H import?	(2 marks)
(ii)	What is the total value of vegetables produced by Country H's producers? Show your work.	(2 marks)
(c)	Suppose the world price is still $200/unit. If Country H's government imposes a tariff of $100 for each unit of vegetable imported, find
	(i)	the change in the quantity of imports.	(2 marks)
	(ii)	the tariff revenue.	(2 marks)
(d)	'The imposition of an effective quota may raise the total value of vegetables imported.' Do you agree? Explain your answer.	(3 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Equilibrium price = $400	(1 mark)
	Equilibrium quantity = 300 units	(1 mark)
(b)	(i)	Country H will consume 600 units of vegetables.	(1 mark)
		The country will import 450 (= 600 - 150) units of vegetables.	(1 mark)
(ii)	Total value of vegetables produced = $200 × 150 = $30,000	(2 marks)
(c)	(i)	The new quantity of imports is 225 (= 450 - 225) units.	(1 mark)
	The quantity of imports decreases by 225 units (from 450 units to 225 units).
	(1 mark)
(ii)	Tariff revenue = $100 × 225 = $22,500	(2 marks)

(d)	Agree. Although the quantity of imported vegetables decreases, the price of the vegetables increases due to the quota restriction. The total value of imported vegetables will increase if the percentage increase in price is greater than the percentage decrease in quantity.	(3 marks)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch612 · Expansion of firms
questions.text:
Country A is a small open economy. It imports a large number of taro cakes from its only trading partner, Country B. Recently, it was rumoured in Country A that some imported taro cakes were contaminated with melamine (三聚氰胺).
(a)	(i)	Country A's government decides to impose a quota on imported taro cakes. With the aid of a diagram, explain how the quota affects the equilibrium price and equilibrium quantity of taro cakes in Country A.	(5 marks)
(ii)	Explain how the imposition of a quota can help improve the quality of imported taro cakes.	(3 marks)

(b)	Suppose there is no trade restriction on taro cakes. Due to the rumour, some people in Country A decide to eat fewer taro cakes. With the aid of a diagram, explain how this affects the equilibrium price, the equilibrium quantity and the domestic production of taro cakes in Country A.	(5 marks)
(c)	Suppose there are only two goods: taro cakes and clothing. If Country A has an absolute advantage in producing taro cakes, briefly explain why Country A can still gain from importing taro cakes.	(4 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	(i)	•	The equilibrium price of taro cakes increases from Pw to Pq.	(1 mark)
•	The equilibrium quantity of taro cakes decreases from Q2 to Q4.	(1 mark)
	(3 marks)
	(ii)	Importers have to pay a cost to compete for quotas. After the addition of a 
unit quota-cost, the money prices of higher quality imports rise by a smaller percentage than the money prices of lower quality imports. In other words, 
the relative prices of higher quality imports drop. By the law of demand, 
Country A will import a greater proportion of higher quality taro cakes. 
Hence, the average quality of imported taro cakes improves.	(3 marks)


(b)	•	The equilibrium price remains unchanged at Pw.	(1 mark)
•	The equilibrium quantity decreases from Q2 to Q3.	(1 mark)
•	The domestic production remains unchanged at Q1.	(1 mark)
	(2 marks)

(c)	Country A may gain from importing taro cakes if it has a comparative disadvantage in producing taro cakes.	(1 mark)
Even if Country A has an absolute advantage in producing taro cakes, it may have a comparative disadvantage in producing taro cakes and a comparative advantage in producing clothing.	(1 mark)
If the international price of taro cakes is lower than Country A's production cost, Country A can obtain taro cakes at a lower cost by importing taro cakes. Thus, it can gain from these imports.	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch612 · Expansion of firms
questions.text:
Country J was hit by an earthquake. Many people died and a nuclear power plant was destroyed. Now, Country J faces a serious problem of radioactive contamination (輻射污染), which will have a long-lasting effect on the environment.
(a)	With the aid of an AS-AD diagram, explain how this affects Country J's output level and price level in the long run.	(8 marks)
(b)	Country H, a small open economy, decides to impose effective quotas on 
Country J's imports. Assume that all world prices remain unchanged. With the aid of a diagram, explain how the quotas affect Country H's domestic price of imported goods and domestic consumption.	(5 marks)
(c)	To help the economy recover, Country J's central bank adopts a monetary policy.
(i)	Which type of monetary policy should the central bank adopt?	(1 mark)
(ii)	Suggest TWO tools of monetary policy which can help Country J's economy recover.	(2 marks)

(iii)	Use the quantity theory of money to evaluate the effectiveness of the policy in the long run.	(3 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	•	The decrease in population and radioactive contamination lead to a decrease in aggregate demand and long run aggregate supply. Also, the destruction of the nuclear energy plant leads to a decrease in the long run aggregate supply.
	(2 marks)
•	In the long run, the output level will decrease.	(1 mark)
•	The change in the price level is uncertain. The price level may increase, decrease or remain unchanged, depending on the magnitude of the decrease in AD and the decrease in LRAS.	(2 marks)
•	Any correct diagram	(3 marks)
	

(b)	•	The domestic price increases from Pw to Pq.	(1 mark)
•	Domestic consumption decreases from Q2 to Q4.	(1 mark)
•	Any correct diagram	(3 marks)

(c)	(i)	Expansionary monetary policy	(1 mark)
(ii)	•	Open market purchases of government bonds
•	Lowering the discount rate
•	Lowering the required reserve ratio
•	Printing money
(Any TWO of the above, 1 mark × 2 = 2 marks)
(iii)	According to the quantity theory of money, real national income is a constant in the long run, always staying at the full employment level. Only the price level changes positively by the same proportion as the nominal money supply. The increase in the nominal money supply will not affect the output level but may cause inflation.	(3 marks)

An earthquake occurs in Country J. After the earthquake, people hold fewer assets in Country J's currency (called the J dollar) and hold more assets in Country H's currency (called the H dollar). Which of the following statements can be used to explain this phenomenon?
A.	The H dollar serves as a better medium of exchange in Country J.
B.	The J dollar cannot serve as a unit of account.
C.	People expect that the inflation rate in Country J will fall.
D.	People expect that the J dollar will depreciate greatly against the H dollar.

questions.topic: B6 · Ch613 · Market and market structure
questions.text:
If the Japanese yen appreciates against the Hong Kong dollar, the price of imported Japanese game consoles in Hong Kong dollars will
A.	increase.
B.	decrease.
C.	remain unchanged.
D.	be uncertain, depending on the price elasticity of demand.

questions.topic: B6 · Ch613 · Market and market structure
questions.text:
Which of the following statements is correct?
A.	When the domestic currency appreciates, domestic prices of imported goods will increase.
B.	When a foreign currency depreciates, the foreign prices of our exported goods will decrease.
C.	Suppose the foreign price of an imported good is a constant. An increase in the domestic price of the imported good implies that the domestic currency has appreciated.
D.	None of the above

questions.topic: B6 · Ch613 · Market and market structure
questions.text:
* If Country A's currency depreciates against Country B's currency, other things being equal,
(1)	prices of imports from Country B, in terms of Country A's currency, will decrease.
(2)	prices of Country B's exports to Country A will remain unchanged.
(3)	Country A will import fewer goods from Country B.
(4)	Country A's aggregate demand will increase.
A.	(1) and (2) only
B.	(1) and (4) only
C.	(2) and (3) only
D.	(3) and (4) only
questions.answerText: Option (2) is incorrect. The prices increase if they are measured in Country A's currency.

questions.topic: B6 · Ch613 · Market and market structure
questions.text:
* Which of the following statements is/are INCORRECT?
(1)	When Country A's currency appreciates, the prices of its imports (in terms of Country A's currency) will increase.
(2)	If Country B's currency depreciates against Country A's currency, the price of Country A's goods in terms of Country B's currency will be higher than the price of the same goods produced in Country B.
(3)	If Country A's currency appreciates against Country B's currency, the total value of Country B's imports from Country A (in terms of Country A's currency) will decrease.
A.	(3) only
B.	(1) and (2) only
C.	(2) and (3) only
D.	(1), (2) and (3)

questions.text:

questions.text:

questions.topic: B6 · Ch613 · Market and market structure
questions.text:
* 'Other things being constant, an increase in the price of foreign currency will lead to an increase in foreign buyers' quantity demanded of our exports.' This statement
A.	is incorrect because it violates the law of demand.
B.	is incorrect because the change in the price of foreign currency will not affect foreign buyers' demand for our exports.
C.	is correct because the increase in the price of foreign currency will lead to an increase in foreign buyers' demand for our exports.

questions.topic: B6 · Ch613 · Market and market structure
questions.text:
* Study the following newspaper cutting.

According to the above information, which of the following situations is LEAST likely to happen?
A.	Country A's currency depreciates.
B.	The purchasing power of Country A's currency decreases.
C.	Country A's consumers buy more imported goods.
D.	Country A's potential GDP increases.
questions.answerText: Options A and B are not the answers. The increase in Country A's money supply will lower the purchasing power of its currency. Thus, the exchange rate (the price) of Country A's currency may decrease.

In Year 1, 1 US dollar can be exchanged for 0.8 renminbi. In Year 2, 1 US dollar can only be exchanged for 0.7 renminbi. Which of the following statements is correct?

(2)	Hong Kong will import less from the mainland.
(3)	The total value (in terms of US dollars) of United States' imports from China increases.

questions.topic: B6 · Ch613 · Market and market structure
questions.text:
If the price of Euros increases from 12 Hong Kong dollars to 20 Hong Kong dollars,
A.	the Hong Kong dollar appreciates against the US dollar.
B.	the Euro appreciates against the Philippine peso.
C.	Hong Kong people will visit Europe less frequently.
D.	European consumers will import fewer goods from the US.
questions.answerText: Option D is incorrect. Under Hong Kong's linked exchange rate system, the appreciation of the Euro against the Hong Kong dollar implies an appreciation of the Euro against the US dollar. In the Euro zone, the prices of goods imported from the US in terms of Euros will decrease. European consumers will import more goods from the US. (Remark: The changes in market exchange rates of non-US currencies against the Hong Kong dollar will closely follow those against the US dollar. However, we cannot say that the changes in market exchange rates of foreign currencies against the US dollar follow those against the Hong Kong dollar.)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch613 · Market and market structure
questions.text:
(a)	Define the exchange rate of a currency.	(2 marks)
(b)	What is a flexible exchange rate system?	(2 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	The exchange rate of a currency is the price of the currency in terms of another currency.	(2 marks)
(b)	Under a flexible exchange rate system, the exchange rate of a currency is determined by the demand for and supply of the currency (i.e., by market forces).
	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch613 · Market and market structure
questions.text:
(a)	List TWO major types of exchange rate systems and explain the difference between them.	(5 marks)
(b)	Suppose the price of 1 Australian dollar relative to the US dollar increases from US$1.05 to US$1.1. Explain whether the US dollar has appreciated or depreciated against the Australian dollar in this case.	(2 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	•	Flexible (or floating) exchange rate system and fixed (or pegged) exchange rate system	(1 mark)
•	Under a flexible exchange rate system, the exchange rate of a currency is determined by the demand for and supply of the currency (or market force).
	(2 marks)
•	However, under a fixed exchange rate system, the exchange rate of a currency is fixed by the central bank.	(2 marks)
(b)	•	The US dollar depreciates against the Australian dollar because	(1 mark)
•	more units of US dollars are needed in exchange for 1 Australian dollar (or the same units of US dollars can be exchanged for fewer units of Australian dollars).	(1 mark)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch613 · Market and market structure
questions.text:
From time to time, the US urges the Chinese government to raise the value of the renminbi. Explain how the rise in the value of renminbi affects
(a)	prices of Chinese goods in terms of US dollars (given their prices in renminbi remain unchanged);	(2 marks)
(b)	the export volume of US goods to China.	(2 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	After the rise in the value of the renminbi (i.e., appreciation of the renminbi), more US dollars are needed in exchange for each unit of renminbi. Hence, when the renminbi prices of Chinese goods remain unchanged, the prices in terms of US dollars will increase.	(2 marks)
(b)	After the rise in the value of the renminbi, the prices of US goods in terms of the renminbi decrease. The quantity demanded of US goods in China increases. 
Hence, the export volume of US goods to China will increase.	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch613 · Market and market structure
questions.text:
Suppose the Euro appreciates against the Hong Kong dollar.
(a)	What is the effect on the price of imported Italian goods in Hong Kong (in terms of Hong Kong dollars)?	(1 mark)
(b)	What is the effect on Hong Kong's total expenditure on imported Italian goods in terms of Euros? Explain your answer with the aid of ONE diagram.	(7 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	The price of imported Italian goods in terms of Hong Kong dollars increases.
	(1 mark)
(b)	•	Since the price of imported Italian goods in terms of Hong Kong dollars increases, the import volume decreases from QM1 to QM2.	(1 mark)
•	The price of imported Italian goods in terms of Euros is assumed to be independent of the Euro's exchange rate. At the same price in terms of Euros, the decrease in the import volume implies that the demand for imported Italian goods decreases.	(2 marks)
•	The demand curve of imported Italian goods shifts leftwards from DM1 to DM2.	(1 mark)
•	Therefore, Hong Kong's total expenditure on imported Italian goods in Euros decreases.	(1 mark)
	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch613 · Market and market structure
questions.text: Suppose Hong Kong dollars appreciate against Australian dollars. Under what situation will Hong Kong's total revenue (in terms of Australian dollars) from exporting goods to Australia increase? Explain with the aid of a diagram.	(6 marks)
questions.answerText:
•	Since Hong Kong dollars appreciate against Australian dollars, the price in Australia of Hong Kong's goods in terms of Australian dollars increases from P1 to P2.	(1 mark)
•	Since Australian consumers now face a higher price (in terms of Australian dollars), their quantity demanded of Hong Kong's goods decreases from Q1 to Q2, according to the law of demand.	(1 mark)
•	If Australian consumers' demand for Hong Kong's goods is inelastic (Ed < 1), Area B will be smaller than Area A. Thus, Hong Kong's total revenue (in terms of Australian dollars) from exporting goods to Australia will increase.	(2 marks)
	(2 marks)

	(7 marks)
questions.answerText:

•	Leftward shift of the demand curve	(1 mark)
•	Decrease in quantity of exports	(1 mark)
•	Decrease in total export value	(1 mark)



Verbal elaboration:
The Hong Kong dollar has appreciated against the Australian dollar.	(1 mark)
The price of Hong Kong's exports in terms of Australian dollars increases. Therefore, Hong Kong's volume of exports decreases.	(1 mark)
Assuming the price of Hong Kong's exports in terms of Hong Kong dollars does not change (at P1), there is a leftward shift of the demand curve from DX1 to DX2.
	(1 mark)
So, the total export value in Hong Kong dollars decreases.	(1 mark)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch613 · Market and market structure
questions.text:
(a)	What is the exchange rate system in Hong Kong?	(1 mark)
(b)	Refer to the table below.

Year	Price of 1 US dollar	
2015	7.8 Hong Kong dollars	
2016	7.7 Hong Kong dollars	

(i)	According to the above table, does the Hong Kong dollar appreciate or depreciate against the US dollar? Explain your answer.	(2 marks)
*(ii)	Explain why in this case note-issuing banks in Hong Kong will buy US dollars from (and sell Hong Kong dollars to) the foreign exchange market.
	(5 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	The linked exchange rate system	(1 mark)
(b)	(i)	The Hong Kong dollar appreciates against the US dollar because the same unit of US dollars can be exchanged for fewer units of Hong Kong dollars.
	(2 marks)
(ii) •	Under the linked exchange rate system, note-issuing banks can sell US dollars for HK dollars to (or buy US dollars with HK dollars from) the Exchange Fund at the fixed rate of US$1 to HK$7.8.	(2 marks)
•	If note-issuing banks use HK$7.7 to buy US$1 in the foreign exchange market and sell US$1 for HK$7.8 to the Exchange Fund, they can gain HK$0.1.	(2 marks)
•	Thus, note-issuing banks have an incentive to buy US dollars from the foreign exchange market.	(1 mark)
(Remark: The mechanism of maintaining the linked exchange rate is NOT required in the syllabus.)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch613 · Market and market structure
questions.text:
Hong Kong has adopted a linked exchange rate system. Suppose the US dollar has appreciated against the Korean won. 
(a)	How will the prices (in terms of Hong Kong dollars) of Hong Kong's imports from Korea change? Briefly explain.	(3 marks)
(b)	With the aid of a diagram, explain under what condition Hong Kong consumers' total expenditure (in terms of Hong Kong dollars) on imports from Korea will decrease.	(4 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Under the linked exchange rate system, the change in the exchange rate of Hong Kong dollars to Korean won will follow that of US dollars to Korean won. Hence, Hong Kong dollars will appreciate against the Korean won and the prices (in terms of Hong Kong dollars) of Hong Kong's imports from Korea will decrease.		(3 marks)
(b)	Indicate on the diagram:
(	Price (in terms of Hong Kong dollars) decreases, quantity demanded increases	(1 mark)
(	Increase in total expenditure < Decrease in total expenditure	(1 mark)
	
	Verbal elaboration:
	When demand is inelastic, the percentage decrease in price is larger than the percentage increase in quantity demanded. Hence, Hong Kong consumers' total expenditure (in terms of Hong Kong dollars) on imports from Korea decreases.
	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch613 · Market and market structure
questions.text:
Suppose the US dollar depreciates against the Euro and Hong Kong imports sausages from Germany.
(a)	Assume the price of German sausages in terms of Euros remains unchanged. Explain how the above event affects the price of imported German sausages in Hong Kong in terms of the following currencies:
(i)	US dollars	(2 marks)
(ii)	Hong Kong dollars	(3 marks)
(b)	What are the effects of the above event on Hong Kong consumers' total expenditure on imported German sausages in terms of Hong Kong dollars (TEM)? Explain your answer with the aid of ONE diagram.	(7 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	(i)	The price in US dollars increases because more units of US dollars are needed to settle the same import price in terms of Euros.	(2 marks)
(ii)	•	Under the linked exchange rate system, the change in the market exchange rate of the Hong Kong dollar against the Euro closely follows that of the US dollar against the Euro. Thus, the Hong Kong dollar depreciates against the Euro.	(2 marks)
•	As a result, in Hong Kong, the price of imported German sausages in terms of Hong Kong dollars increases.	(1 mark)

(b)	•	Since the price of imported German sausages in terms of Hong Kong dollars (Pd) increases, according to the law of demand, Hong Kong consumers' quantity demanded of imported Germany sausages decreases. The volume of imported German sausages (QM) decreases from QM1 to QM2.	(2 marks)
•	The change in TEM is uncertain, depending on Hong Kong consumers' price elasticity of demand for imported German sausages (EM).	(1 mark)
•	If EM > 1 (i.e. demand is elastic), the percentage drop in QM is larger than the percentage rise in Pd. Thus, TEM drops. / If EM = 1 (i.e. demand is unitarily elastic), the percentage drop in QM is equal to the percentage rise in Pd. Thus, TEM remains unchanged. / If EM > 1 (i.e. demand is inelastic), the percentage drop in QM is smaller than the percentage rise in Pd. Thus, TEM rises.	(2 marks)
•	Any correct diagram	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch613 · Market and market structure
questions.text:
Suppose the US dollar depreciates against the Korean won and Hong Kong exports garments to Korea.
(a)	Assume the price of Hong Kong-made garments in terms of Hong Kong dollars remains unchanged. Explain how the above event affects the price of Hong Kong-made garments in terms of Korean won.	(3 marks)
(b)	What are the effects of the above event on Hong Kong exporters' total revenue from exporting garments to Korea in terms of Hong Kong dollars (TRX)? Explain your answer with the aid of ONE diagram.	(6 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	•	Under the linked exchange rate system, the change in the market exchange rate of the Korean won against the Hong Kong dollar closely follows that against the US dollar. Thus, the Hong Kong dollar depreciates against the Korean won.	(2 marks)
•	As a result, the price of Hong Kong-made garments in terms of Korean won decreases.	(1 mark)
(b)	•	Since the price of Hong Kong-made garments in terms of Korean won decreases, the export volume (QX) increases from QX1 to QX2.	(1 mark)
•	The price of Hong Kong-made garments in terms of Hong Kong dollars (Pd1) is assumed to be independent of the exchange rate. At the same price in terms of Hong Kong dollars, the increase in the export volume implies that Korea's demand for Hong Kong-made garments increases. The demand curve of Hong Kong-made garments shifts rightwards from DX1 to DX2.	(2 marks)
•	Therefore, TRX increases.	(1 mark)
	(2 marks)

questions.text:

questions.text:
Suppose some Hong Kong restaurants provide dishes with imported ingredients, and all of the dishes are sold to foreign visitors. Explain how this will affect Hong Kong's
(a)	the visible trade balance;	(2 marks)
(b)	the invisible trade balance;	(2 marks)
(c)	the current account balance.	(2 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Importing the ingredients is a debit entry in the goods account. It worsens the visible trade balance.	(2 marks)
(b)	Selling the dishes to foreign visitors is regarded as exports of services. It is a credit entry in the services account and improves the invisible trade balance.
	(2 marks)
(c)	Restaurant production creates value-added. Thus, the increase in the invisible trade balance must be greater than the decrease in the visible trade balance. This improves the current account balance.	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch613 · Market and market structure
questions.text:
Explain how each of the following items is treated in Hong Kong's current account or capital and financial account.
(a)	A Hong Kong businessman donates $1 million to a charitable organisation in Libya (利比亞).	(2 marks)
(b)	A famous scholar from the US works in Hong Kong on a three-month contract as a visiting lecturer at a Hong Kong university.	(2 marks)
(c)	An American company raises funds in Hong Kong to finance its investment project in the US. (Remark: You are NOT required to discuss how the interest payments involved are recorded.)	(2 marks)
(d)	A Hong Kong resident flies on Cathay Pacific to Shanghai for business.	(2 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	The donation is a Hong Kong resident's current transfer sent abroad. This is recorded on the debit side of Hong Kong's current account.	(2 marks)
(b)	This involves buying factor services from abroad. The wage paid to the scholar is recorded on the debit side of Hong Kong's current account.	(2 marks)
(c)	This is Hong Kong's investment abroad and results in an outflow of foreign currencies to the US. The funds raised are recorded on the debit side of Hong Kong's capital and financial account. 	(2 marks)
(d)	This case does not involve an external transaction, so this is neither recorded in Hong Kong's current account nor its capital and financial account.	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch613 · Market and market structure
questions.text:
Country X faces a balance of payments deficit in 2015.
(a)	Explain whether this means Country X's accounting balance of payments is in deficit.	(2 marks)
(b)	How will the official reserves of Country X change? Explain.	(2 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	No,	(1 mark)
	the accounting balance of payments must be balanced.	(1 mark)
(b)	The central bank will sell an equivalent amount of foreign currency to the foreign exchange market to cover the deficit. Hence, the official reserves will decrease.
	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch613 · Market and market structure
questions.text:
Study the following table which shows the balance of payments (BoP) position of an economy.

questions.topic: B6 · Ch613 · Market and market structure
questions.text:
Explain whether the following statements are NECESSARILY true.
(a)	A country will have a current account deficit when it has a capital and financial account surplus.	(2 marks)
(b)	A country has a current account surplus when its net exports are positive.
	(2 marks)
questions.answerText:
(a)	Yes. In the accounting balance of payments, the sum of the current account balance and the capital and financial account balance must be zero. Hence, when one is in surplus, the other must be in deficit.	(2 marks)
(b)	Not necessarily true. If the sum of net factor income from abroad and net current transfers is negative and its absolute value is greater than net exports, the current account balance will become negative.
	Current account balance = Net exports + Net factor income from abroad + Net current transfers	(2 marks)

questions.topic: B6 · Ch613 · Market and market structure
questions.text:
* Peter: If there is a balance of payments deficit, the current account must be in deficit.
Pan: No. A balance of payments must be balanced. The current account will be in deficit only if the capital and financial account is in surplus.
Explain whether Peter and Pan are correct.	(8 marks)
questions.answerText:
Peter's statement is incorrect.
•	The market balance of payments is composed of the current account balance and the net change in capital and financial non-reserve assets.	(1 mark)
•	The current account can be in surplus even if there is a balance of payments deficit.	(1 mark)
•	This happens when the decrease in capital and financial non-reserve assets is larger than the amount of the surplus in the current account.	(1 mark)
Comment on Pan's statements:
•	The first statement is correct if the balance of payments refers to the accounting balance of payments.	(1 mark)
•	The second statement is correct.	(1 mark)
•	By definition,
Accounting BoP =  + 	(1 mark)
•	As the accounting BoP must be equal to zero,
Current account balance = - Capital and financial account balance	(1 mark)
•	This implies that the current account must be in deficit (surplus) when the capital and financial account is in surplus (deficit).	(1 mark)
